title: LLM Foundations
description: Foundation models, language modeling and the complete LLM lifecycle.

lessons.title: Foundation models, LLMs & generative AI
lessons.subtitle: Define the boundaries of each term, then connect pretraining to real deployment decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. A pretrained model can write text and classify reviews. Which labels—foundation model, LLM, generative model—apply, and why?
  2. Does every foundation model use a Transformer? Does every LLM generate useful text?
  3. Why does a single broadly pretrained model support tasks absent as explicit labels in its training set?
  4. What changes when you replace a task-specific classifier with a prompt-driven foundation model?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Three overlapping, nonidentical ideas. A foundation model is broadly pretrained and adaptable across downstream tasks; its modality may be text, image, audio, or combinations. An LLM models sequences of linguistic tokens (frequently code and other serialized data as well). Generative AI describes systems that produce new content by learning a distribution or a conditional mapping; it includes image diffusion and audio generation. Many decoder-only LLMs belong to all three groups, but a contrastively trained vision-language foundation model may not be a text generator.

Pretraining: θ* = argminθ 𝔼x∼D[ℒ(x; θ)] → reusable representation and/or conditional distribution

Pretraining usually optimizes a proxy objective, not a direct “truth” objective. That distinction explains why fluent generation, calibrated confidence, verifiable factuality, and tool-use safety require separate work. Pretraining does not install a database of guaranteed correct statements; knowledge is distributed imperfectly across learned parameters.

Traditional task-specific ML

Collect task-labeled examples → engineer or learn features → train model → fixed output contract. Easy to constrain, but new tasks often need new training.

Foundation-model engineering

Select pretrained model → define task with prompts/context/tools → evaluate → optionally adapt weights → deploy with guardrails and monitoring. Faster task reuse, new failure surface.

Changing the interface from per-task weights to natural-language instructions is profound, but the resulting model is stochastic and may follow unwanted instructions from retrieved or user-controlled text. Production systems therefore separate model capability, grounding, authorization, and evaluation.

sections.heading: Interview-ready spoken answer
sections.html: A foundation model is a broadly pretrained reusable model; an LLM is a language-centered instance, and generative AI is the broader class of content-creating systems. Broad pretraining transfers representations across tasks, so engineering shifts from fitting a model per task toward context design, adaptation, retrieval, evaluation, and controlled deployment. Reuse is powerful, but factuality and security are not guaranteed by pretraining.

sections.html:
1. A vision encoder produces vectors. Is it a foundation model even if it never generates a sentence? Explain adaptation.

sections.heading: Production scenario
sections.html:
Scenario: A company wants support classification, summarization, and reply drafting. A team suggests one large LLM for every request.

Plan: Define per-task correctness and failure cost; measure simple baselines (rules or small classifiers), LLM quality, p95 latency, data-handling risk, and per-request cost on the same held-out set. Route deterministic classification to a cheaper verified path if it meets targets, while drafting can use a generative model with retrieval and review.

Acceptance: Maintain an explicit gold set by workflow; compare task-specific error rates and cost at matched quality, report confidence intervals, and test refusal, PII, and prompt-injection cases before traffic rollout. Do not invent “one-model” savings without a measured baseline.

sections.html:
• Foundation ≠ language ≠ generative; know the overlaps.
  • A training objective is a proxy, not a factuality guarantee.
  • Evaluate tasks separately even when a common model serves all of them.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Describe how the development lifecycle differs between a 2018 custom NLP classifier and a modern LLM feature.
  2. Where do prompts end and software-enforced policy begin?
  3. When does fine-tuning beat retrieval or deterministic software?
  4. How do you establish return on model complexity rather than rely on vendor benchmark claims?
sections.text: Describe how the development lifecycle differs between a 2018 custom NLP classifier and a modern LLM feature. Where do prompts end and software-enforced policy begin? When does fine-tuning beat retrieval or deterministic software? How do you establish return on model complexity rather than rely on vendor benchmark claims?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
The major shift is separation of learned general capability from application-specific state. Pretraining is an expensive upstream activity; application teams compose a pretrained model with retrieval, business logic, APIs, schemas, auth, and evaluators downstream. This is an engineering abstraction, not a claim that no custom training is needed.

  1. Specify the task: Inputs, output schema, who can invoke it, cost of false positives/negatives, failure policy.
  2. Establish baselines: Rules, search, small models, hosted LLM, and human workflow where relevant.
  3. Supply missing knowledge: Retrieval for mutable facts; tools for live or exact calculations; fine-tuning for recurring behavior/style/domain patterns.
  4. Build a harness: Validation, permission checks, rate limiting, retries, caching, deterministic operations, logging, and human approval for irreversible actions.
  5. Evaluate and roll out: Golden tests, adversarial and multilingual slices, calibration where meaningful, shadow testing, canaries, rollback.

Why this design works: A language model is good at interpreting ambiguous instructions and synthesizing text, while conventional software is superior at enforcing invariants, transactions, and permissions. A good architecture allocates responsibility accordingly.

NeedFirst-choice mechanismTypical failure
Fresh private factsRetrieval plus permissionsStale or unauthorized context
Stable response formatSchema-constrained decoding + validatorSemantically wrong valid JSON
Exact arithmeticVerified tool / deterministic codeBad tool arguments
Consistent specialized behaviorPrompt baseline then fine-tune if supported by evalsOverfit and forgetting

sections.heading: Interview-ready spoken answer
sections.html: Foundation models turn many ML applications into systems engineering problems: we reuse learned capabilities and invest in grounding, reliable APIs, data contracts, evaluation, and safety boundaries. I use the simplest baseline that meets the requirement, then add RAG, fine-tuning, or agents only if evaluation identifies a measurable gap.

sections.heading: Production scenario
sections.html:
Scenario: A support assistant answers with outdated prices and occasionally reveals another tenant’s policy.

Diagnose: Split answer accuracy into retrieval currency, retrieval authorization, grounding, and model generation. Trace document IDs, version timestamps, effective user identity, and source attribution per response.

Fix: Enforce tenant/ACL filters at retrieval and again at data access; add version-aware indexing and cited responses. Do not rely on “do not reveal private data” prompt text as the authorization boundary.

Validate: Cross-tenant access tests must return zero unauthorized documents; measure freshness delay and answer faithfulness on a timestamped golden dataset. Roll out with a kill switch.

  • Prompt instructions are not security boundaries.
  • Choose RAG for mutable knowledge, tools for exact state, fine-tuning for repeated behavior.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. What exactly is updated during next-token pretraining?
  2. If an LLM is trained on a billion sentences, does it retrieve the nearest sentence at runtime?
  3. Why can cross-entropy improve while factuality on a specialized task remains poor?
  4. Where does sampling enter relative to the Transformer forward pass?
sections.text: What exactly is updated during next-token pretraining? If an LLM is trained on a billion sentences, does it retrieve the nearest sentence at runtime? Why can cross-entropy improve while factuality on a specialized task remains poor? Where does sampling enter relative to the Transformer forward pass?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Training path. (1) Text is tokenized into integer IDs; (2) chunks are arranged as training sequences; (3) embeddings, positional information, attention, and MLP layers compute hidden states; (4) a language-model head produces a logit for each vocabulary token at each position; (5) the target is the actual next token in the data; (6) cross-entropy measures prediction error; (7) backpropagation computes gradients and an optimizer updates parameters. The same weights are shared across positions, and attention provides contextual interactions.

L(θ) = −(1/N) Σt=1…N log pθ(xt | x<t)

For the true token y, cross-entropy equals −log p(y); a probability of 0.8 yields about 0.223 nats, while 0.1 yields about 2.303 nats. Gradients push the distribution toward observed continuation tokens, not toward an external truth oracle. Sequence correlations let the network internalize syntax, code patterns, statistical facts, and some procedures.

Inference path. Freeze weights; tokenize prompt; run the model to get logits for the next token; transform logits into a probability distribution; select a token via greedy or stochastic decoding; append token; repeat until a stopping condition. Serving frameworks usually cache earlier K/V projections so later steps do not recompute the entire prefix. The cache stores contextual intermediate activations, not a second copy of model weights.

Important trap: Next-token training does not mean the model literally predicts whole words, stores its entire dataset verbatim, or searches the internet automatically. Text generation is conditionally autoregressive; the deployment may add external retrieval or tools.

sections.heading: Interview-ready spoken answer
sections.html: An LLM is trained to assign high probability to the next token conditioned on earlier tokens. It runs the training sequence through a Transformer, computes vocabulary logits, applies cross-entropy against observed next tokens, and updates weights through backpropagation. At inference the weights stay fixed; the system selects one token from the predicted distribution, appends it, and repeats. Fluent prediction is not itself a correctness guarantee.

A strong response should justify the mechanism, name limits, offer alternatives, and explain how to measure a claim.

sections.heading: Production scenario
sections.html:
Scenario: A domain assistant speaks fluently but produces unsupported contract clauses.

Hypotheses: Missing evidence, misleading retrieved passages, sampling variance, or model prior overriding context. Instrument document coverage, cited spans, model/prompt version, decoding parameters, and claim-to-source entailment. Test retrieval oracle passages to isolate retrieval versus generation.

Options: Tighten retrieval, enforce evidence-linked claims and abstention, evaluate a specialized model, or require human review. Do not assume lower temperature makes fabricated claims true.

Acceptance: On a held-out set with unanswerable cases, report factual-support rate, false-answer rate, and abstention recall; compare against pre-change baselines.

lessons.title: Autoregressive models & next-token prediction
lessons.subtitle: Master conditional factorization, teacher forcing, decoding dependence, and latency consequences.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Write the probability of a sequence as a product of conditional probabilities.
  2. What is teacher forcing, and why can training run token positions in parallel while inference is sequential?
  3. Does causal attention mean input tokens are processed serially during prefill?
  4. Where does exposure bias arise and when does it matter?
sections.text: Write the probability of a sequence as a product of conditional probabilities. What is teacher forcing, and why can training run token positions in parallel while inference is sequential? Does causal attention mean input tokens are processed serially during prefill? Where does exposure bias arise and when does it matter?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
An autoregressive (AR) model factorizes a joint sequence distribution using the chain rule. For tokens x₁...xₜ, it uses the left prefix to predict each next token, normally with a causal mask preventing positions from reading future tokens.

p(x₁, …, xₜ) = ∏t=1…T p(xt | x1, …, xt−1)

Teacher forcing: During training, feed the entire ground-truth sequence, shifted by one target position. Although each position is only allowed to depend on its prefix, causal attention allows the GPU to evaluate predictions for many token positions in a single parallel forward pass. During generation, the next token is unknown, so it must be generated before the following token can be conditioned on it. This creates a serial dependency even when an individual step is GPU-parallel.

Cost: For full dense attention, attention score work during prefill has O(T²·d) flavor, while single-token decode attends across its current cached context, O(T·d) attention work per step (details depend on head shape). Long generation also carries a KV-cache memory burden approximately proportional to layers × context × KV-heads × head-dim × bytes. This distinction matters when sizing throughput.

Failure: Training mostly sees real prefixes, while decoding consumes its own sampled outputs; distribution shift can amplify early mistakes. A hallucinated premise in one step can influence later steps. Mitigations depend on task: constrained decoding, external verification, robust training, and evidence-grounding.

sections.heading: Interview-ready spoken answer
sections.html: Autoregressive models factor sequence probability into next-token conditionals. During training, teacher forcing supplies the correct prefix so causal Transformer positions can be evaluated in parallel. During inference each newly sampled token becomes part of the prefix, so output steps are sequential; a KV cache avoids unnecessary recomputation of earlier attention states.

sections.heading: Production scenario
sections.html:
Scenario: Interactive code completion misses the latency target even though GPU utilization appears moderate.

Instrument: Separate time to first token, queue delay, prefill time, tokens/s in decode, generation length, and KV-cache usage. A 2,000-token answer may simply be dominated by serial output generation.

Fix options: Cap unnecessary output length, use an adequately sized faster model, dynamic batching, appropriate speculative decoding, or workload-specific prefix reuse. Validate task completion at matched output budgets: aggressively shortening output can reduce utility.

Acceptance: Report p50/p95 TTFT and per-token latency, task success, throughput, and cost per completed task under a documented concurrency distribution.

lessons.title: Autoregressive vs. masked language modeling
lessons.subtitle: Contrast objectives, context visibility, output behavior, and suitable tasks.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why can BERT inspect both left and right context but a causal next-token decoder cannot?
  2. Could a masked encoder generate a paragraph just by sampling next tokens? What would be missing?
  3. Explain masked token prediction mathematically and its training/inference mismatch.
  4. Which objective would you choose for intent classification versus free-form answer generation?
sections.text: Why can BERT inspect both left and right context but a causal next-token decoder cannot? Could a masked encoder generate a paragraph just by sampling next tokens? What would be missing? Explain masked token prediction mathematically and its training/inference mismatch. Which objective would you choose for intent classification versus free-form answer generation?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Autoregressive objective: predict the next token using only earlier tokens, maximizing p(xₜ | x₍<t₎). Attention masking enforces causality. This naturally supports left-to-right open-ended decoding and streaming.

Masked language modeling (MLM): corrupt selected positions with a mask or replacement, then predict the original token from both left and right observed context, as in BERT-style encoder pretraining. A common illustrative loss is:

LMLM = −Σi∈M log pθ(xi | corrupted(x), i)

The MLM loss covers masked positions M; it is not generally a normalized joint probability of all tokens, and filling multiple masks independently may miss dependencies between them. Importantly, SentencePiece is tokenization, not a modeling objective; do not confuse the input encoder with a language-model training task.

DimensionAutoregressive decoderMasked encoder
VisibilityLeft prefix via causal attentionLeft and right observed tokens
Primary targetNext token at each positionReconstruct selected masked tokens
Natural fitFree-form generation, code completionClassification, token tagging, contextual encoding
Inference limitationSerial generation stepsNo native left-to-right generator head/objective

Encoder-decoder denoising models, such as T5-style systems, can instead combine rich input understanding with autoregressive output generation. Bidirectional attention does not automatically mean better quality for every task: it changes what information is visible and what objective the model learned.

sections.heading: Interview-ready spoken answer
sections.html: Autoregressive modeling learns the distribution of the next token from earlier tokens and aligns directly with streaming generation. Masked language modeling hides selected tokens and uses both surrounding sides to reconstruct them, which is useful for contextual representations and understanding tasks. A BERT-style masked encoder is not automatically a general-purpose paragraph generator; architecture and training objective must align with the desired output.

sections.heading: Follow-up pressure test
sections.html:
1. Can you compute a joint sequence likelihood from independent MLM predictions in the same way as AR factorization?
  2. Why doesn't bidirectional attention inherently leak future tokens for a classification task?
  3. What architectural change lets an encoder represent source text while another network produces a sequence?

lessons.title: Encoder-only, decoder-only & encoder-decoder Transformers
lessons.subtitle: Choose architecture from data flow, attention masks, and output characteristics—not model branding.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Draw data flow and attention patterns for all three Transformer families.
  2. What exactly is cross-attention in an encoder-decoder model?
  3. Why can encoder-decoder translation outperform a naive decoder-only setup on some constraints?
  4. When do you need contextual embeddings instead of generation?
sections.text: Draw data flow and attention patterns for all three Transformer families. What exactly is cross-attention in an encoder-decoder model? Why can encoder-decoder translation outperform a naive decoder-only setup on some constraints? When do you need contextual embeddings instead of generation?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Encoder-only: Source tokens attend bidirectionally to other source tokens (subject to padding and other task masks). Layers build contextual representations. Classification often pools a designated output or uses sequence representations; token tagging uses per-token states. Typical examples include BERT-style encoders.

Decoder-only: A single causal stack maps prompt plus generated prefix to next-token logits. The prompt and output occupy one token stream. This unification simplifies prompting, in-context learning, chat, and streaming, but output tokens are produced sequentially and must be constrained for strict formats.

Encoder-decoder: An encoder processes the source; a causal decoder attends to its own earlier target tokens and attends across the entire encoded source via cross-attention: Q comes from decoder states, while K,V come from encoder states. This is naturally suited to source-conditioned transformations such as translation and summarization, including objectives trained for those workflows.

Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵀ / √dk + mask) V

Practical design questions include input-output asymmetry, sequence lengths, deployment ecosystem, and evaluation. Decoder-only models can also excel at translation or classification; the architecture is a strong inductive bias, not an absolute capability boundary.

Complexity nuance: A self-attention layer over length n typically constructs O(n²) token-pair scores in the straightforward implementation; FlashAttention reduces memory traffic and avoids materializing the full scores, but does not generally make dense exact attention asymptotically linear in arithmetic cost.

I choose based on the output contract, latency, task training, and measured quality—not a rigid architecture slogan.

lessons.title: RNNs vs. Transformers
lessons.subtitle: Reason from computation graphs to scaling, memory, and long-range dependency behavior.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why can a Transformer process training positions in parallel but a vanilla RNN cannot?
  2. Is attention always cheaper than recurrence for long sequences?
  3. What does the longest sequential dependency path imply for optimization?
  4. Which architecture might win for tiny streaming devices or extremely long sequences?
sections.text: Why can a Transformer process training positions in parallel but a vanilla RNN cannot? Is attention always cheaper than recurrence for long sequences? What does the longest sequential dependency path imply for optimization? Which architecture might win for tiny streaming devices or extremely long sequences?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
RNN computation: an RNN updates a hidden state in sequence: hₜ = f(Wₕhₜ₋₁ + Wₓxₜ). This creates a length-T sequential path through time, inhibiting training parallelism across positions. Vanishing/exploding gradients complicate long-range dependencies; gated LSTM/GRU variants improve stability but retain recurrence.

Transformer computation: self-attention allows position i to interact directly with another accessible position j in a layer. During training all positions can be projected and processed in large matrix operations. Causal masks preserve valid autoregressive information flow without requiring an RNN-style sequential hidden-state update during prefill.

PropertyRNN / gated recurrenceDense self-attention Transformer
Across-position trainingSequential recurrent dependencyHighly parallel within a layer
Long-range interactionThrough hidden-state chainDirect token-pair interaction
Long-context computeOften O(T·d²) recurrent computeO(T²·d + T·d²) typical per layer
Working state at inferenceFixed-size hidden state for a standard RNNGrowing KV cache for causal attention

These complexities are simplified: embedding size, head dimensions, layers, variants, kernel efficiency, and hardware control practical crossover points. New state-space or hybrid architectures change the comparison. It is incorrect to say Transformers always beat every recurrent approach at any context length.

sections.html: An RNN compresses its history into a recurrent hidden state, which creates a serial dependency across time. A Transformer uses attention to let each position directly mix information from other permitted positions, so training can parallelize across the sequence and optimize long-range interactions more effectively. The trade-off is quadratic dense attention computation and growing KV state; recurrence or hybrid methods may win in tight-memory or streaming settings.

A strong response should justify the mechanism, name limits, offer alternatives, and explain how to measure a claim.

sections.heading: Production scenario
sections.html:
Scenario: A wearable needs streaming anomaly detection on long sensor traces with strict memory limits.

Plan: Benchmark a gated RNN, lightweight attention, and possibly a modern state-space model on the same event-labeled stream. Measure detection recall, delay to detect, battery/energy, on-device peak memory, and robustness under sensor dropout.

Choice: If far-back exact interactions matter, attention may help; if constant-memory streaming is paramount, recurrence may dominate. Validate against the real device, not only desktop GPU speed.

  • Attention has direct interactions but costly long-context scaling.
  • Hardware and task shape, not fashion, determine the winner.

lessons.title: Inside ChatGPT: request-to-response lifecycle
lessons.subtitle: Separate what is general to LLM-backed chat systems from product-specific internals that are not public.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Trace a chat request from client input through token generation and streaming UI.
  2. Which components are inside the model, and which belong to the serving application?
  3. Where might tools or retrieval enter without changing the base model weights?
  4. Explain TTFT, KV reuse, stop conditions, and failure handling in one coherent flow.
sections.text: Trace a chat request from client input through token generation and streaming UI. Which components are inside the model, and which belong to the serving application? Where might tools or retrieval enter without changing the base model weights? Explain TTFT, KV reuse, stop conditions, and failure handling in one coherent flow.

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Reference architecture, not a claim about ChatGPT’s private implementation. (1) Client submits text and conversation context; (2) server authenticates, authorizes, and applies rate limits; (3) an orchestrator forms model messages and may select a model; (4) a tokenizer converts serialized context into token IDs; (5) prompt processing (prefill) builds hidden states and usually KV cache; (6) final prompt position yields next-token logits; (7) decoding samples/selects output tokens iteratively; (8) the application may invoke tools and re-enter generation; (9) output is streamed, validated/filtered where configured, persisted, and rendered.

TTFT ≈ queue + input handling + prefill + first decode + network/stream overhead

API providers may implement tool calls as a structured output event followed by a server-side tool execution and a subsequent model turn. A model has no inherent permission to browse a user's filesystem, call a database, or guarantee a transaction; the surrounding application grants and enforces those capabilities.

Failure boundaries include truncation, context overflow, malformed tool arguments, authorization errors, timeouts, partial stream disconnects, retries that duplicate side effects, and stop condition bugs. Production handling should use request IDs, bounded deadlines, idempotency keys for writes, and clear error statuses.

What we cannot infer: The exact ChatGPT model routing, internal prompts, kernel scheduling, caching, or proprietary safety implementation for any specific request. These vary and are not fully observable from the client. Explain the standard architecture without presenting product-specific speculation as fact.

The service streams tokens and may orchestrate retrieval or tool calls between model turns. The application—not the model weights—handles permissions, persistence, deadlines, and tool side effects. I would distinguish this standard design from proprietary implementation details I cannot verify.

  2. If the network disconnects after a payment tool call, how do you prevent duplicate charges?
  3. Does enabling streaming reduce total compute or only perceived responsiveness?

A strong response should justify the mechanism, name limits, offer alternatives, and explain how to measure a claim.

sections.heading: Production scenario
sections.html:
Scenario: Users see responses stop after a tool invocation; some retries duplicate actions.

Diagnose: Trace client request ID → orchestration turn → tool call ID → tool outcome → resume step; record disconnects, deadlines, and whether tool calls were acknowledged. Separate interrupted streams from model completion failures.

Fix: Persist workflow state; add idempotency keys and a deduplication ledger for side effects; handle reconnects with safe resume and clear UX. Retrying a full conversation blindly is unsafe for write operations.

Acceptance: Exactly-once business effect under replay tests (achieved through idempotent processing), no unauthorized tool calls, and monitored completion rate and p95 end-to-end latency.

  • TTFT includes queueing and network as well as inference.
  • Never assert private ChatGPT internals as verified facts.

lessons.title: Open-source, open-weight & closed-source deployment trade-offs
lessons.subtitle: Reason about licenses, risk, TCO, customization, and hosting reality.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why is downloadable model weight access not synonymous with open-source?
  2. How do you calculate when self-hosting beats pay-per-token APIs?
  3. Which privacy claims require contractual and operational verification?
  4. What does a migration plan look like if a model provider or license changes?
sections.text: Why is downloadable model weight access not synonymous with open-source? How do you calculate when self-hosting beats pay-per-token APIs? Which privacy claims require contractual and operational verification? What does a migration plan look like if a model provider or license changes?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Terminology: An open-source model has a license and accompanying accessible materials that satisfy relevant open-source criteria; in AI, the scope may include code, weights, and training details, and definitions differ. An open-weight model provides downloadable parameters, but may restrict commercial use, redistribute restrictions, or omit training data/code. A closed model typically gives hosted API access without weights. Treat each license and provider policy as its own contract.

Decision axisHosted proprietary APISelf-hosted open-weight
Upfront operationsLow; provider manages servingGPU, deployment, observability, security
Unit economicsUsage-based and predictable at low volumeCan improve at sustained utilization; idle capacity costs
Model controlLimited to exposed API settingsMore control over weights, quantization, tuning
Data boundariesProvider contract, geography, retention policiesControl of own infrastructure, shared responsibility
Failure modesRate limits, API outages, upstream changesGPU failure, OOM, patching, capacity issues
Illustrative monthly TCO ≈ GPU hours × $/GPU-hour + ops + storage + network + observability

Compare that against API input/output-token charges on your actual request lengths and cache hit rates. Benchmark under peak concurrency and at matched quality; price per token alone obscures batch throughput and idle GPU hours. Regulatory or privacy suitability requires legal/security review, not a marketing label.

APIs reduce time to market and capacity burden; self-hosting increases control but introduces GPU utilization and reliability risks. I use workload-specific TCO and rollback plans instead of assuming either is always cheaper or safer.

Scenario: An enterprise wants to move confidential summarization from a hosted provider to local inference.

Plan: Inventory data sensitivity, retention requirements, licenses, eval suite, prompt lengths, and traffic. Evaluate a shortlist of open-weight models with quantization variants on identical test documents.

Risks: Quantization-induced quality loss, underutilized GPUs, missing hardware redundancy, model provenance, logging leaks. Introduce traffic shadowing and a reversible switch.

Acceptance: Meet agreed factuality and throughput thresholds, prove data-flow restrictions via audit and network tests, and show 30-day modeled TCO with sensitivity to utilization.

lessons.title: SLMs, LLMs & Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)
lessons.subtitle: Compare parameter scale, inference-time computation, latency, and practical model routing.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Is an LRM always larger in parameter count than a non-reasoning LLM?
  2. How can inference-time compute improve complex task performance without retraining?
  3. When should an SLM outperform a stronger LLM on product utility?
  4. What would you evaluate before turning on a longer reasoning budget?
sections.text: Is an LRM always larger in parameter count than a non-reasoning LLM? How can inference-time compute improve complex task performance without retraining? When should an SLM outperform a stronger LLM on product utility? What would you evaluate before turning on a longer reasoning budget?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
SLM: A small language model is usually chosen for lower memory footprint, faster/local inference, predictable cost, or a narrow specialty. There is no universal parameter-count cutoff. LLM: A broad term for higher-capacity language models, also without a fixed public numerical boundary. LRM: Usually refers to language models designed or optimized for more capable multi-step reasoning, often through specialized training and/or inference-time computation; an LRM need not be the largest model by parameter count.

Inference-time compute: Hard questions can benefit from generating intermediate reasoning tokens, searching over candidate solutions, using verifiers, or invoking tools. This spends extra compute at inference rather than relying only on a single immediate answer. Gains are task-dependent; longer reasoning can also introduce errors, excessive latency, and cost. It does not guarantee truth or faithful explanations of internal computations.

Expected task utility = quality benefit − λ·latency − μ·cost − ν·risk (illustrative objective)

Routing: Use a deterministic fast path for trivial extraction, a smaller validated model for bounded tasks, and a stronger reasoning-capable model for harder multi-step inputs. A classifier for complexity is itself imperfect: route conservatively when mistakes are expensive and keep a fallback or escalation path.

Request shapeCandidate pathWhat to measure
Tag a short support ticketRule / compact encoder / SLMF1, latency, price
Draft a nuanced policy explanationGeneral-purpose LLM + retrievalFaithfulness, review time
Solve multi-step symbolic reasoningReasoning-capable LLM + verifierVerified success, budget, tail latency

Model names and labels change faster than these design principles. Do not assume “reasoning” is a guaranteed separate architecture; often the underlying model remains Transformer-based autoregressive generation, augmented by training and inference-time strategy.

title: Tokenization & Embeddings
description: Tokens, subword algorithms, vector representations, and positional encoding.

lessons.title: Tokenization: why language becomes IDs
lessons.subtitle: Trace text → tokenizer → discrete token IDs → embedding lookup, and identify the information the interface can lose.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. An LLM consumes integers rather than strings. What converts the bytes in a request into model input?
  2. Does one token equal one word, character, or Unicode code point?
  3. Why can two visually identical strings tokenize differently?
  4. Which invariants must hold between a model and its tokenizer?
sections.text: An LLM consumes integers rather than strings. What converts the bytes in a request into model input? Does one token equal one word, character, or Unicode code point? Why can two visually identical strings tokenize differently? Which invariants must hold between a model and its tokenizer?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Core mechanism. Neural layers operate on numerical arrays. A tokenizer defines a finite vocabulary V and an encoding procedure that maps input strings (possibly after normalization and pre-tokenization) to integer token IDs t₁,…,tₙ. A vocabulary entry may represent a full word, subword, whitespace-containing substring, punctuation, one byte, or special control token. IDs are identifiers, not meaningful scalar measurements.

encode: text → (t₁,…,tₙ), tᵢ ∈ {0,…,|V|−1}; X = E[t] ∈ ℝⁿˣᵈ
  1. Normalize if configured: Unicode normalization/case folding may change characters; exact behavior depends on tokenizer. Avoid assuming normalization happens.
  2. Pre-tokenize if configured: split or mark boundaries around words, digits, punctuation, and whitespace. Regex rules differ across families.
  3. Subword segmentation: apply learned merge rules (BPE), vocabulary scoring (WordPiece or unigram), or another method.
  4. Map to IDs and insert special tokens: apply BOS/EOS, chat role delimiters, padding, or multimodal markers according to the template and model.
  5. Lookup embeddings: retrieve learned vectors for each ID, then supply position information and Transformer layers.

Round-trip nuance. Byte-complete encodings can reconstruct original UTF-8 bytes for ordinary text when no lossy normalization or cleanup intervenes. Unknown-token replacement or Unicode normalization may destroy exact reversibility. Decoding from tokens need not perfectly recreate the input across all tokenizers.

Operational implications. Context limits, API bills, KV-cache allocation, and attention work depend on token counts, not character counts. The model must use its exact trained vocabulary, merge ordering, special-token IDs, and chat template. A tokenizer mismatch can produce valid-looking IDs that mean different strings to the model, damaging quality without crashing.

Compute surface

Embedding lookup costs O(n·d) reads; standard full attention has O(n²·d) attention arithmetic (ignoring implementation-specific kernels), so token inflation can be disproportionately expensive.

Failure surface

Normalization mismatches, accidental addition of role tokens, surrogate handling, and OOV policy cause prompt-length variance or semantic corruption.

The segmentation affects context length, cost, and sometimes correctness; tokenizer versions, special-token conventions, and input templates must stay aligned with the model.

lessons.title: Byte Pair Encoding: training, merges & encoding
lessons.subtitle: Derive greedy frequency merges, apply their learned rank ordering to unseen strings, and examine byte-level variants.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Walk me through training one round of BPE using pair counts.
  2. Why does greedy BPE not always produce globally minimal token count?
  3. What is the difference between character BPE and byte-level BPE?
  4. What happens to unknown vocabulary terms under byte-level BPE?
sections.text: Walk me through training one round of BPE using pair counts. Why does greedy BPE not always produce globally minimal token count? What is the difference between character BPE and byte-level BPE? What happens to unknown vocabulary terms under byte-level BPE?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Training. Begin with a base alphabet of symbols: in a word-based teaching example, characters plus an end-of-word boundary; in GPT-style byte-level systems, potentially the 256 raw byte values combined with specific pre-tokenization rules. Count adjacent pairs inside the units permitted by preprocessing, choose the most frequent pair, introduce a new symbol for the concatenation, replace nonoverlapping occurrences, and record that merge. Repeat until a vocabulary or merge budget is reached.

pair* = argmax₍a,b₎ Σs∈corpus count((a,b) adjacent in s)

Toy example: low low lower contains repeated l·o, o·w, and l·o·w patterns. After merging l+o→lo, we recount pairs, perhaps then merge lo+w→low. Exact tie results depend on the specified tie-breaking rule; the lab makes that rule deterministic and visible.

Inference. The encoder starts from the tokenizer's initial symbols, then performs only learned merges, respecting their rank/order and preprocessing. Some implementations choose the currently highest-priority adjacent merge iteratively; optimized tokenizers use heaps or rank-based algorithms. Do not relearn frequencies from a user's prompt at inference time. Greedy highest-frequency training is not the same as finding the globally shortest segmentation for arbitrary future text.

Illustrative training cost: O(M·N) for naïve rescan of N symbols over M merges; optimized counts update locally.

Byte-level benefits and limits: A full set of 256 initial byte tokens allows encoding arbitrary UTF-8 sequences without an [UNK] token. It does not imply efficient segmentation: rare multi-byte characters may require many tokens. Spaces, newlines, regex boundaries, and special-token treatment remain model-specific. Raw byte BPE, byte-to-Unicode remapping, and SentencePiece byte fallback are distinct engineering choices.

Implementation traps: pair counts must be weighted by word occurrence frequency when training on compressed word-count corpora; overlapping pairs cannot be merged twice in one pass; merge ranks are reproducibility-critical; Unicode code points and UTF-8 bytes are different alphabets; and adding merges usually changes IDs or segmentation unless vocabulary mapping is coordinated.

Illustrative pseudocode
symbols = initialize_symbols(corpus)
merges = []
repeat M times:
    pair = most_frequent_adjacent_pair(symbols)
    if pair does not exist: break
    symbols = replace_nonoverlapping(symbols, pair)
    merges.append(pair)  # ordered ranks

encode(text):
    tokens = initialize_symbols(text)
    for pair in merges:
        tokens = replace_nonoverlapping(tokens, pair)
    return token_ids(tokens)

At inference we apply the learned merges to new text; we never compute a fresh corpus vocabulary per user request. Byte-level BPE can represent any UTF-8 string, but rare scripts and emojis may still expand into many tokens, affecting latency and context budgets.

sections.heading: Production scenario
sections.html:
Incident: A tokenizer retrain using new domain records unexpectedly changes thousands of production prompts.

Diagnosis: Compare old/new merge tables, vocab IDs, token counts and semantic task outcomes on a fixed evaluation suite, segmented by language and prompt template. Determine whether the model's input/output embedding matrices were resized and adapted.

Mitigation: Treat tokenizer+weights+template as one deployable artifact; train/adapt embeddings for new IDs and assess regressions. Avoid swapping tokenizers into frozen models as a drop-in performance fix.

Acceptance: Versioned fixtures reproduce exact IDs; task quality is non-inferior on agreed slices; token-efficiency improvement is reported with confidence intervals and no hidden regression in rare-language subsets.

lessons.title: WordPiece, SentencePiece & byte-level strategies
lessons.subtitle: Distinguish the segmentation algorithm from the tokenizer framework and from its base alphabet.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Is SentencePiece a competitor algorithm to BPE?
  2. How does WordPiece choose subwords at encoding time?
  3. Why do WordPiece vocabularies often include ##-prefixed continuation tokens?
  4. What is the practical difference between an unknown-token system and byte fallback?
sections.text: Is SentencePiece a competitor algorithm to BPE? How does WordPiece choose subwords at encoding time? Why do WordPiece vocabularies often include ##-prefixed continuation tokens? What is the practical difference between an unknown-token system and byte fallback?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Three different axes are often conflated: (1) vocabulary-learning algorithm (BPE, WordPiece, unigram language model), (2) input units (bytes, Unicode characters, normalized text), and (3) tokenizer implementation/framework (e.g., SentencePiece). SentencePiece can train unigram or BPE segmenters directly from raw sentences with whitespace represented explicitly, often as ▁; it is not a single alternative algorithm.

ApproachTraining intuitionTypical encoding ruleImportant edge
BPEMerge frequent neighboring symbolsApply stored merge ranksDepends on base symbols and pre-tokenizer
WordPieceSelect subword vocab by probabilistic/likelihood-inspired criterion; details vary across implementationsGreedy longest-match-first within a word in standard BERT-style implementationsUncovered word may collapse to [UNK]
SentencePiece unigramFit pruned probabilistic vocabularyFind likely segmentation via dynamic programming/Viterbi, possibly samplingNormalization and fallback configuration matter
Byte-level BPEBPE over byte-derived initial symbolsRanked byte-level mergesArbitrary bytes encodable; long sequences still possible

WordPiece example (illustrative vocabulary): Suppose play, ##ing, and ##er exist; playing can be play + ##ing. ## denotes continuation within the word, not literal input characters. If a word has no complete decomposition using valid pieces, BERT-like encoders may produce one [UNK] for the entire word, losing identity of individual characters. Some variants use other fallbacks, so verify the actual model.

SentencePiece example: The token ▁New can explicitly encode a word boundary. Its normalization pipeline can make Unicode behavior different from a GPT-style regex pre-tokenizer. Unigram segmentation selects the most probable sequence of pieces, not necessarily the fewest tokens. Stochastic segmentations can be used for training augmentation when configured.

Unigram decoding: s* = argmax₍s∈Seg(x)₎ Σu∈s log P(u)

Selection: Evaluate compression, reversibility, multilingual coverage, stable templates, special-token safety, implementation latency, and alignment with the model's training data. A popular library's name alone says nothing about its fallback guarantees.

Scenario: A document indexing team observes that biological identifiers and names disappear from downstream QA.

Diagnose: Serialize the source text and compare tokenizer output for the exact identifiers. If a WordPiece encoder emits [UNK], information is lost before the Transformer ever sees it; if byte BPE creates many tokens, information remains but may be truncated later.

Remediate: Preserve original exact strings in lexical indexes and structured metadata; add appropriate domain-adapted encoders only after confirming compatible model training.

Validate: Exact-identifier recall, percent unknown tokens, token counts by domain slice, and downstream answer exact-match on held-out data.

lessons.title: Vocabulary size, efficiency & unknown handling
lessons.subtitle: Quantify compression and memory consequences without mistaking fewer tokens for better semantics.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why doesn't maximizing vocabulary size always reduce inference cost?
  2. How do you quantify token efficiency fairly across languages?
  3. How do you estimate added embedding memory when growing a vocabulary?
  4. What tests catch silent unknown-token information loss?
sections.text: Why doesn't maximizing vocabulary size always reduce inference cost? How do you quantify token efficiency fairly across languages? How do you estimate added embedding memory when growing a vocabulary? What tests catch silent unknown-token information loss?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Compression versus coverage. More vocabulary entries generally allow frequently occurring strings to be represented as larger pieces, reducing sequence length for the corpus they fit. But each new vocabulary row needs a learned vector, and often a corresponding output projection row. Rare-token embeddings may be poorly trained. Vocabulary growth can increase final vocabulary projection/softmax work, especially without specialized kernels or weight tying.

Input embedding parameters = |V|·d; memory (weights only) = |V|·d·bytesPerElement
Example: ΔV = 32,000, d = 4,096, bf16 → 32,000 × 4,096 × 2 = 262,144,000 bytes ≈ 250 MiB

If the output projection is untied, another comparable matrix may be needed. Training with Adam also allocates gradients and optimizer states. The above is only input embedding weights, not a full training memory estimate.

Metrics: tokens per document and per language; bytes/token on the same raw text set; tokens per semantic unit or reference text; unknown-token rate; p50/p95/p99 length inflation; truncation rate; and downstream task success. Interpret bytes/token cautiously: UTF-8 characters in different scripts naturally use different byte lengths. Comparing raw tokens per character without accounting for script and normalization may be misleading.

Very small vocabulary

Fewer parameters, robust reuse of fragments, but long sequences create more attention/KV-cache traffic.

Very large vocabulary

Potentially shorter sequences on familiar strings, but larger embedding/head costs and poorer statistics for rare token rows.

Unknown-token handling: closed character/subword alphabets may use [UNK]; full byte initial alphabets represent any UTF-8 byte sequence; byte fallback in character-based systems acts only if enabled and implemented. Unknown terms are not the same as unknown tokens: a model can process a novel word's bytes while lacking conceptual knowledge of it.

Latency trade-off: approximate full-attention arithmetic grows like O(n²·d), but flash-style implementations can change memory traffic without eliminating dense attention arithmetic. Decode KV-cache memory grows O(n·L·Hkv·dhead), so tokenizer inefficiency affects serving concurrency.
sections.text: Compression versus coverage. More vocabulary entries generally allow frequently occurring strings to be represented as larger pieces, reducing sequence length for the corpus they fit . But each new vocabulary row needs a learned vector, and often a corresponding output projection row. Rare-token embeddings may be poorly trained. Vocabulary growth can increase final vocabulary projection/softmax work, especially without specialized kernels or weight tying. Input embedding parameters = |V|·d; memory (weights only) = |V|·d·bytesPerElement Example: ΔV = 32,000, d = 4,096, bf16 → 32,000 × 4,096 × 2 = 262,144,000 bytes ≈ 250 MiB If the output projection is untied, another comparable matrix may be needed. Training with Adam also allocates gradients and optimizer states. The above is only input embedding weights , not a full training memory estimate. Metrics: tokens per document and per language; bytes/token on the same raw text set; tokens per semantic unit or reference text; unknown-token rate; p50/p95/p99 length inflation; truncation rate; and downstream task success. Interpret bytes/token cautiously: UTF-8 characters in different scripts naturally use different byte lengths. Comparing raw tokens per character without accounting for script and normalization may be misleading. Very large vocabulary Potentially shorter sequences on familiar strings, but larger embedding/head costs and poorer statistics for rare token rows. Unknown-token handling: closed character/subword alphabets may use [UNK] ; full byte initial alphabets represent any UTF-8 byte sequence; byte fallback in character-based systems acts only if enabled and implemented. Unknown terms are not the same as unknown tokens : a model can process a novel word's bytes while lacking conceptual knowledge of it. Latency trade-off: approximate full-attention arithmetic grows like O(n²·d), but flash-style implementations can change memory traffic without eliminating dense attention arithmetic. Decode KV-cache memory grows O(n·L·H kv ·d head ), so tokenizer inefficiency affects serving concurrency.

lessons.title: Token embeddings: IDs to trainable vectors
lessons.subtitle: Explain the embedding lookup, gradient updates, and why token vectors alone are not sentence meaning.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. What is the exact operation that maps token ID 17 to a vector?
  2. How are embedding rows learned during language-model training?
  3. Why do identical token IDs have the same initial embedding yet different contextual hidden states?
  4. How can a token embedding matrix serve as an output head?
sections.text: What is the exact operation that maps token ID 17 to a vector? How are embedding rows learned during language-model training? Why do identical token IDs have the same initial embedding yet different contextual hidden states? How can a token embedding matrix serve as an output head?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Embedding lookup is an indexed gather, not an external semantic search. With a vocabulary of V tokens and model width d, the embedding parameter matrix E ∈ ℝ^(V×d) has one row per token ID. For a token sequence t of length n, the input tensor is X[i,:]=E[tᵢ,:]. A one-hot-vector matrix multiplication is mathematically equivalent but wasteful in implementation.

X = one_hot(t)·E ≡ gather(E, t) ; X shape = [n, d]

Learning. Rows begin random or otherwise initialized and are updated by gradients from the language-model objective. The model is not handed a semantic dictionary of tokens. Tokens that appear in similar and useful predictive contexts often develop related representations, but their geometry depends on the objective, training data, architecture, and anisotropy. The embedding of a subword is not guaranteed to have a standalone stable natural-language meaning.

Contextualization: the row for bank is initially identical regardless of sentence. After attention and feed-forward mixing, hidden states for river bank and bank loan can diverge. Never conflate static input token embeddings with contextual token representations or task-trained sentence embeddings.

Gradients and weight tying: if a token ID appears in a batch, the input embedding gather delivers a gradient to its selected row(s). But when the same matrix is tied to the output projection, language-model logits h·Eᵀ can produce gradients across many output rows. So “only selected embedding rows are updated” is not generally true for tied output weights.

LM logits z = hWoutᵀ + b ; with tied weights Wout = E (dimension-compatible designs)

Production concerns: input dtype, quantization, vocabulary resizing, padding-vector conventions, optimizer states, and device placement. If token IDs change order, even identical-looking model weights can map words to incorrect vectors. Initial token embeddings are not sufficient evidence for semantic similarity; use task-aligned contextual embedding models when doing retrieval.

lessons.title: Embedding dimensions, geometry & representation
lessons.subtitle: Calculate parameter and activation memory, explain similarities, and separate token-vector geometry from retrieval embeddings.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why doesn't increasing embedding dimension necessarily improve accuracy?
  2. Derive embedding memory and compare it with activations for a long batch.
  3. What do cosine similarity and dot product imply if vector norms differ?
  4. Can the model use low-rank or factored embeddings without losing the external token interface?
sections.text: Why doesn't increasing embedding dimension necessarily improve accuracy? Derive embedding memory and compare it with activations for a long batch. What do cosine similarity and dot product imply if vector norms differ? Can the model use low-rank or factored embeddings without losing the external token interface?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Model width. An embedding maps each discrete token ID into d_model coordinates. These coordinates are learned features, not 4,096 individually human-labeled meanings. Model width influences the sizes of Q/K/V and MLP projections, residual streams, and activation memory. Tying dimensions across modules simplifies residual addition but is not mandated by every architecture.

Embedding weights: V·d; input activations: B·n·d·s bytes (s = bytes per stored element)
Illustration: V=64k,d=2048,bf16 → 64,000×2048×2=262,144,000 bytes ≈250 MiB

A batch of 8 sequences × 4,096 tokens × 2,048 width × bf16 adds 8×4096×2048×2 = 134,217,728 bytes = 128 MiB just for one such activation tensor, excluding attention state, gradients, and temporary buffers. A serving system must account for weights, KV cache, and kernels separately.

Geometry: cos(a,b)=a·b/(||a||·||b||) ignores magnitude; dot(a,b) depends on both angle and norm. If all vectors are normalized, cosine and dot-product ranking coincide. Raw token embeddings are often anisotropic and not optimized to encode sentence semantic similarity.

Alternatives: factorized embeddings decompose a large V×d matrix into V×r and r×d, saving parameters if r ≪ d. Product quantization or other low-precision representations may save memory at an accuracy/decode-complexity cost; rank/precision choices must be evaluated.

Debugging: unusual token norms, untrained rows, out-of-range IDs, pad-token leakage, and tokenizer/version mismatch can cause severe failures. Use targeted probes and task evaluations rather than overinterpreting 2D projection plots: PCA/t-SNE visualizations can distort global distances.

lessons.title: Why Transformers need position information
lessons.subtitle: Prove the permutation issue and distinguish absolute and relative location schemes.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Without a position signal, which aspect of token ordering can self-attention recover?
  2. What does permutation equivariance mean for position-free self-attention?
  3. Is a causal mask by itself a full position representation?
  4. Where in the pipeline can positional information enter?
sections.text: Without a position signal, which aspect of token ordering can self-attention recover? What does permutation equivariance mean for position-free self-attention? Is a causal mask by itself a full position representation? Where in the pipeline can positional information enter?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism. Plain self-attention performs the same projection and matching operation for each input position. With no positional signal or position-dependent mask, permuting the input token rows permutes the output rows in the same way; self-attention has no built-in preference for order.

SelfAttention(PX) = P·SelfAttention(X) (without position-dependent mask; P is a permutation matrix)

The softmax attention formula uses content-based Q and K products; absent position, dog bites man and man bites dog contain the same token multiset, yet require different interpretation. Positional methods inject index/relative-distance information so that the model can distinguish such arrangements.

Important nuance: a strictly causal mask does break arbitrary permutation equivariance by exposing differing prefix sets. So the statement “decoder self-attention has no order signal whatsoever without embeddings” is too strong. Nevertheless, causal visibility alone is a limited/implicit position cue; explicit or structured positional mechanisms improve the representation of relative and absolute order.

Where position enters: (a) add a position vector to input token embeddings; (b) modify Q/K projections with RoPE; (c) add relative position bias to attention logits; (d) use other learned or fixed relative mechanisms. These are architectural alternatives, not ingredients that must all coexist.

Additive: xᵢ = E[tᵢ] + pᵢ ;   Relative logit bias: score(i,j)=qᵢ·kⱼ/√dₖ + b(i−j)

Cost: additive position vectors add one vector per token; attention-relative methods may require computing biases or rotations but often integrate efficiently into fused kernels. Position mechanism, context length, and training distribution jointly determine long-range performance. “Theoretically supports n positions” does not mean calibrated accuracy at that n.

sections.html: Without positional information, unrestricted self-attention is permutation equivariant: reordering inputs simply reorders outputs. A decoder causal mask supplies a limited structural order cue, but explicit positional methods are still useful for distinguishing sequence locations and distances. We can add position vectors, bias attention scores by relative distance, or rotate queries and keys with RoPE. The choice affects extrapolation and computation.

lessons.title: Learned vs. sinusoidal positional embeddings
lessons.subtitle: Write the sinusoid equations and reason about limits of trainable position tables.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Derive the sinusoidal positional vector and its dimension pairing.
  2. What changes when you input position 20,000 into a 4,096-row learned absolute position table?
  3. Does sinusoidal encoding guarantee extrapolation to unseen context lengths?
  4. Why can pairs of sinusoidal frequencies help represent relative displacement?
sections.text: Derive the sinusoidal positional vector and its dimension pairing. What changes when you input position 20,000 into a 4,096-row learned absolute position table? Does sinusoidal encoding guarantee extrapolation to unseen context lengths? Why can pairs of sinusoidal frequencies help represent relative displacement?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Learned absolute positional embeddings use a trainable table P∈ℝ^(Lmax×d), with xᵢ=E[tᵢ]+P[i]. This has simple implementation and lets the training objective adapt positions, but a standard table has a fixed maximum row index; using unseen indices needs interpolation, extension, or an architecture change. Table cost is Lmax×d parameters.

Sinusoidal encoding from the original Transformer uses fixed sin/cos features at geometrically spaced wavelengths (for even d):

PE(pos,2i) = sin(pos / 100002i/d)
PE(pos,2i+1) = cos(pos / 100002i/d), for i=0,…,d/2−1

Each two-dimensional pair rotates with angular frequency ωᵢ=10000^(−2i/d). Basic trigonometry gives sin(a+b) and cos(a+b) as linear combinations of sin/cos at a. This makes relative offsets accessible to a suitable downstream function; it does not automatically solve all extrapolation or ambiguity problems, especially beyond trained ranges.

Example d=4, position 2: frequencies are ω₀=1 and ω₁=1/100, producing [sin 2, cos 2, sin 0.02, cos 0.02]. Adjacent coordinates are paired; switching their order is a convention issue only if consistently implemented throughout training and inference.

Debugging: verify off-by-one positions, padding offsets, caching position IDs, left-padding, and packed sequences. A model might produce numerically valid logits with wrong relative positions and silently lose accuracy.

sections.html: Learned positional embeddings add a trainable vector from a finite position table. Sinusoidal encodings add deterministic sin/cos features at different frequencies, so position vectors can be computed outside the training length. Their algebra supports relative offsets, but a mathematical encoding defined for longer positions is not proof the trained model generalizes there. I'd validate position IDs, padding, and length-shift quality before claiming extended context support.

Sinusoidal encodings add deterministic sin/cos features at different frequencies, so position vectors can be computed outside the training length. Their algebra supports relative offsets, but a mathematical encoding defined for longer positions is not proof the trained model generalizes there. I'd validate position IDs, padding, and length-shift quality before claiming extended context support.

Incident: Quality falls after a serving change from right-padding to left-padding.

Hypothesize: Position IDs now include pad offsets differently; cache lengths do not align with the continuation; or attention masks changed.

lessons.title: Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE)
lessons.subtitle: Work through Q/K rotation pairs, prove the relative-distance dot-product property, and discuss long-context caveats.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why rotate queries and keys rather than adding a position vector to token embeddings?
  2. Show mathematically why RoPE attention depends on relative displacement.
  3. What does the RoPE base parameter change?
  4. What fails when you naively extend a RoPE-based model far beyond its trained range?
sections.text: Why rotate queries and keys rather than adding a position vector to token embeddings? Show mathematically why RoPE attention depends on relative displacement. What does the RoPE base parameter change? What fails when you naively extend a RoPE-based model far beyond its trained range?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Operations. In RoPE-based attention, project residual states into Q and K, partition a configured rotary subdimension into 2D pairs, and rotate each pair by a position-dependent angle. Values V are normally not rotated by standard RoPE. For pair index m, frequency ωₘ=base^(−2m/d_rot); at sequence position p, the angle is p·ωₘ.

R(θ) = [[cos θ, −sin θ],[sin θ, cos θ]];
q'ₚ = R(pωₘ)qₚ ; k'ₛ = R(sωₘ)kₛ
(q'ₚ)ᵀk'ₛ = qₚᵀR((s−p)ωₘ)kₛ

Derivation: R(a)ᵀR(b)=R(b−a), because rotations are orthogonal. Thus the positional contribution to Q/K compatibility depends on the relative index difference, rather than requiring an absolute-position lookup row. Rotating both positions by a common offset leaves each pair's dot product unchanged if Q/K content vectors are held fixed. In an actual causal Transformer, shifting tokens and masks may change contextual content, so this algebra is not a full-system output invariance claim.

Implementation: reshape Q/K to heads, rotate configured components (interleaved vs. split-half layouts vary), ensure the cached keys retain their original absolute position rotations, and use the current continuation position when appending a query. Position-ID mistakes cause long-response quality degradation despite otherwise correct KV caching.

Advantages: no learned absolute table is necessary, and the mechanism gives a useful relative phase structure. Trade-offs: high-frequency phase aliasing, training-length distribution shift, choice of RoPE base, numeric precision, kernel layout, and attention-head rotary fractions influence long-context behavior. Position interpolation and RoPE scaling are adaptation strategies, not universal fixes.

Illustrative pair rotation
def rotate_pair(x0, x1, pos, omega):
    theta = pos * omega
    return (x0*cos(theta) - x1*sin(theta),
            x0*sin(theta) + x1*cos(theta))

q_rot = rotate_pair(*q, query_position, omega)
k_rot = rotate_pair(*k, key_position, omega)
score = dot(q_rot, k_rot) / sqrt(d_head)

sections.heading: Interview-ready spoken answer
sections.html: RoPE rotates pairs of query and key coordinates by angles proportional to token position, with multiple frequencies across a head. Since the transpose of one rotation times another equals a rotation by their difference, the resulting Q–K dot product encodes relative position. It avoids a finite learned absolute position table, but trained context limits and cache-position correctness still matter. Extending length requires evaluation and possibly a scaling strategy.

sections.html:
1. If you add 100 to both position IDs, must the entire model output stay identical? Strong answer: only the isolated RoPE pair score for fixed content is invariant; not the entire causal computation.
  2. What happens if cached K is rotated at position 4, then re-rotated as position 5? Strong answer: phase mismatch and corrupted attention.
  3. Why is RoPE not the same as learned positional embeddings? Strong answer: alters Q/K angular geometry after projection, not additive input vectors.

Strong response criteria appear in each prompt. State assumptions and explain how you would verify claims.

sections.heading: Production scenario
sections.html:
Incident: Short completions are accurate, but after thousands of generated tokens an assistant begins repeating or misusing distant facts.

Profile: Compare full-sequence reference decoding against incremental KV-cache decoding, log safe position-index traces and head configuration, verify RoPE base/scaling parameters in serving artifacts, and test boundary lengths.

Possible root causes: offset/rotation mismatch in cached keys, wrong rotary-dimension layout, phase errors after sliding-window truncation, or distribution shift beyond training length.

Fix: Correct position bookkeeping, use a verified kernel/reference implementation, and evaluate any length-extension strategy on controlled retrieval/reasoning tasks. Acceptance: Cache versus full-pass logits agree within precision tolerance for in-range fixtures; long-context task metrics meet explicitly agreed thresholds.

  • Relative-position property is an exact dot-product identity for fixed content.
  • Cache position alignment and long-context generalization are separate concerns.

lessons.title: Diagnosing multilingual, code & domain tokenization failures
lessons.subtitle: Use exact-token instrumentation to distinguish fragmentation, truncation, and information destruction.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why can the same number of visible characters produce radically different token counts?
  2. How do you separate out-of-vocabulary replacement from fragmentation?
  3. Why do code and structured identifiers stress general-purpose tokenizers?
  4. When would you retrain a tokenizer, fine-tune the model, or avoid modifying the weights?
sections.text: Why can the same number of visible characters produce radically different token counts? How do you separate out-of-vocabulary replacement from fragmentation? Why do code and structured identifiers stress general-purpose tokenizers? When would you retrain a tokenizer, fine-tune the model, or avoid modifying the weights?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Failure taxonomy. (1) Fragmentation: uncommon text turns into many byte/subword tokens; content is still encodable but expensive. (2) Lossy fallback: [UNK] erases distinctions. (3) Normalization collisions: different Unicode strings map to the same normalized representation, sometimes by design. (4) Boundary mistakes: tokenizer or pre-tokenizer splits identifiers, indentation, whitespace, escape sequences, or numbers in ways that harm structured extraction. (5) Truncation: the prompt is shortened after token-budget enforcement, silently dropping critical context. (6) Training coverage: even perfect encoding does not imply conceptual knowledge.

Examples: Bangla, Devanagari, CJK text, emojis with skin-tone modifiers and zero-width joiners, chemical formulae, invoice IDs, source code symbols and mixed-case identifiers can have high token expansion under a tokenizer trained predominantly on other distributions. Their actual counts depend on the chosen tokenizer; never attribute one toy count to production models.

  1. Capture a privacy-safe reproduction: escaped original string, UTF-8 byte count, code-point count, visually rendered example, normalization form and tokenizer artifact hash.
  2. Inspect output: token IDs and their decoded bytes/pieces, [UNK] count, continuation markers and post-template prompt length.
  3. Slice the data: p50/p95 tokens per document by language, domain and document type, and truncation rate at the real context budget.
  4. Trace the effect: compare downstream exact-match, citation fidelity, code compilation or name-entity recall against a stable gold set.
  5. Apply the minimal remedy: preserve exact terms in lexical search, adjust pre-tokenization only in a compatible model pipeline, use chunking/retrieval, choose a multilingual/code-specialized model, or retrain/adapt tokenizer and model jointly when ROI justifies it.

Evaluation design: report paired examples, bootstrap confidence intervals for quality and length outcomes where appropriate, monitor p95 latency, model memory and token charges, and set hard correctness thresholds for IDs and code. More aggressive merges may shorten text yet worsen representation learning if data for a newly minted token is scarce.

IDs vanish from answerCheck truncated span and retrieval logToken budget / lexical grounding
Low quality with normal token countTask-level error analysisModel training / prompt / data, not necessarily tokenizer

sections.html: I'd debug multilingual or domain-specific failures by inspecting the exact string-to-token mapping before changing the model. I'd distinguish reversible fragmentation from unknown-token replacement, normalization collisions, and budget truncation. Then I'd measure token inflation and downstream task accuracy by language or domain. The safest fix is often retrieval, preserved exact text, or a compatible specialist model rather than swapping the tokenizer under frozen embeddings.

1. If a tokenizer has no [UNK], why can entity extraction still fail? Strong answer: fragmentation, truncation, inadequate learning, or model behavior.

  3. Why is code indentation special? Strong answer: whitespace/control tokens can be semantically meaningful, so cleanup must not be assumed safe.

sections.heading: Production scenario
sections.html:
Scenario: A code assistant is deployed for a mixed Bangla/English developer team. p95 prompt tokens rise and exact function names occasionally change in generated edits.

Instrument: Token histograms by language and file type, identifier span offsets, parse/compile success, round-trip tokenizer fixtures, truncation position, and error concentration in comments vs. executable code.

Remediation order: (1) ensure stable tokenizer/model pair and correct chat template; (2) preserve code verbatim and remove only genuinely redundant prompt material; (3) reserve input/output budgets; (4) evaluate code-focused and multilingual-compatible models; (5) consider tokenizer retraining only with aligned model adaptation.

Acceptance: Task success measured by tests, exact-identifier preservation, lower validated length tails, and no worsening on paired language slices. Report numerical results only after experiment.

  • More tokens ≠ necessarily worse semantics, but usually higher system cost.

title: Transformer Architecture
description: Decode every operation inside a Transformer forward pass.

lessons.title: Transformer architecture: components and purpose
lessons.subtitle: Trace parallel sequence processing through token representations, attention, MLPs, residual paths, and the language-model head.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why did attention-based Transformers replace recurrence as the default architecture for large-scale language modeling?
  2. What does the attention layer compute that an FFN cannot?
  3. Which parts are tokenwise and which mix information across positions?
  4. What does decoder-only mean, and does it forbid cross-attention?
sections.text: Why did attention-based Transformers replace recurrence as the default architecture for large-scale language modeling? What does the attention layer compute that an FFN cannot? Which parts are tokenwise and which mix information across positions? What does decoder-only mean, and does it forbid cross-attention?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Start with the computation graph, not the buzzword. A Transformer is a deep stack of content-dependent token-mixing operations and per-position nonlinear feature transformations. A decoder-only causal LM processes token IDs T∈ℕ[B,N] and produces logits Z∈ℝ[B,N,V]. Embedding lookup maps IDs into the residual stream X∈ℝ[B,N,D]; position information is supplied by a model-dependent mechanism (learned absolute, RoPE, relative bias, etc.). Each block updates the residual stream with attention and an FFN/MLP. A final normalization and projection form next-token scores.

X⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾ = U + FFN(Norm₂(U)),   U = X⁽ˡ⁾ + Attention(Norm₁(X⁽ˡ⁾)) (representative pre-norm block)
  1. Embedding: map a token ID to a learned D-vector. Numeric IDs do not carry scalar meaning.
  2. Attention: each query position computes scores against allowed key positions, normalizes scores, and combines their values. It is the principal cross-token communication channel in a standard decoder block.
  3. MLP: independent, parameter-shared nonlinear transformation at each token location. Standard FFNs do not directly exchange information between tokens.
  4. Residual path: carry an additive identity route through depth, helping information flow and gradients.
  5. Normalization: control feature scale; exact arrangement (pre/post) and norm algorithm vary.
  6. Output head: map final hidden vectors to V vocabulary logits. Weights may be tied to the input embedding table.

Why scale? Across positions, attention matrix multiplication can be parallelized during prefill—unlike a sequential hidden-state recurrence. This does not make full attention free: score interaction count grows quadratically with sequence length, and autoregressive generation still requires a dependency on preceding tokens. Hardware-efficient matrix operations and specialized attention kernels are crucial.

Architecture boundary: the original 2017 Transformer is an encoder–decoder model. A GPT-style decoder-only model uses causal self-attention without the original encoder–decoder cross-attention sublayer; multimodal/hybrid decoders may add cross-attention. Encoder layers commonly use bidirectional attention; do not conflate attention visibility and model family.

Engineering benefits

Parallel sequence computation, flexible contextual mixing, scale-friendly accelerator kernels, reusable pretrained representations.

Costs & failures

Quadratic full-attention work, expensive prefill at large N, long-sequence sensitivity, numerical mask bugs, throughput-vs-latency contention.

1. Does the FFN communicate information between tokens? Strong response: no, independent per-position computation; previous attention can inject context.

  3. Why is the word decoder misleading here? Strong response: causal autoregressive architecture, not necessarily the original seq2seq decoder.

Answer by explaining the mechanism, the trade-off, and how you would test the claim.

sections.html: Incident: A refactor runs without exceptions but model loss increases. Inspect: compare layerwise norm outputs, QKV split order, tensor axis names, mask values, target shift, output logits against a minimal reference at short N.   2. Derive WQ/WK/WV shapes for D=768 and H=12.
  3. Why do we need three projections rather than one shared embedding?
  4. Show exactly which axis QKᵀ contracts and which axis softmax normalizes.
