sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Core derivation. For one residual stream X∈ℝ[B,N,D], define Q=XW_Q, K=XW_K, V=XW_V. In canonical MHA the flattened projections each have width D, and three matrices are each [D,D]; they are often computed by one fused weight W_QKV∈ℝ[D,3D]. Reshape into heads of dimension dₕ=D/H. Queries and keys live in a learned compatibility space while values carry the vectors to be mixed. Q, K, and V are computed from the same token sequence in self-attention but have different learned parameters.

qᵢ = W_Qᵀ xᵢ,  kⱼ = W_Kᵀ xⱼ,  vⱼ = W_Vᵀ xⱼ;
aᵢⱼ = softmaxⱼ( qᵢᵀkⱼ / √dₖ + mᵢⱼ );   oᵢ = Σⱼ aᵢⱼ vⱼ

Dimension example: with D=768 and H=12, dₕ=64. W_Q,W_K,W_V are each [768,768] in one common parameterization. XW_Q is [B,N,768], reshaped to [B,12,N,64]. Q @ K.transpose(-2,-1) gives [B,12,N,N]. A @ V returns [B,12,N,64]. After concatenation and output projection W_O∈ℝ[D,D], the result returns to [B,N,D].

Why separate roles? A token can be good at matching a preceding token without sending the same representation to the output. Separate Q/K/V let the model learn asymmetric search and transported content. In other variants, K/V head counts can be reduced (GQA/MQA), dₖ and dᵥ may differ, projections may include bias, and RoPE may rotate only a fraction of Q/K features. Do not assume every LLM uses a pure [D,D] projection per role.

Data flow vs. semantics: the weights are data-dependent per input because dot-products involve token features, but the linear projection weights are fixed after training. Attention probabilities are neither causal explanations nor automatically interpretable features; they are operational weights for mixing values.

Self-attention projections + output: approximately 4D² weight parameters per layer, assuming H·dₕ = D and no biases.

Debugging: assert head divisibility; ensure last axes in matmul are [-2,-1]; compare fused and unfused projections; check contiguous/transpose reshape; verify QK orientation and scale. Common bug: taking softmax over query dimension instead of keys.

sections.heading: Interview-ready spoken answer
sections.html: Q, K, and V are learned, separate projections of the hidden states. Each query scores permitted keys, the scale and mask are applied, softmax normalizes across key positions, and the resulting weights form a weighted sum of value vectors. With D=768 and 12 heads, each head is 64-dimensional in standard MHA, producing per-head N×N compatibility matrices. Separate projections let matching and transported information have different learned representations.

lessons.title: Scaled dot-product attention and √dₖ
lessons.subtitle: Derive the variance argument for attention scaling, investigate softmax saturation, and distinguish scaling from masking.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why is the denominator √dₖ rather than dₖ?
  2. What assumptions justify the variance argument and when do they fail?
  3. Does scaling by √dₖ guarantee stable attention at all network depths?
  4. If dₖ=64, how should raw dot products and softmax probabilities change?
sections.text: Why is the denominator √dₖ rather than dₖ? What assumptions justify the variance argument and when do they fail? Does scaling by √dₖ guarantee stable attention at all network depths? If dₖ=64, how should raw dot products and softmax probabilities change?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Attention scores: for a query q∈ℝ[dₖ] and key k∈ℝ[dₖ], define unscaled s=q·k=Σᵢ qᵢkᵢ. Under the simplifying assumptions that components are independent, zero-mean and unit-variance, E[s]=0 and Var(s)=dₖ. Standard deviation therefore grows as √dₖ. Dividing by √dₖ makes the score variance approximately one in this idealized case.

Var(Σᵢ qᵢkᵢ) = Σᵢ Var(qᵢkᵢ) = dₖ;  score = (q·k)/√dₖ

Why it matters to gradients. When logits become large relative to one another, softmax becomes near one-hot. Off-winning entries receive tiny derivatives, and the system may have a harder optimization problem. Scaling reduces dependence of typical logit magnitude on head width at initialization. It is not a proof of correct calibration; learned Q/K statistics, normalization, temperatures, and biases matter in trained systems.

Worked example: for dₖ=64, divide raw QK scores by 8. A raw score row [8,4,0] becomes [1,.5,0], which produces a noticeably more distributed softmax. Applying a mask is separate: if key j is in the future, its score should be prohibited (−∞), so its normalized weight is exactly zero in the ideal math.

Numerics: use a stable softmax (subtract maximum of finite logits) and account for fused kernels or mixed-precision accumulation. A row with all keys masked is an edge case—some implementations return NaN or require special safe handling. In causal self-attention with correctly shaped nonempty sequences, the diagonal generally provides at least one valid key, but combined padding masks can create fully masked rows.

Cost: QKᵀ is roughly 2BN²D FLOPs using multiply+add=2 and summed head width D. The scale is cheap relative to matrix products; key factors for performance include sequence length, memory traffic, and kernel fusion.

Invalid intuition

“Scaling makes Q and K unit vectors.” No: it scales scores rather than normalizing vector length.

Alternative

Cosine attention or learned temperature can change score calibration, but changes model behavior and must be evaluated rather than casually substituted.

lessons.title: Self-attention vs cross-attention
lessons.subtitle: Identify which sequence supplies queries, which supplies keys and values, and why mask geometry changes.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Draw Q/K/V data flows for self-attention and cross-attention.
  2. If decoder tokens have length N and encoder tokens length M, what is the score shape?
  3. Why does standard decoder-only language modeling not require cross-attention?
  4. What do cached K/V represent in encoder–decoder cross-attention?
sections.text: Draw Q/K/V data flows for self-attention and cross-attention. If decoder tokens have length N and encoder tokens length M, what is the score shape? Why does standard decoder-only language modeling not require cross-attention? What do cached K/V represent in encoder–decoder cross-attention?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Self-attention: the query, key and value vectors are projected from the same sequence representation. With X∈ℝ[B,N,D], one head computes Q=XW_Q, K=XW_K, V=XW_V, so the score map has shape [B,H,N,N]. For a decoder LM, the upper triangle is masked: each position may see itself and its predecessors. Bidirectional encoder self-attention typically admits all nonpadding positions.

Cross-attention: queries come from the decoder-side representation X_dec∈ℝ[B,N,D_dec]; keys and values come from an external memory X_mem∈ℝ[B,M,D_mem] (often encoder outputs). Projection matrices can be rectangular to create compatible head widths. The score shape is [B,H,N,M]. Each decoder position can query all permitted memory slots, unless application constraints impose an additional mask.

Self: softmax(QₓKₓᵀ/√d) Vₓ   |   Cross: softmax(Q_dec K_memᵀ/√d) V_mem

Architectural uses: original Transformer sequence-to-sequence decoder has causal self-attention and cross-attention over encoder states. Decoder-only LMs instead encode prompt context in their causal self-attention stream. Vision-language or speech systems may add cross-attention to externally encoded features; simply sending multimodal tokens in a combined sequence is another design. Model labels alone do not guarantee a specific cross-attention layer.

Latency trade-offs: self-attention prefill mixing costs roughly O(BN²D). Cross-attention over memory M costs O(BNMD), plus external encoder work and memory/KV management. Static cross-attention K/V can often be computed once and reused during generation; dynamic memory invalidates reuse. Access-control masking over retrieved snippets must be enforced before the model can attend to restricted material, not merely hidden by later softmax tricks.

Mask nuance: for cross-attention, a triangular causal mask over the N×M matrix generally makes no sense unless memory elements are temporally aligned. Common masks prevent attending to padding or prohibited memory entries. Always check what “True” means for the particular attention API: PyTorch's SDPA uses True for allowed entries, while some other MHA masks use the opposite convention.

Always check what “True” means for the particular attention API: PyTorch's SDPA uses True for allowed entries, while some other MHA masks use the opposite convention.

sections.html: Self-attention uses Q, K, and V projected from the same sequence, so an N-token input gives an N×N score map per head; a decoder masks future keys. Cross-attention uses decoder queries against external encoder or memory keys and values, giving an N×M map. It enables conditional generation from a separate representation but adds memory and compute, and usually has a different masking policy.

lessons.title: Causal masking and leakage prevention
lessons.subtitle: Make future-token information unavailable at the attention-score level; validate with adversarial prefix-invariance tests.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why is a causal mask required for parallel teacher-forced training?
  2. Show the attention logit mask for sequence length 4.
  3. Why is multiplying post-softmax attention by a 0/1 mask incorrect?
  4. Can a masking bug produce excellent training loss and terrible generation?
sections.text: Why is a causal mask required for parallel teacher-forced training? Show the attention logit mask for sequence length 4. Why is multiplying post-softmax attention by a 0/1 mask incorrect? Can a masking bug produce excellent training loss and terrible generation?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Objective and visibility. A causal language model estimates p(x₁,…,xₙ)=∏ₜ p(xₜ|x₍₁:ₜ₋₁₎). During teacher-forced training, all input positions are processed in parallel; without masking, position t could read target token xₜ₊₁ from a future location and cheat. A triangular bias enforces the conditional-information boundary inside each self-attention layer.

M[i,j] = 0 if j≤i, otherwise −∞;  A = softmax((QKᵀ)/√dₕ + M)   (softmax over keys j)
Example: sequence N=4; rows are queries, columns are keys
         k₀   k₁   k₂   k₃
q₀       ✓    ×    ×    ×
q₁       ✓    ✓    ×    ×
q₂       ✓    ✓    ✓    ×
q₃       ✓    ✓    ✓    ✓

Why before softmax? If an invalid logit is left in the normalizing denominator, even multiplying its final probability by zero wastes probability mass and changes the other weights unless you renormalize. The standard safe approach is a large negative/additive forbidden bias before the normalization; fused kernels implement this logically without materializing a full mask.

Correctness invariant: changing token IDs at positions greater than t must not change logits for positions ≤t, assuming a deterministic eval-mode model and unchanged position/padding metadata. This is a powerful unit test because it catches both direct and indirect leakage across multiple layers.

Packing/padding: a plain causal lower-triangle is insufficient when packing independent documents into one tensor; without a block-diagonal or segment-aware mask, later segments can see earlier documents. Left padding, cached decode offsets, and chunked prefill make mask alignment nontrivial. Avoid fully masked query rows where possible; implementations differ in handling them.

Complexity: in full prefill the mask changes which interactions are valid, but a naïvely materialized N×N score tensor still costs O(N²) memory; fused and sparse-aware kernels may reduce intermediate storage.

sections.html: The causal mask enforces the factorization of next-token prediction while processing all training positions in parallel. For query i, only keys j≤i are allowed; future-score entries are effectively −∞ before softmax. I verify correctness by mutating suffix tokens and asserting that earlier-position logits remain unchanged. I also test packed sequences, padding, and cache offsets because those can leak data even when a triangular mask exists.

  3. How does packed training change the mask? Strong response: document boundary/segment-awareness plus causal visibility.

Hypothesis: future tokens leaked during teacher forcing. Test: replace suffix tokens and recompute prefix logits at each layer in eval mode; inspect masks with asymmetric lengths and packed examples. Repair: correct masked attention score construction and add automated leakage tests to CI. Acceptance: strict prefix invariance within numeric tolerance, no cross-document attention in packed samples, and realistic holdout autoregressive evaluation.

  • Suffix mutation must not affect prefix logits.
  • Packing and cache-position offsets are high-risk leakage surfaces.

lessons.title: Multi-Head Attention: representation and output projection
lessons.subtitle: Explain head partitioning, concatenation, output mixing, head diversity limitations, and practical variants.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why multiple attention heads instead of one larger head?
  2. What is the output shape after concatenating heads and why do we need W_O?
  3. Do heads necessarily learn unique linguistic relationships?
  4. Does increasing head count with fixed D reduce the N² work?
sections.text: Why multiple attention heads instead of one larger head? What is the output shape after concatenating heads and why do we need W_O? Do heads necessarily learn unique linguistic relationships? Does increasing head count with fixed D reduce the N² work?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Standard setup. For hidden width D and H heads, split projected features into H vectors of dimension dₕ = D/H. Each head independently computes an attention distribution and weighted value mixture. Concatenate all H outputs into D features, then apply a learned output projection W_O∈ℝ[D,D]. This lets the next residual stream combine information from the different head subspaces.

headₕ = softmax(Qₕ Kₕᵀ / √dₕ + M) Vₕ;  MHA(X)=Concat(head₁,…,head_H) W_O

Mechanistic rationale: multiple learned projections can route different kinds of information—short-range copying, delimiter matching, code structure, or long-distance relations—through different subspaces. This is a capability, not a guarantee: heads may be redundant, specialized, or change roles across checkpoints. Claims about named “syntax heads” require mechanistic evidence and controlled ablations.

Complexity under fixed D: summing H head attentions still performs roughly 2BN²D score multiplications plus another 2BN²D weighted-value multiplications. Full QKV + output projection is about 8BND² FLOPs (multiply and add counted separately). Increasing H while keeping D fixed mainly changes dₕ and the number/shape of attention matrices; it does not proportionally multiply the leading N²D arithmetic, but unoptimized kernel launch/softmax costs, cache metadata, and memory traffic can increase.

Parameter comparison: in standard dense MHA with fixed D, W_Q,W_K,W_V,W_O total 4D² weights independent of H. However, per-head learned biases, relative features, architecture-specific projections, and GQA/MQA change this picture.

GQA/MQA boundary: module 6 covers detailed GQA, but at a high level, reducing the number of K/V heads can shrink decode KV-cache memory and bandwidth. It changes inference bottlenecks but is not mathematically identical to full MHA without retraining or conversion.

Debugging: use head-specific heatmaps and tests, not only averaged head attention. An average can conceal a faulty head. Check mask broadcasting to all heads, head-dimension scale, contiguous layouts, and output projection orientation.

lessons.title: Feed-Forward Networks: GELU, SiLU, SwiGLU
lessons.subtitle: Compare the per-position MLP formulas, activation behavior, parameter costs, and gated variants.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Does the FFN mix token positions?
  2. Derive the two-layer GELU MLP and the three-projection SwiGLU variant.
  3. How do you compare hidden expansion sizes fairly across different FFN types?
  4. Where do FFNs dominate Transformer compute?
sections.text: Does the FFN mix token positions? Derive the two-layer GELU MLP and the three-projection SwiGLU variant. How do you compare hidden expansion sizes fairly across different FFN types? Where do FFNs dominate Transformer compute?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
What FFNs do: attention aggregates information between positions; an FFN applies the same learned nonlinear function to each position separately. Given X∈ℝ[B,N,D], a conventional MLP expands to F features and projects back to D:

FFN_GELU(x)=W_down · GELU(W_up x+b_up)+b_down

In row-vector convention this is GELU(X W_up + b_up) W_down + b_down with shapes [D,F] and [F,D]. GELU roughly gates negative inputs smoothly; the exact Gaussian-CDF form is GELU(z)=z·Φ(z), with common approximate implementations. ReLU uses max(0,z) and has a discontinuous derivative at zero. SiLU/Swish is z·sigmoid(z).

SwiGLU: compute two independent branches of width F: U=XW_up and G=XW_gate. Multiply the up branch by a SiLU-transformed gate, then return to D: SwiGLU(X) = (SiLU(G) ⊙ U) W_down. The elementwise gate can learn richer conditional feature selection at extra projection cost.

Weights: GELU MLP ≈ 2DF;  SwiGLU ≈ 3DF (bias-free);   F_SwiGLU≈(2/3)F_GELU gives similar parameter count.

Example: if D=4096, a GELU MLP with F=16384 has about 2×4096×16384=134.2 million weight parameters. A comparable-parameter SwiGLU width is approximately 10923, because it has three large projection matrices. Exact hidden-width rounding matters for hardware efficiency and tensor parallel layouts.

Compute: approximately 4BNDF FLOPs for GELU projections and 6BNDF for SwiGLU projections using the same F (multiply+add=2). At short sequence lengths, dense linear layers and model-weight bandwidth can dominate serving; at long prefill N, attention's N² term may become important. MoE replaces dense FFN with routed expert computation in some architectures.

Failures: mistakenly applying an activation to the residual sum, omitting a gate multiplication, using the wrong tensor order in fused kernels, FP16 overflow with large activations, or comparing expansions at unequal parameter budgets. Debug with scalar activation plots, shape assertions, finite-value tests, and reference parity.

lessons.title: Residual connections and gradient propagation
lessons.subtitle: Reason about identity paths, Jacobians, training depth, and the effect of normalization placement.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why does residual addition help train deep Transformer stacks?
  2. Write the local Jacobian of y=x+F(x).
  3. Do residual connections guarantee no vanishing/exploding gradients?
  4. How can residual scaling alter optimization?
sections.text: Why does residual addition help train deep Transformer stacks? Write the local Jacobian of y=x+F(x). Do residual connections guarantee no vanishing/exploding gradients? How can residual scaling alter optimization?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Residual route: instead of forcing a sublayer to replace its input, compute y=x+F(x), where F can be attention or an MLP branch. The identity route allows the residual stream to carry information forward even if a residual branch is initially small or poorly conditioned.

y=x+F(x);   ∂y/∂x=I+J_F(x);   ∂𝓛/∂x=(I+J_F)ᵀ∂𝓛/∂y

Why it helps: the gradient includes a direct identity contribution rather than passing exclusively through a long product of nonlinear Jacobians. However, the total gradient is still a sum of paths and can exhibit cancellation, explosion, or instability. Saying “residuals solve vanishing gradients” without caveats is incomplete.

Stacked residuals: for x_{l+1}=x_l+F_l(x_l), telescoping gives x_L=x_0+Σ_l F_l(x_l); this offers an additive interpretation, but since every branch depends on previous states, it is not a set of independent corrections. In backprop, many identity-plus-branch paths contribute.

Pre-norm interaction: in x+F(Norm(x)), the bypass does not pass through a normalization operator. In post-norm Norm(x+F(x)), gradients are transformed by normalization after each residual sum. This is part of why many deep GPT-like models choose pre-norm, though precise stability and quality depend on initialization, scaling, and architecture.

Residual scaling and initialization: some models scale residual branches at initialization, use gating, or choose layer-dependent multipliers to control depth-dependent activation growth. This is not interchangeable with dropping residuals: it trades stability, representation update strength, and optimization dynamics.

Validation: inspect gradient norm per block and branch, activation RMS by depth, optimizer loss curve, exploding/vanishing flags, and loss sensitivity to residual scale. Use a zeroed-branch test: if F(x)=0, pre-norm residual sublayer should return x exactly within floating-point behavior.

This is not interchangeable with dropping residuals: it trades stability, representation update strength, and optimization dynamics. Validation: inspect gradient norm per block and branch, activation RMS by depth, optimizer loss curve, exploding/vanishing flags, and loss sensitivity to residual scale. Use a zeroed-branch test: if F(x)=0 , pre-norm residual sublayer should return x exactly within floating-point behavior.

This supplies a direct gradient route and helps preserve information through depth. It does not mathematically guarantee stable optimization; normalization placement, residual scales, activation growth, and initialization still matter. I would monitor layerwise activation RMS and gradient norms rather than assume residuals prevent every instability.

lessons.title: LayerNorm vs RMSNorm: exact computation
lessons.subtitle: Compute normalization across the feature dimension and reason about mean subtraction, parameters, and numerical stability.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Write LayerNorm and RMSNorm equations for the last dimension.
  2. What is the difference between centering and scaling?
  3. When is RMSNorm a reasonable replacement and when is it not drop-in?
  4. How do epsilon placement and half-precision accumulation affect results?
sections.text: Write LayerNorm and RMSNorm equations for the last dimension. What is the difference between centering and scaling? When is RMSNorm a reasonable replacement and when is it not drop-in? How do epsilon placement and half-precision accumulation affect results?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
LayerNorm normalizes each token independently across its D hidden features (not across the batch), typically with a trainable scale γ and bias β. Compute μ=(1/D)Σᵢxᵢ and σ²=(1/D)Σᵢ(xᵢ−μ)², then LN(x)ᵢ=γᵢ(xᵢ−μ)/√(σ²+ε)+βᵢ.

LN(x)ᵢ = γᵢ (xᵢ−μ)/√(σ²+ε) + βᵢ;  RMSNorm(x)ᵢ = γᵢ xᵢ/√(mean(x²)+ε)

RMSNorm divides features by their root-mean-square magnitude and usually learns only γ. It does not subtract the feature mean, so the normalized output is not generally zero-mean. This can reduce operations and is used in many modern decoder LMs, but its behavior is not mathematically equivalent to LayerNorm.

Example: x=[1,2,3], with unit γ and zero β. LayerNorm subtracts μ=2 and divides by sqrt(2/3+ε), yielding approximately [-1.2247,0,1.2247]. RMSNorm divides by sqrt(14/3+ε), yielding about [0.4629,0.9258,1.3887]. The outputs differ in both mean and direction.

Data flow: normalization preserves shape [B,N,D]. It computes statistics over only the last D dimension; accidentally normalizing over sequence or batch can create training/inference mismatch and even violate causality if future tokens influence normalization of earlier ones.

Numerical issues: use epsilon inside the square root as defined by the selected implementation, especially near zero variance. Many kernels accumulate sums/means in FP32 when input is BF16/FP16. Choice of ε, bias and weight conventions, cast locations, and normalization axis affect checkpoints and inference parity. Never swap LayerNorm for RMSNorm in an existing pretrained model without validating or adapting weights.

Performance: both are O(BND) in feature reads/elementwise operations; differences often involve memory traffic, fusion, and GPU kernel overhead. Neither eliminates quadratic attention.

lessons.title: Pre-Norm vs Post-Norm Transformer blocks
lessons.subtitle: Derive update order, explain gradient-route differences, and compare stability and representational trade-offs.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Show the exact equations for pre-norm and post-norm residual blocks.
  2. Why is pre-norm common in deep causal decoders?
  3. Is post-norm always worse or unusable?
  4. Does using pre-norm eliminate the need for an output normalization?
sections.text: Show the exact equations for pre-norm and post-norm residual blocks. Why is pre-norm common in deep causal decoders? Is post-norm always worse or unusable? Does using pre-norm eliminate the need for an output normalization?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Pre-norm applies normalization before the sublayer and adds its output directly to the residual stream. A representative attention+FFN block is:

u = x + Attn(Norm₁(x));   y = u + FFN(Norm₂(u))

Post-norm instead normalizes after each sublayer's residual addition:

u = Norm₁(x + Attn(x));   y = Norm₂(u + FFN(u))

Key optimization difference: pre-norm's main bypass x→x+branch is an exact identity addition at each block; post-norm routes even the skip contribution through the norm Jacobian. The latter can make deep optimization more sensitive to initialization, LR warmup, and layer depth. Most contemporary autoregressive LMs use pre-norm-like layouts or closely related variants, but post-norm designs can train successfully with proper recipe and may differ in final-layer representation behavior.

Do not confuse normalization type and placement: RMSNorm vs LayerNorm is one axis; pre-norm vs post-norm is a separate axis. A decoder can be pre-LayerNorm or pre-RMSNorm, and may apply a final norm before the LM head. The norm before the attention branch and the norm before FFN usually have separate learned parameters.

Memory and speed: both layouts have comparable leading-order FLOPs and parameter counts for matching sublayers; differences lie in kernel fusion, activation checkpointing, and training stability. The main trade-off is optimization behavior rather than a guaranteed major inference-cost reduction.

Common mistakes: applying the same norm twice to wrong state, adding residual after normalization in a supposed post-norm implementation, forgetting final norm in a pre-norm stack, silently loading weights trained under a different layout. Compare outputs with a hand-constructed block where attention/FFN return zeros to expose update-order differences.

I also distinguish norm placement from LayerNorm versus RMSNorm and verify any final normalization before loading or exporting a checkpoint.

lessons.title: Transformer compute, memory, and scaling complexity
lessons.subtitle: Estimate projection, FFN, and attention FLOPs; distinguish persistent weights, ephemeral attention activations, and KV cache.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. When do projection/FFN costs exceed the N² attention cost?
  2. Estimate attention score memory for B=4,H=32,N=4096 in FP16.
  3. Why can FlashAttention remove an N² memory bottleneck without making attention arithmetic linear?
  4. How do prefill and single-token decode complexity differ with a KV cache?
sections.text: When do projection/FFN costs exceed the N² attention cost? Estimate attention score memory for B=4,H=32,N=4096 in FP16. Why can FlashAttention remove an N² memory bottleneck without making attention arithmetic linear? How do prefill and single-token decode complexity differ with a KV cache?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Variables: B sequences, N tokens, model width D, heads H, head size dₕ=D/H, FFN width F, and blocks L. The following approximations treat a multiplication plus addition as 2 FLOPs, count weights without biases, and describe a standard dense full-attention layer. Hardware kernel FLOP conventions and actual activation memory vary.

Operation (per block)Approx FLOPs / paramsReason
Q,K,V,output projections8BND² FLOPs; 4D² weights4 dense D×D maps
QKᵀ and AV4BN²D FLOPsTwo sequence-mixing matrix products
GELU FFN4BNDF FLOPs; 2DF weightsTwo dense projections
SwiGLU FFN6BNDF FLOPs; 3DF weightsThree dense projections
Materialized scores/probsO(BHN²) elementsOne N×N tensor per head
Compute/block (GELU) ≈ 8BND² + 4BN²D + 4BNDF
Weights/block (GELU) ≈ 4D² + 2DF

Memory example: B=4,H=32,N=4096 gives 4×32×4096²=2,147,483,648 attention-score elements. At 2 bytes each, that is about 4 GiB for one materialized attention-score tensor per block (before accounting for softmax copies, gradients, activations, and allocations). This illustrative memory footprint is why O(N²) intermediates can be a blocker.

FlashAttention nuance: IO-aware tiled attention can compute mathematically equivalent dense attention while avoiding materialization of the full score/probability matrices in HBM. It reduces memory traffic and the dominant attention intermediate-memory footprint, not the fundamental count of pairwise dot products in dense full attention. Sliding-window/sparse attention changes the actual interaction pattern and potentially arithmetic.

KV cache: after prefill, incremental decoding at one step attends one new query to N existing keys, giving attention work roughly O(BND) per new token per layer rather than recomputing N×N for old tokens. Per-layer KV elements are 2BNH_kv dₕ; multiply by layers and bytes/element for cache allocation. Heads for K/V may differ from Q heads in GQA.

What model size means: block weights plus embeddings and output head (tied or untied), biases/norms, and optional router/experts give model parameter totals. Parameter bytes + KV bytes + runtime/activation overhead must fit accelerator memory. Real latency also reflects batch scheduling, bandwidth, layout, and kernel choice, not FLOPs alone.

title: Generation & Context
description: Decode logits, sampling, context windows, and structured generation.

lessons.title: From hidden states to vocabulary logits
lessons.subtitle: Follow the exact final projection, tensor dimensions, weight tying, and per-token score semantics.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Given [B,N,D] hidden states and vocabulary V, derive the output tensor and parameter count with/without tied embeddings.
  2. Why are logits not probabilities, and why does the last row drive next-token inference?
  3. What happens to memory and bandwidth when V is 200k instead of 32k?
  4. Can a positive logit be less likely than a negative logit? Explain.
sections.text: Given [B,N,D] hidden states and vocabulary V, derive the output tensor and parameter count with/without tied embeddings. Why are logits not probabilities, and why does the last row drive next-token inference? What happens to memory and bandwidth when V is 200k instead of 32k? Can a positive logit be less likely than a negative logit? Explain.

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Trace the decoder to the next token. After L causal Transformer blocks, the final position contains a context-dependent hidden vector hₜ ∈ ℝᴰ. The output projection W_out ∈ ℝᴰˣⱽ forms unnormalized scores zₜ = hₜ W_out + b, so a batch of full-sequence outputs has shape [B,N,V]. In some models a final RMSNorm or LayerNorm precedes the projection. At generation time, only the last unconsumed token-position logits are needed for deciding the next token; training typically scores many positions in parallel.

H ∈ ℝ[B,N,D], W_out ∈ ℝ[D,V]   →   Z = H W_out + b ∈ ℝ[B,N,V]
  1. Obtain hidden states: token embeddings, positions, causal attention and MLPs produce H.
  2. Normalize and project: compute the matrix product to V candidate-token scores per position.
  3. Apply rules: optional vocabulary constraints, bad-token masks, and repetition/logit biases transform logits, depending on implementation.
  4. Compute probabilities: apply temperature and stable softmax to finite logits.
  5. Select a token: greedy, beam search, or stochastic sampling.
  6. Advance: append the token, update per-layer KV cache, and repeat until EOS/stop/budget.

Weight tying: input embedding E ∈ ℝ[V,D]; tying uses W_out=Eᵀ and saves approximately VD independent parameters. Untied output adds another VD (biases excluded). With V=128,000,D=4096, one untied matrix is about 524.3 million parameters, or 1 GiB at 2 bytes each; the final output activation for B=1 and one step is another V scores, and a full [B,N,V] logit tensor can be huge if materialized unnecessarily.

Complexity: full sequence output projection is O(BNDV) operations, incremental projection O(BDV). The large vocabulary matrix may influence decoding memory bandwidth and top-k selection time. Sharded vocabularies must account for globally correct normalization/selection. Traps: reading logits as confidence scores, accidentally projecting a padding position, using wrong last-token indices in a padded batch, confusing output tokens with Unicode words, and assuming weight-tying is mandatory. A logit difference—not its absolute sign—drives the probability ratio.
sections.text: Trace the decoder to the next token. After L causal Transformer blocks, the final position contains a context-dependent hidden vector hₜ ∈ ℝᴰ . The output projection W_out ∈ ℝᴰˣⱽ forms unnormalized scores zₜ = hₜ W_out + b , so a batch of full-sequence outputs has shape [B,N,V] . In some models a final RMSNorm or LayerNorm precedes the projection. At generation time, only the last unconsumed token-position logits are needed for deciding the next token; training typically scores many positions in parallel. H ∈ ℝ[B,N,D], W_out ∈ ℝ[D,V]   →   Z = H W_out + b ∈ ℝ[B,N,V] Obtain hidden states: token embeddings, positions, causal attention and MLPs produce H . Normalize and project: compute the matrix product to V candidate-token scores per position. Apply rules: optional vocabulary constraints, bad-token masks, and repetition/logit biases transform logits, depending on implementation. Compute probabilities: apply temperature and stable softmax to finite logits. Select a token: greedy, beam search, or stochastic sampling. Advance: append the token, update per-layer KV cache, and repeat until EOS/stop/budget. Weight tying: input embedding E ∈ ℝ[V,D] ; tying uses W_out=Eᵀ and saves approximately VD independent parameters. Untied output adds another VD (biases excluded). With V=128,000,D=4096 , one untied matrix is about 524.3 million parameters, or 1 GiB at 2 bytes each; the final output activation for B=1 and one step is another V scores, and a full [B,N,V] logit tensor can be huge if materialized unnecessarily. Complexity: full sequence output projection is O(BNDV) operations, incremental projection O(BDV) . The large vocabulary matrix may influence decoding memory bandwidth and top-k selection time. Sharded vocabularies must account for globally correct normalization/selection. Traps: reading logits as confidence scores, accidentally projecting a padding position, using wrong last-token indices in a padded batch, confusing output tokens with Unicode words, and assuming weight-tying is mandatory. A logit difference—not its absolute sign—drives the probability ratio.

sections.heading: Interview-ready spoken answer
sections.html: Final hidden states have width D, but the LM head projects each into V vocabulary logits. These are relative scores, not probabilities; at inference I select from the correct final position, apply decoding constraints and softmax, choose a token, then advance the autoregressive state. For a large vocabulary I budget the D×V projection and avoid materializing all [B,N,V] logits when only the final row is required. Weight tying can reuse the input embedding matrix.

  3. How much memory does [B,N,V] cost? Strong answer: B×N×V×dtype bytes, distinct from model parameters.

lessons.title: Softmax and token probability distributions
lessons.subtitle: Derive stable softmax, probability ratios, entropy, log probabilities, and numerical edge cases.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why does softmax subtract the maximum logit?
  2. Derive the odds ratio between two tokens from logits.
  3. What happens if every vocabulary candidate is masked?
  4. How would you check whether model probabilities are calibrated?
sections.text: Why does softmax subtract the maximum logit? Derive the odds ratio between two tokens from logits. What happens if every vocabulary candidate is masked? How would you check whether model probabilities are calibrated?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Logits can be any finite real scores. Softmax converts their differences into a categorical distribution. For token i and V available tokens, pᵢ = exp(zᵢ) / Σⱼexp(zⱼ). Dividing numerator and denominator by exp(m) with m=maxⱼ zⱼ gives a numerically stable equivalent. Additive shifts zᵢ+c change no probabilities; rescaling logits does.

pᵢ = exp(zᵢ−m) / Σⱼ exp(zⱼ−m),   m=maxⱼzⱼ
log(pᵢ/pⱼ)=zᵢ−zⱼ  (for allowed tokens)

Worked example: logits [2,1,0] yield probabilities approximately [0.665,0.245,0.090]. Exp(2)/exp(1)=e gives the relative odds of the first versus second tokens. log_softmax is preferable when aggregating sequence log-likelihoods because multiplying many small probabilities underflows. Entropy H(p)=−Σpᵢlog pᵢ describes spread, not factual uncertainty, evidence sufficiency, or calibrated confidence.

  1. Suppress invalid candidates with true −∞ logits or a suitably safe mask implementation.
  2. Scale/transform logits as required by decoding strategy.
  3. Find the finite maximum per batch row; exponentiate shifted logits.
  4. Divide by the total finite mass and sample or take argmax.
  5. Use logsumexp to compute stable log probabilities for beam scoring and diagnostics.

Calibration: highly peaked token probabilities do not establish that a full answer is true. To assess confidence on a defined downstream task, measure reliability diagrams, expected calibration error where applicable, selective prediction risk-coverage, and task-specific held-out labels. Edge cases: all −∞ logits cause undefined normalization; NaNs propagate; mixed precision can underflow very small terms; tokenizer-specific special tokens may require masking. A production decoder must verify at least one eligible token remains after hard constraints.

These probabilities are useful for decoding but are not a trustworthy measure of factual correctness or answer-level calibration.

lessons.title: Greedy decoding versus beam search
lessons.subtitle: Distinguish local next-token decisions from approximate sequence-level search and its failure modes.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Give a two-step sequence where greedy decoding misses the most likely complete sequence.
  2. How do beam width, length normalization, and EOS termination influence output?
  3. Why is beam search often unpopular in open-ended chat generation?
  4. What is its time and KV-cache cost?
sections.text: Give a two-step sequence where greedy decoding misses the most likely complete sequence. How do beam width, length normalization, and EOS termination influence output? Why is beam search often unpopular in open-ended chat generation? What is its time and KV-cache cost?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Greedy: choose argmaxᵢ P(yₜ=i | y<ₜ,x) at each step. It optimizes each next-token decision, not the sequence probability ∏ₜP(yₜ|y<ₜ,x). Beam search: keep the best W partial hypotheses ranked by accumulated token log-probabilities; expand each with candidate tokens, prune to W, and continue until a termination rule applies. It is an approximate search, not exhaustive global optimization unless exhaustive width is used.

score(y₁:T) = Σₜ log P(yₜ | y<ₜ,x)
illustrative length-adjusted: score_α(y)=score(y)/Tᵅ

Concrete counterexample: the first-step options have P(A)=0.55, P(B)=0.45. After A the best second token has probability 0.33, while after B a terminal token has probability 0.99. Greedy picks A then its best continuation, around 0.1815; a beam that keeps B can find B→EOS with likelihood 0.4455. These are fabricated values illustrating search, not actual model probabilities.

  1. Initialize beam with the prompt, total log-probability zero, and no generated tokens.
  2. For each active hypothesis, run next-token inference and propose candidate successors.
  3. Add log probabilities to parent scores; apply clearly documented length/coverage/constraint scoring.
  4. Preserve finished hypotheses while continuing unfinished ones; implementations differ in how they normalize and when they stop early.
  5. Return a finished hypothesis selected under the chosen rule, checking that a degenerate unfinished beam is not treated as a valid completion.

Engineering costs: with width W, up to W continuations require compute and KV states each step, although shared prefixes can reuse cache storage until branching. Beam search increases latency/memory and can intensify generic or repetitive outputs in open-ended conversation. Length normalization may change ranking and beam pruning. It is useful in constrained translation, transcription, or sequence tasks when likelihood is a reasonable quality proxy. It is not a guaranteed quality improvement; compare against sampling and task metrics rather than treating larger beams as automatically better. Beam size one is greedy only if scoring and special termination handling match.

sections.html: Greedy picks the highest-probability next token and can miss a better whole sequence. Beam search tracks multiple partial continuations using summed log probabilities and optional length normalization. That improves approximate sequence search for some constrained tasks but costs more decode compute and KV memory and can worsen blandness in open-ended chat. I decide using task evaluation, not beam width alone.

  3. How would you make beams efficient? Strong answer: share common prefix KV, prune early, cap width/length, benchmark latency.

  • Likelihood is not a universal proxy for factuality, diversity, or helpfulness.

lessons.title: Temperature and probability reshaping
lessons.subtitle: Understand the exact logit scaling, entropy behavior, and why temperature is not a reliability switch.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Derive Pᵀ(i) for logits and show what happens as T approaches zero or infinity.
  2. Does temperature=0 always mean perfectly repeatable production output?
  3. Where should temperature sit relative to top-p filtering?
  4. When might high temperature be useful and harmful?
sections.text: Derive Pᵀ(i) for logits and show what happens as T approaches zero or infinity. Does temperature=0 always mean perfectly repeatable production output? Where should temperature sit relative to top-p filtering? When might high temperature be useful and harmful?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Temperature transforms relative logits before categorical sampling. For T>0, define pᵢ(T)=exp(zᵢ/T)/Σexp(zⱼ/T). When T<1, logit differences are magnified, making the top alternatives more dominant; T>1 flattens the distribution. For a unique largest logit, T→0⁺ concentrates all mass on its argmax; for T→∞, mass approaches uniform over eligible finite-logit candidates.

log(Pᵀ(i)/Pᵀ(j)) = (zᵢ−zⱼ)/T  (T>0)

Example: logits [2,1,0] at T=1 give about [0.665,0.245,0.090]. At T=0.5, they become approximately [0.867,0.117,0.016]. At T=2, they become approximately [0.506,0.307,0.186]. Temperature changes the relative probabilities but not the rank order of distinct finite logits. If T=0 is supported by an API, it normally selects a greedy path as a special case; you must not divide by zero in the formula.

Combining filters: a pedagogical implementation may apply temperature scaling before deriving the top-p nucleus and apply top-k to remove lower-ranked candidates. Filtering order and whether providers also apply repetition or presence penalties first are provider-specific. Top-k selection is rank-invariant under positive temperature, but top-p set membership is not: p depends on temperature-scaled mass. Verify a provider’s contract before porting presets.

Production: lower T can help consistency in bounded extraction/classification but cannot repair missing information, flawed retrieval, unsupported claims, or a misaligned system instruction. T=0 is not a universal bitwise-determinism guarantee; hardware kernels, nondeterministic reductions, model routing/version changes, ties, or external tool state may change the output. For ideation you may accept wider diversity; for regulated decisions you should use deterministic validation, evidence checks, and task-specific evals regardless of T.

lessons.title: Top-k and Top-p (nucleus) sampling
lessons.subtitle: Compute candidate filtering correctly and understand dynamic vs fixed support sizes.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. For a toy probability vector, compute exact top-k and top-p allowed sets.
  2. Why must top-p include the token that crosses the cumulative threshold?
  3. How does temperature change nucleus membership?
  4. What guard is needed when all candidates have been masked?
sections.text: For a toy probability vector, compute exact top-k and top-p allowed sets. Why must top-p include the token that crosses the cumulative threshold? How does temperature change nucleus membership? What guard is needed when all candidates have been masked?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Top-k: keep the k highest-ranked eligible token scores and set others to −∞; renormalize the retained distribution. It imposes a fixed candidate count even when the distribution is extremely sharp or flat. Top-p: sort eligible tokens by descending probability, retain the smallest nonempty prefix whose cumulative original mass is at least p, then renormalize that prefix. It adapts the candidate count to probability concentration.

Sₚ = smallest ranked prefix S such that Σᵢ∈S P(i) ≥ p
P_filtered(i) = P(i) / Σⱼ∈S P(j)   if i∈S; otherwise 0

Example: P=[0.50,0.25,0.15,0.07,0.03]. Top-k with k=2 keeps the first two tokens, which renormalize to [0.667,0.333]. Top-p with p=0.80 retains three tokens because 0.50+0.25=0.75 is insufficient and adding 0.15 reaches 0.90; renormalized mass is approximately [0.556,0.278,0.167]. For p=0.5, only the first token survives. The threshold-crossing token must remain included.

  1. Start from valid logits, apply compatible penalties/masks/temperature per the chosen implementation.
  2. If using top-k, retain the highest k currently eligible tokens.
  3. Compute stable probabilities over remaining candidates.
  4. If using top-p, sort by descending probability and keep the smallest mass-covering prefix.
  5. Normalize again and sample using a controlled random-number generator.

Failure cases: small k can eliminate rare but necessary identifiers, JSON characters, domain terms, or end tokens; high p with a flat tail permits nonsensical low-probability tokens. Top-p can become effectively greedy with a highly peaked distribution. Some implementations use min_p, typical sampling, or nucleus threshold variations; do not assume identical parameter semantics across platforms. Sorting all V logits may be expensive, and top-k/top-p implementations often use partial selection/fused kernels. Compare quality under the actual task rubric and log the exact processor chain for reproducibility.

It imposes a fixed candidate count even when the distribution is extremely sharp or flat. Top-p: sort eligible tokens by descending probability, retain the smallest nonempty prefix whose cumulative original mass is at least p , then renormalize that prefix. It adapts the candidate count to probability concentration. Sₚ = smallest ranked prefix S such that Σᵢ∈S P(i) ≥ p P_filtered(i) = P(i) / Σⱼ∈S P(j)   if i∈S; otherwise 0 Example: P=[0.50,0.25,0.15,0.07,0.03] . Top-k with k=2 keeps the first two tokens, which renormalize to [0.667,0.333] . Top-p with p=0.80 retains three tokens because 0.50+0.25=0.75 is insufficient and adding 0.15 reaches 0.90 ; renormalized mass is approximately [0.556,0.278,0.167] . For p=0.5, only the first token survives. The threshold-crossing token must remain included. Start from valid logits, apply compatible penalties/masks/temperature per the chosen implementation. If using top-k, retain the highest k currently eligible tokens. Compute stable probabilities over remaining candidates. If using top-p, sort by descending probability and keep the smallest mass-covering prefix. Normalize again and sample using a controlled random-number generator. Failure cases: small k can eliminate rare but necessary identifiers, JSON characters, domain terms, or end tokens; high p with a flat tail permits nonsensical low-probability tokens. Top-p can become effectively greedy with a highly peaked distribution. Some implementations use min_p , typical sampling, or nucleus threshold variations; do not assume identical parameter semantics across platforms. Sorting all V logits may be expensive, and top-k/top-p implementations often use partial selection/fused kernels. Compare quality under the actual task rubric and log the exact processor chain for reproducibility.

I pay attention to the exact temperature/filter order, EOS eligibility, and schema-constrained outputs because overly aggressive filtering can eliminate valid completions.

lessons.title: Repetition penalties and decoding failure modes
lessons.subtitle: Distinguish repeated-token score processing from n-gram, lexical, and task-level consistency controls.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why can repetition penalties damage code generation and exact quotation?
  2. How does a sign-aware repetition penalty modify positive versus negative logits?
  3. What causes looping besides sampling parameters?
  4. How would you trace a repetition regression step by step?
sections.text: Why can repetition penalties damage code generation and exact quotation? How does a sign-aware repetition penalty modify positive versus negative logits? What causes looping besides sampling parameters? How would you trace a repetition regression step by step?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Repetition is not one defect. It may be a token loop (the the the), repeated n-gram, recursive plan/tool loop, repetitive sentence style, or an intentionally repeated identifier that a task requires. There are several distinct logit processors:

ControlMechanismTrade-off
Repetition penalty rFor seen token i, illustrative: zᵢ←zᵢ/r if zᵢ≥0, else zᵢ←r zᵢ (r>1).Suppresses seen tokens even when valid repetition is required.
Presence penaltySubtract a fixed amount if token appeared at least once.Reduces reuse, ignores frequency.
Frequency penaltySubtract amount proportional to prior token count.Progressively discourages frequent necessary tokens.
No-repeat n-gramHard-mask a token if it would complete a repeated n-gram.Can prohibit valid grammar, labels, or quotations.
Length/stop controlsStop at EOS, safe delimiter, or max tokens.Prevents endless runtime, not necessarily bad content.

Mechanism details: a sign-aware penalty avoids accidentally increasing the probability of a previously seen negative-logit token; the exact formula and whether it covers prompt tokens or only generated output are implementation-specific. Additive frequency penalties modify logits, not probabilities. They should be applied before sampling normalization. Detect repeated text both at token level and normalized sentence/task level because byte/subword boundaries hide semantic loops.

Diagnosis: log token_id, raw and processed logit ranks, cumulative history counts, stop reason, generation length, prompt suffix and temperature/top-p settings; correlate repetition with prompt template, model version, and tool observations. If repeated reasoning is caused by stale context or a controller reissuing tool calls, decoder penalties do not fix the underlying state machine. Prefer constrained planners, state-change checks, or task-specific termination. Evaluation: exact-n-gram repetition rate together with correctness, code compilation, named-entity preservation, and human preference. Lowering repetition at the cost of breaking data fidelity is not an improvement.

sections.html: I separate token-level degeneration from application-level loops. Repetition, presence, frequency, and no-repeat n-gram penalties modify candidate logits or masks, but they can damage identifiers, quotations, and source fidelity. I inspect token traces and compare repetition rates with task correctness, and use explicit agent-state/stop logic when the repetition is caused by a workflow loop rather than token sampling.

Instrument: token-level run length, repeated 3/4-gram rates, summarization input ordering, output truncation, and model stop reason. Hypotheses: generation loop, duplicated retrieved context, missing EOS, or failure in streaming stop detection. Options: deduplicate inputs, fix stop conditions, tune penalties with exemptions, or impose a finite structured outline. Acceptance: repetition decreases while key numbers, citations, and factual fidelity remain stable or improve.

lessons.title: EOS, stop tokens, and stop sequences
lessons.subtitle: Define model token termination, API string matching, streaming boundaries, and completion invariants.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Differentiate an EOS token ID from a user-supplied multi-character stop string.
  2. Why can a streamed stop delimiter straddle two network chunks?
  3. How do max_new_tokens and context-window limits interact?
  4. What happens when stop filtering accidentally removes a structural JSON delimiter?
sections.text: Differentiate an EOS token ID from a user-supplied multi-character stop string. Why can a streamed stop delimiter straddle two network chunks? How do max_new_tokens and context-window limits interact? What happens when stop filtering accidentally removes a structural JSON delimiter?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
EOS is a learned special token ID. At each autoregressive step the model may assign a probability to an end-of-sequence token. When sampled, a decoder stops according to its completion protocol. Chat models may use multiple trained end markers (end-of-message/end-of-turn/tool handoff) whose meanings are determined by model and conversation format. A stop sequence is typically an API-level text string or token pattern checked by the serving layer, and may encode into multiple tokens. A max token budget is an external hard limit; reaching it is not semantic completion.

Stop mechanismWho controls itWhat to validate
EOS/end-turn tokenModel vocabulary + trained chat templateCorrect token IDs, template, and generation stop reason
Stop sequenceClient/server decoderStreaming prefix buffers, overlaps, and unicode boundaries
Output token limitServing runtimeTruncation vs completed semantic unit
Context limitModel/runtime capacityInput+generation positional budget, caching/eviction logic
Tool-call endStructured control protocolCorrect turn handoff, no user-visible partial tool syntax

Streaming algorithm: the wire layer may deliver arbitrary byte chunks; token/text boundaries are not guaranteed. An incremental matcher needs to keep a suffix long enough to match a stop prefix that spans chunks. For string stop patterns, maintain an incremental UTF-8 decoder and a bounded suffix/prefix automaton; avoid emitting text that may later be recognized as part of a withheld stop delimiter. Never assume chunk.includes(stop) catches cross-chunk matches. The exact output-inclusion behavior for stop strings is API-specific.

Failure modes: prematurely stopping inside code/quotes, EOS being masked out, misconfigured chat template leaking control tokens, never-ending generation due to disabled EOS, and JSON validity failures when tokens are cut off by max budget. Always expose a structured finish reason (model end, external stop, length, error, tool handoff). A downstream caller should treat “length” as an incomplete result, not a success.

sections.html: The EOS token is a model-specific learned token that can terminate generation. A stop sequence is a serving-layer pattern, possibly spanning multiple tokens or streamed chunks; it requires incremental matching. Output-token and context limits are independent hard safeguards, and a length-limited response can be incomplete. I preserve finish reasons so callers can distinguish clean completion from truncation or a tool handoff.

  2. Is stop sequence always a single token? Strong answer: no, tokenizer may split it.
  3. What if model emits EOS inside an incomplete JSON object? Strong answer: treat as incomplete/invalid and recover safely.

Mechanism → trade-off → concrete verification. Do not hand-wave.

sections.heading: Production scenario
sections.html: Incident: A streaming transcript service includes internal </turn> delimiters in responses when traffic is routed through a new proxy. Hypothesis: the proxy flushes substrings before stop matching and misses split delimiters. Instrument: raw token stream in secure tests, transport chunk boundaries, finish reason, and final assembled response. Fix: incremental delimiter matcher and withholding buffer; unit-test every split position, repeated prefixes, and multibyte UTF-8. Acceptance: zero leaked delimiters on exhaustive synthetic splits and no spurious dropped content.

• EOS is a token ID; API stop strings may span multiple tokens/stream chunks.
  • Length-limit termination is incomplete, not equivalent to successful EOS.
  • Streaming must preserve incremental matching state and report finish reason.

lessons.title: Context windows: architectural versus practical limits
lessons.subtitle: Distinguish model-position capacity, request budgets, attention/KV costs, and actual usable context quality.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Does a model advertised at 128k context necessarily handle 128k input plus 128k output?
  2. Why is context length a quality problem as well as a memory/latency problem?
  3. Estimate KV-cache growth with N, L, H_kv, and head dimension.
  4. What happens if the runtime context setting exceeds the model’s trained regime?
sections.text: Does a model advertised at 128k context necessarily handle 128k input plus 128k output? Why is context length a quality problem as well as a memory/latency problem? Estimate KV-cache growth with N, L, H_kv, and head dimension. What happens if the runtime context setting exceeds the model’s trained regime?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
The context window is the amount of token-position history the model/runtime can attend over within its supported configuration, generally including current prompt tokens and generated continuation. Different APIs may reserve output capacity separately; apply the actual service's documented limits rather than assuming the advertised number is available for all of the input. Position mechanisms (learned positions, RoPE scaling/interpolation, sliding-window layers), KV capacity, server prefill policies, and model training all affect the operational maximum.

N_system + N_history + N_retrieval + N_user + N_overhead + N_reserved_output ≤ W

Why it gets expensive: dense prefill attention interaction count is O(N²) per layer, while per-token KV cache storage grows approximately linearly with context length: bytes_KV ≈ 2 × B × N × L × H_kv × d_head × bytes_per_element for normal full-cache layout. For illustrative B=1,N=32,768,L=32,H_kv=8,d_head=128,bpe=2, KV memory is 4 GiB. Compute time also depends on model width, hardware and attention algorithm; actual allocator overhead may increase peak usage. Long-context attention quality is not guaranteed by size alone.

Model capacity vs effective accuracy: a model can accept long sequences but be less reliable at finding, integrating, or comparing facts buried far apart, with positional extrapolation or attention sink effects complicating behavior. The “lost in the middle” literature reports task- and model-dependent position sensitivity; do not call it universal. Evaluate at different N and gold-evidence positions, including distractors and conflicting facts.

Decision options: pass everything for small stable corpora when reliability and price allow; perform retrieval, deterministic filtering, document hierarchy, windowing, or recursive aggregation for large corpora. Compare retrieval misses against long-context misses; RAG introduces its own chunking and citation failures. If an end-to-end task truly needs cross-document global analysis, hybrid retrieval plus selected comprehensive passages may win over a tiny context budget. Extrapolating a RoPE context beyond validated lengths must be treated as a quality experiment, not a free config upgrade.

lessons.title: Truncation, sliding windows, and summarization
lessons.subtitle: Implement bounded-context strategies without silently losing obligations, entity links, or factual provenance.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Compare oldest-first truncation, recency windows, retrieval, and hierarchical summaries.
  2. How would you guarantee system instructions survive context compaction?
  3. What should an incremental summary store besides prose?
  4. How can you know whether compaction lost information needed later?
sections.text: Compare oldest-first truncation, recency windows, retrieval, and hierarchical summaries. How would you guarantee system instructions survive context compaction? What should an incremental summary store besides prose? How can you know whether compaction lost information needed later?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
When requests grow: keep a protected high-priority system/developer envelope; budget the current task, user turn, tool schema and output reserve; then allocate remaining tokens among recent history, durable user-approved facts, summaries, and retrieved evidence. Naive tail truncation is fast and simple, but can remove critical constraints established early. Head+tail retention protects introductions and recency but misses middle dependencies. Sliding windows are especially effective for local conversational continuity but not long-range global tasks.

StrategyOperational behaviorFailure pattern
Oldest-first truncateDrop prior messages once budget exceededForgets commitments and earlier entity definitions
Sliding recent-turn windowKeep most recent K turns/tokensCannot answer queries about older details
Running summaryReplace prior text with compact representationFact distortion; subtle constraints overwritten
Retrievable episode storageIndex older turns, fetch relevant segmentsRetrieval miss, staleness and access mismatches
Hierarchical map-reduceSummarize chunks then aggregate summariesGlobal relationships lost across boundaries

Practical compaction state: track immutable instructions, current task and constraints, entities/aliases, factual claims with source IDs/timestamps, unresolved questions, explicit user preferences (with authorized retention), pending actions, and per-field uncertainty. Summaries should mark unsupported inferences, and old source excerpts should remain retrievable when the application has permission. Store summary version and token count. Distinguish message logs (durable DB), model current context (ephemeral text), and GPU KV cache (inference optimization); these are not interchangeable memories.

Pipeline: tokenize request exactly → choose safety margin → preserve high-priority messages → select recent turns and relevant old episodes → compact older content into bounded structured summary → validate invariants → pack evidence under budget → generate. For extremely long source docs, use heading-aware chunking and aggregation with evidence provenance, plus extraction-first strategies for table values. Evaluate recall of old commitments, exact identifiers, topic-switch resilience, answer faithfulness, context cost, and latency; measure against a full-history oracle on selected tests rather than simply tracking tokens saved.

Evaluate recall of old commitments, exact identifiers, topic-switch resilience, answer faithfulness, context cost, and latency; measure against a full-history oracle on selected tests rather than simply tracking tokens saved.

sections.html: I treat context compaction as a state-preservation problem, not just text shortening. I always reserve instructions, current request and output budget; preserve exact entities, commitments and source pointers; then select recent turns plus relevant older events or a structured summary. I validate that important facts survive compaction and test conversational continuity and factual accuracy, since a cheaper shorter prompt is not necessarily a better system.

lessons.title: Lost in the middle and long-context reliability
lessons.subtitle: Measure evidence-position effects, distractor sensitivity, and interventions that preserve grounding.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How would you design an experiment demonstrating lost-in-the-middle rather than retrieval failure?
  2. Why can beginning/end positions be easier for some models than middle positions?
  3. Why is reordering evidence not always harmless?
  4. How do you separate model long-context errors from bad document packing?
sections.text: How would you design an experiment demonstrating lost-in-the-middle rather than retrieval failure? Why can beginning/end positions be easier for some models than middle positions? Why is reordering evidence not always harmless? How do you separate model long-context errors from bad document packing?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Phenomenon: in some long-context retrieval/QA evaluations, model accuracy varies depending on where decisive evidence appears—often lower when relevant evidence is buried among unrelated middle passages. This is an observed behavior of particular models/tasks/configurations, not a theorem that every Transformer always ignores the middle. Training distributions, attention patterns, distractors, recency/primacy effects, positional generalization, and prompt formatting may contribute.

Controlled test: construct the same answerable query, the same unique supporting passage, and a fixed set of distractors. Move only the position of that passage (front, quarter, middle, three-quarter, end), holding total token length, wording, and answer target constant. Repeat across multiple randomized fixtures and lengths; measure exact answer accuracy, citation precision, hallucination, and abstention. Evaluate with and without retrieval/reranking and with source-position annotations. This distinguishes retrieval not finding a passage from generator failing to use an already-present passage.

accuracy(position, N) = correctly_answered(position,N) / tested_queries(position,N)

Mitigations: rank and limit evidence instead of dumping everything, put core evidence near the relevant user instruction when robust in tested model, reorganize into labeled sections and short citations, ask targeted per-document extraction then compose a justified response, or use explicit tool retrieval. Splitting complex requests into multiple reasoned subqueries can help if you preserve linking evidence. Beware: rearranging documents can alter chronology, temporal precedence, regulatory priority, or negations; attach metadata and test conflicting sources. Front-loading answer-bearing snippets may improve a single benchmark but can cause evidence cherry-picking if the prompt omits counterexamples.

Performance: shortening irrelevant context reduces prefill and KV usage, but retrieval/reranking incurs its own latency and recall risk. Report p95 input tokens, retrieval recall@k, citation validity, answer exactness, and cost stratified by passage position. A “passage moved to first slot” toy demonstration is only an illustration until model measurements substantiate it.

sections.html: Lost in the middle is a task-dependent decrease in using relevant evidence at certain positions in long input contexts. To diagnose it, I hold query, passage, distractors, and total length constant while moving the gold passage across positions; then compare answer accuracy and citations. I usually test selective retrieval/reranking and labeled evidence packing, but I verify that reordering does not destroy chronology or source priority.

sections.html:
1. Does the model architecture mathematically force a U-shaped accuracy curve? Strong answer: no, empirical phenomenon.

  3. Why might retrieval worsen things? Strong answer: evidence recall miss and hidden access/freshness constraints.

Mechanism → trade-off → concrete verification. Do not hand-wave.

Hypotheses: source text parse errors, distractor conflicts, position sensitivity, or evidence drowning. Instrument: original evidence offsets, packed positions, question type, cited source versions, and long-context score by position bucket. Mitigate: clause-aware extraction/reranking, explicit provenance, and evidence-bucket tests. Acceptance: narrow the accuracy gap between position buckets while maintaining citation and contradiction-handling quality under identical test cases.

  • Evaluate gold evidence placement while controlling every other input.
  • Prioritize relevance and provenance; do not treat reordering as universally safe.

lessons.title: Multi-turn conversation and long-lived context
lessons.subtitle: Maintain conversation state, tool results, topic switches, and cache correctness under bounded prompts.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Describe state flow for a chatbot that handles multiple topics over 100 turns.
  2. What is the difference between message history, summary memory, vector memory, and KV cache?
  3. How do you handle a user switching topics and later returning to an unresolved task?
  4. What does concurrency-safe conversation state require?
sections.text: Describe state flow for a chatbot that handles multiple topics over 100 turns. What is the difference between message history, summary memory, vector memory, and KV cache? How do you handle a user switching topics and later returning to an unresolved task? What does concurrency-safe conversation state require?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
A reliable chat system has more state than a prompt string. Its durable store has message IDs, roles, timestamps, attachment access scopes, tool-call IDs/results, conversation/thread ownership, and versioned summaries. A request handler loads and authorizes that state, builds a model-specific chat template, budgets tokens, selects relevant evidence, invokes the model, streams output, and only commits the new assistant turn when appropriate. GPU KV cache is an ephemeral acceleration layer for repeated prefix computation; it is not a durable conversation database.

request_t = pack(policy, active_task, recent_turns, summaries, retrieved_episodes, user_t, tools)

Topic switching: identify active intent and entity references without assuming the previous subject always carries over. Keep a structured task ledger with pending goals, current state, dependent facts, and last update. When the user returns to an older task, retrieve the relevant episode/task summary rather than concatenating hundreds of turns. Resolve ambiguous pronouns carefully. Names or instructions from one workspace/tenant must not silently leak into another.

Operational details: use optimistic versions or per-thread serialization to avoid two concurrent requests both reading the same state and overwriting each other. Record message IDs before async tool execution; make side-effecting tool calls idempotent where possible. If a model times out mid-stream, track partial response state and safely resume/retry without duplicating external actions. Tool outputs are untrusted content and should not be promoted to system instructions. Apply ACL filters both when retrieving memories and when rendering citations.

Evaluation: long-horizon entity resolution, exact-value retention, topic-switch recovery, multithread isolation, stale-summary detection, tool-call replay protection, and per-turn latency. Separate input packing quality from retrieval quality and generation quality by logging token breakdown and sources. A 100-turn chatbot can still handle turn 101 by storing state intelligently without replaying all 100 turns verbatim.

sections.html: I store authorized conversation history and task state durably, then assemble a bounded per-turn prompt using policies, the active goal, recent messages, and relevant retrieved past episodes. I keep GPU KV caches separate because they only accelerate inference. For topic switches, I track unresolved tasks and rehydrate the right context. I also protect against concurrent writes, tool retries, cross-tenant leakage, and misleading summaries.

  2. What if two messages are sent simultaneously? Strong answer: version/serialization/merge policy and tool idempotency.
  3. How do you prevent memory leakage? Strong answer: scoped storage, ACL checks, audit trail, and injection boundaries.

Mechanism → trade-off → concrete verification. Do not hand-wave.

Acceptance: high topic-switch accuracy on designed multi-turn tests, zero cross-user leakage, and no doubled side effects during retries.

  • KV cache is inference reuse, not user memory.

lessons.title: Structured outputs and JSON Schema constraints
lessons.subtitle: Compare prompting, post-validation, repair retries, tool calls, and token-level grammar constraints.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How does constrained decoding differ from “Please output valid JSON”?
  2. Why can syntactically valid JSON still be wrong or unsafe?
  3. How do tokenizers complicate token-level JSON grammar constraints?
  4. What do you do when the model refuses or emits an incomplete object?
sections.text: How does constrained decoding differ from “Please output valid JSON”? Why can syntactically valid JSON still be wrong or unsafe? How do tokenizers complicate token-level JSON grammar constraints? What do you do when the model refuses or emits an incomplete object?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Four levels of enforcement: (1) prompt instructions and few-shot examples encourage a shape; (2) postprocessing parses and validates after generation; (3) structured-output or tool-call APIs impose a contract through provider mechanisms; (4) grammar-/automaton-constrained decoding masks next-token candidates that would make a prefix invalid under a grammar/schema-aware state. In practice these layers can be combined. They give different guarantees.

allowed_t = { token i | parse_prefix(output₍≤t₎ + decode(i)) remains valid and completable }

Decoder mechanism: compile the JSON/schema constraints into a parser-state representation (FSM/CFG/structured validator as appropriate), track the incremental output prefix, ask the tokenizer-aware constraint engine which token IDs remain legal, mask all others to −∞, then sample. A single token can contain multiple characters (punctuation, escape sequences), so constraints must validate the decoded token string and UTF-8/tokenizer semantics, not assume one character per token. If the grammar excludes all candidates, raise a controlled error rather than inventing a compliant value.

JSON Schema caveats: real engines support different subsets: required fields, enums, types, nesting, unions, references, patterns, and length constraints may vary. Valid JSON is only syntax; schema-valid content can still fabricate invoice_amount, violate a permission boundary, mis-map an entity, or contradict evidence. Use domain validation (range, cross-field checks, database references, provenance) after parsing. Streaming output may be incomplete until EOS; don't apply an entire-object validator to every intermediate chunk as though it were final.

Retry and failure control: classify failures (parse, schema, domain, unsupported evidence, provider refusal, length). Retry boundedly with targeted error feedback only when safe, and avoid rerunning side-effecting tools. For strict contracts, let users edit invalid or missing fields rather than defaulting to confident invented values. Metrics: parse-success %, schema-valid %, semantic field precision/recall, hallucinated-field %, rejection/abstention rate, retries per request, added latency and cost.

  3. What can go wrong with automatic repair? Strong answer: hidden semantic changes, repeated API cost, replaying side effects.
