lessons.title: Mixtral and DeepSeek architecture case studies
lessons.subtitle: Read architecture reports critically and compare mechanisms, not model marketing.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How exactly does Mixtral route tokens while sharing the attention layers?
  2. Contrast Mixtral GQA with DeepSeek-V3 MLA and DeepSeekMoE.
  3. What do total vs activated parameter counts say—and not say—about inference cost?
sections.text: How exactly does Mixtral route tokens while sharing the attention layers? Contrast Mixtral GQA with DeepSeek-V3 MLA and DeepSeekMoE. What do total vs activated parameter counts say—and not say—about inference cost?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism & data flow

The original Mixtral 8×7B model uses eight feedforward experts per MoE layer and selects two for each token; self-attention is shared. Its published parameter accounting is ~47B total and ~13B active per token. DeepSeek-V3 reports 671B total, ~37B activated per token, a DeepSeekMoE layout with routed and shared experts, and Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA). MLA projects input hidden states into a shared compressed KV latent stored for decoding, with an additional decoupled positional key component, instead of ordinary K,V per attention head. DeepSeek-V3 also reports an auxiliary-loss-free load-balancing strategy. DeepSeek-R1 is primarily a reasoning-oriented training/post-training story; do not confuse it with a unique attention kernel.

Algorithms and mathematics

Mixtral MoE layer y=Σ_{e∈Top2(router(x))}g_e FFN_e(x). DeepSeek-V3 MLA cached state per token schematically c_KV ∈ R[d_c] plus position-dependent k_R ∈ R[d_R], rather than 2×Hkv×Dh full K,V vectors. Actual parameter/kernel savings require specific architecture dimensions.

Architecture & alternatives

Mixtral shows top-2 routing with GQA in a conventional decoder. DeepSeek-V3 combines expert sparsity with latent KV compression. GQA shares KV heads; MLA uses a low-rank KV representation, which has different implementation and training semantics.

Implementation or pseudocode

Inspect official model config and publication version. Distinguish published architecture from provider-served model aliases, quantization, expert parallel layouts and undocumented serving patches.

Compute, memory, latency and cost

Total model weights still need placement; active FLOPs, memory bandwidth and communication drive time per token. Do not infer latency or VRAM directly from “37B activated.”

Failures, misconceptions and mitigations

Common errors: 8×7B=56B for Mixtral ignores shared parameters; MLA is not equivalent to storing GQA K/V. Treat performance claims across different tests/hardware as non-comparable without matched evaluation.

lessons.title: Recursive Language Models (RLMs)
lessons.subtitle: Treat large input as an external environment that can be inspected programmatically.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why is the RLM concept more accurately a recursive inference strategy than a new attention layer?
  2. How does code-based slicing reduce context pressure?
  3. What happens when recursive subcalls lose context or repeat work?
sections.text: Why is the RLM concept more accurately a recursive inference strategy than a new attention layer? How does code-based slicing reduce context pressure? What happens when recursive subcalls lose context or repeat work?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism & data flow

In the 2025 Recursive Language Models work, a model uses a controller to inspect a long prompt or data artifact as an external environment instead of packing it all into the immediate model context. It may write operations to search, subset, summarize or transform the stored text and recursively invoke the LLM on smaller pieces. Intermediate results return to the controller which integrates them. Recursive scope, call limits and evidence provenance matter; the model cannot reason about bytes never visited unless its tool chooses them.

Algorithms and mathematics

Total work ≈ Σ_i tokens(subcall_i)×model_cost + controller/tool overhead. The maximum context per individual call can remain below C even if external data length N≫C; this is an orchestration property, not a change to per-call Transformer attention.

Architecture & alternatives

RAG retrieves indexed evidence efficiently when the query has a clear retrieval signal. RLM-style recursive exploration can suit complex aggregation, long code/data inspection and hierarchical analyses but incurs controller and subcall variance.

Implementation or pseudocode

Use immutable source handles, line/offset references, deterministic slicing tools and recursion depth/token budgets. Record tool traces, subcall inputs, source provenance and partial outputs. Avoid executing untrusted generated code without a sandbox.

Compute, memory, latency and cost

Additional tool calls and recursive LLM requests may cost more and have long-tail latency. Cache repeated subresults; parallelize independent queries only when correctness permits.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigations

Failure cases: missed relevant slice, circular recursion, false summaries, prompt injection from source content, and uncertain provenance. “Arbitrarily long” means the controller can access long external input, not guaranteed exhaustive reasoning.

lessons.title: Diffusion Language Models vs autoregressive generation
lessons.subtitle: Explain masked iterative refinement without assuming a free parallel-speed advantage.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. What is the forward corruption process in a masked diffusion LM?
  2. How does iterative denoising differ from causal left-to-right sampling?
  3. When is parallel token updating genuinely faster end-to-end?
sections.text: What is the forward corruption process in a masked diffusion LM? How does iterative denoising differ from causal left-to-right sampling? When is parallel token updating genuinely faster end-to-end?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism & data flow

Masked discrete diffusion language models such as LLaDA train on text corrupted by masking a selected fraction of token positions. A model predicts original tokens at masked locations under the corruption distribution. Generation starts from many masked positions and repeatedly predicts replacements or remasks uncertain positions over a schedule, allowing non-left-to-right editing. This differs from autoregressive factorization p(x)=∏p(x_t|x_<t). The number of refinement steps, predictions per step, remasking policy and conditional guidance determine latency and quality.

Algorithms and mathematics

Autoregressive: log pθ(x₁:N)=Σ_t log pθ(x_t|x_<t). Illustrative masked diffusion training: sample mask fraction τ, sample Mτ, minimize E[Σ_{i∈Mτ}w(τ)·(−log pθ(x_i|corrupted x,τ))]; weighting and exact objective vary by diffusion formulation.

Architecture & alternatives

AR generation naturally streams one token at a time with KV reuse; diffusion can update tokens in parallel but performs multiple full-sequence denoising passes. DLM may help controllable editing or bidirectional refinement; serving kernels and task quality decide feasibility.

Implementation or pseudocode

Implement a toy masked denoising loop with a fixed-length sequence and confidence remasking. Verify no gold-token leakage in train targets and benchmark final accuracy under varying step counts.

Compute, memory, latency and cost

An N-token diffusion sample with K denoising steps can still cost K Transformer passes over N positions; do not infer speedup from predicting several tokens at once. AR decode uses incremental KV but has sequential dependency.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigations

DLM outputs can oscillate under remasking; stopping too early reduces coherence. Evaluation must cover perplexity comparability caveats, controllability, end-to-end tokens/sec and factual accuracy—not architectural novelty alone.

title: Inference & Infrastructure
description: Serving engines, hardware economics, latency, and scaling.

lessons.title: Prefill vs. decode: computation and data flow
lessons.subtitle: Distinguish bulk prompt processing from one-token incremental inference.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Trace a chat completion from admission through prefill to the final streamed token.
  2. Why does the prefill stage compute K/V for all input tokens but decode only for the newest token?
  3. Where do tokenization, queueing, detokenization and EOS handling show up in TTFT?
sections.text: Trace a chat completion from admission through prefill to the final streamed token. Why does the prefill stage compute K/V for all input tokens but decode only for the newest token? Where do tokenization, queueing, detokenization and EOS handling show up in TTFT?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism & data flow

At request arrival, the router formats chat messages and tokenizes them, queues the request, and assigns a scheduler slot. Prefill runs the prompt through all Transformer layers using causally masked attention. It produces hidden states and K/V tensors for valid prompt positions, inserts their K/V into the cache, and obtains a distribution for the first output token. Decode then loops: sample the next token, run one-token Q/K/V and FFN projections, append new K/V, attend with Q against cached history, stream detokenized bytes, and stop at EOS, stop sequence or length budget. Mixed batches may contain prefill chunks and decoding requests simultaneously. Prompt-prefix caching can avoid recomputing *matching* stable prefixes; it is not universal response caching.

Equations and assumptions

Prefill attention score pairs per head = N(N+1)/2 for full causal N-token input (efficient kernels need not materialize them). Decode step t attends to N+t cached keys. Generation latency ≈ queue + prefill + Σ_t decode(t) + network/stream overhead. The exact first-token reporting boundary is service-defined.

Architecture alternatives

Whole-prompt prefill offers efficient GEMMs but can block decoding if scheduled monolithically. Chunked prefill interleaves work; prefill/decode separation isolates resource allocation but introduces KV transfer.

Implementation & instrumentation

Instrument tokenizer time, prompt length, queue wait, prefill kernel time, KV allocation, per-step decode and network flush. Separate end-of-prefill from first externally delivered token. Guard capacity at admission.

Latency, memory, compute & cost

Prefill has parallel positions and sizable matrix operations; decode is sequential across generated tokens and repeatedly reads weight/KV state. Output length can dominate end-to-end time despite short prompts.

Edge cases & failure modes

Don’t say prefill “generates all tokens”; it computes prompt hidden states and normally initiates the first sample. Cached prefixes must match positions, attention masks, model version and tenancy rules.

lessons.title: Why prefill is usually compute-bound and decode often bandwidth-bound
lessons.subtitle: Derive arithmetic intensity instead of repeating a slogan.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Use a roofline argument to explain a low-batch decode bottleneck.
  2. What changes the compute/bandwidth balance as concurrent batch size rises?
  3. Why can attention KV reads dominate long-context decoding even with GQA?
sections.text: Use a roofline argument to explain a low-batch decode bottleneck. What changes the compute/bandwidth balance as concurrent batch size rises? Why can attention KV reads dominate long-context decoding even with GQA?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism & data flow

For a dense linear layer Y=XW, a large prefill input X has many rows, enabling a GPU to reuse W across a large matrix multiplication; math per fetched weight rises. At decode batch one, a thin vector-matrix operation still needs to read most W but does relatively little work per weight. HBM traffic can cap tokens/sec even if tensor cores are mostly idle. Decode also streams historical KV through attention; as context and active sequences grow, KV bytes/step grow. At high concurrency, batched decode turns vectors into GEMMs and raises weight reuse, so “decode is always bandwidth-bound” is not universally true.

Equations and assumptions

Idealized dense matmul: FLOPs ≈ 2·M·K·N; bytes for weights ≈ K·N·b. Weight-only arithmetic intensity ≈ 2M/b FLOP/byte (ignores input/output, caches and fusion). Roofline time ≥ max(FLOPs / achievable_FLOPs_s, bytes / achievable_HBM_B_s).

Architecture alternatives

More batching often boosts total throughput but can raise individual request latency. Quantizing weights reduces bytes but dequantization and unsupported kernels may erase gains. Faster memory devices or better partitioning help bandwidth-bound decode.

Implementation & instrumentation

Collect profiler roofline evidence: SM/tensor-core occupancy, achieved HBM bandwidth, GEMM shapes, kernel launch time and tokens/second at batch sizes 1, 4, 16. Profile attention/MLP separately.

Latency, memory, compute & cost

When effective arithmetic intensity sits below the hardware ridge point (peak compute/peak bandwidth), memory transfer limits a kernel; above it, compute may dominate. Hardware theoretical peaks are upper bounds, not observed performance.

Edge cases & failure modes

An algorithm can move between regimes by batch/sequence length, quantization, kernel fusion, weight residency and parallelism. Keep units straight: GB/s decimal vs GiB/s binary.

lessons.title: TTFT, TPOT, end-to-end latency, and throughput
lessons.subtitle: Treat latency percentiles and throughput as different workload-level quantities.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Define TTFT, TPOT, ITL, request throughput and token throughput precisely.
  2. Explain why average TPOT can hide a single 2-second inter-token stall.
  3. Design a fair benchmark comparing engines with different request lengths and arrival processes.
sections.text: Define TTFT, TPOT, ITL, request throughput and token throughput precisely. Explain why average TPOT can hide a single 2-second inter-token stall. Design a fair benchmark comparing engines with different request lengths and arrival processes.

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism & data flow

For each user request, record request arrival, queue exit, first streamed output, every subsequent token delivery, and final completed response. TTFT is time from request start to the first observable token, often including processing and network; its definition must be consistent. Inter-token latency (ITL) is elapsed time between consecutive token arrivals. TPOT is commonly output-generation time divided by number of subsequent tokens; implementations vary in denominators, so state the convention. Throughput may mean requests/s, total generated tokens/s, or combined input + output tokens/s. Compare distributions by prompt/output length, concurrent requests, cache hits and cold/warm models.

Equations and assumptions

For output tokens delivered at t₁…tₒ, TTFT=t₁−t_request; ITLᵢ=tᵢ−tᵢ₋₁ for i≥2; TPOT≈(tₒ−t₁)/(O−1) for O>1; response latency=tₒ−t_request. Little’s law L=λW holds under steady stable conditions.

Architecture alternatives

Low TTFT and low TPOT may trade off under scheduler priorities: decode-first protects live streams, while aggressive prefill improves admission and fresh-request TTFT. Tail latency is user-facing, not optional.

Implementation & instrumentation

Use timestamp instrumentation at model server and client for SSE chunks; do not confuse raw tokens with arbitrary byte chunks. Benchmark open-loop offered-load curves as well as fixed-concurrency closed-loop tests.

Latency, memory, compute & cost

At fixed load, increasing active concurrency can improve generated tokens/s until memory, scheduler or HBM saturates; beyond saturation queues and tail latencies explode. Report goodput: rate meeting quality and latency SLO.

Edge cases & failure modes

Token streaming may coalesce multiple tokens; first byte can be metadata rather than text. Cross-provider TTFT measurements may use different clock boundaries.

lessons.title: Why the first token can be slower
lessons.subtitle: Localize first-token delays without claiming each first token is inherently more expensive.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Enumerate first-token path costs and identify which change under prompt caching.
  2. When might the first token be faster than subsequent tokens?
  3. What experiments separate cold-start from long-prompt TTFT?
sections.text: Enumerate first-token path costs and identify which change under prompt caching. When might the first token be faster than subsequent tokens? What experiments separate cold-start from long-prompt TTFT?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism & data flow

First-token delivery typically requires request validation, prompt construction, tokenization, scheduling, potentially cold model loads or graph capture, full prompt prefill, a first output projection and sampling, then network write. Subsequent steps reuse prompt KV and process only a new input token, but their attention history grows. For very short prompts or heavily loaded mixed traffic, it is possible for TTFT to be small and future tokens to stall due to scheduling or memory pressure. A tokenizer bottleneck does not disappear by deploying FlashAttention.

Equations and assumptions

TTFT = queue + preprocess + cold-start(optional) + prefill + first-token sample/delivery. For full attention prefill compute grows roughly quadratically with N in attention scores; dense projection FLOPs grow linearly with N (for fixed model dims).

Architecture alternatives

Reducing prompt size or leveraging valid prefix cache tackles prefill. Prewarming weights and compilation handles cold starts. Scheduling changes tackle queue delay. Streaming transport must flush appropriately.

Implementation & instrumentation

Run four matched traces: cold/warm model × cache-hit/miss, with short/long prompts. Measure each stage at server and client boundaries.

Latency, memory, compute & cost

A long 32k prompt with 10-token answer is first-token dominated; a 128-token prompt with 4k-token answer is decode dominated. Different optimization budgets follow.

Edge cases & failure modes

Comparing first and later token *latency* is meaningful only under the same concurrency and output streaming semantics. Cache hit is not synonymous with answer hit.

lessons.title: KV caching and incremental decode
lessons.subtitle: Calculate work avoided by reusing past keys and values.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Explain precisely which tensors are cached per layer and which are recomputed.
  2. Why does a KV cache not eliminate attention work over historical positions?
  3. Demonstrate cached vs uncached output parity with causal masking.
sections.text: Explain precisely which tensors are cached per layer and which are recomputed. Why does a KV cache not eliminate attention work over historical positions? Demonstrate cached vs uncached output parity with causal masking.

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism & data flow

At each decoder layer, the input prompt produces key and value projections for all positions. On subsequent generation steps, previous K/V remain valid because causal self-attention prevents past hidden states from depending on future generated tokens. The new token produces its Q, K and V; its query attends to cached K/V plus current K/V. Keeping caches avoids repeated historical projections and full-prefix Transformer passes. A cache must be keyed to the exact model, positions, attention mask, rope offsets, and request/prefix identity. Paged KV allocators manage where tensors reside, not the mathematical K/V contents.

Equations and assumptions

Per-request KV elements = 2 × n_layers × sequence_tokens × n_kv_heads × head_dim. Multiply by bytes/value and active requests for memory. With a fixed cache, new-token self-attention score work per layer/head is O(T) rather than rerunning full O(T²) attention for every prefix.

Architecture alternatives

Cache choices include dynamic contiguous, static reserved, block-paged, shared-prefix, quantized, sliding and CPU-offloaded variants. Offloading relieves VRAM but adds transfer latency.

Implementation & instrumentation

Validate against an uncached full forward on tiny fixed input using identical weights, positions, causal mask and deterministic sampling; test prefix changes, forks, cancellations and model upgrades.

Latency, memory, compute & cost

KV cost increases linearly with live cached token count for full attention, and memory admission is limited by sum across active sequences, not just maximum sequence length.

Edge cases & failure modes

Reusing K/V across different tenants or altered prompt content can leak context. Naively retaining entire multimodal KV also grows quickly. A cache may improve throughput while reducing max batch due to memory.

lessons.title: GPU memory: weights, activations, workspace and KV
lessons.subtitle: Build a realistic serving budget before selecting hardware.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Can an 8B BF16 model fit into a 16-GiB GPU in production? Justify every reserve.
  2. What is the difference between allocated, reserved and free GPU memory?
  3. How do batch, token count, attention layout and quantization alter memory?
sections.text: Can an 8B BF16 model fit into a 16-GiB GPU in production? Justify every reserve. What is the difference between allocated, reserved and free GPU memory? How do batch, token count, attention layout and quantization alter memory?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism & data flow

Weight memory is parameters × stored bits plus quantization scales/zeros, tied weights, padding and miscellaneous tensors. KV memory scales with total active tokens and KV-head dimensions. Inference activations are smaller than in training because no backward graph is kept, but prefill intermediate tensors, logits, attention kernels, temporary workspaces, CUDA graphs, fragmentation and runtime library state still use VRAM. Tensor parallelism shards portions of weights and caches, but interconnect buffers and unsharded modules remain. Budget headroom for output-token growth, requeues and bursts, not just average token count.

Equations and assumptions

VRAM_budget ≥ params×weight_bytes + Σ_requests(2L·Hkv·Dh·Treq·kv_bytes) + prefill_activations + workspaces + allocator_slack + graph_memory. Example: 8B BF16 ≈ 16.0 GB ≈ 14.9 GiB weights alone; 32L/8KV/128/BF16/8,192 tokens = 1 GiB cache.

Architecture alternatives

Quantization lowers weight capacity but can lower quality; GQA lowers KV specifically; paging reduces fragmentation; CPU KV offload swaps bandwidth for memory. All can coexist.

Implementation & instrumentation

Collect actual `memory_allocated`, `memory_reserved`, nvidia-smi process bytes, GPU traces and peak-per-stage usage. Measure at maximum allowed prompt, output and concurrent request mix.

Latency, memory, compute & cost

Peak memory can be greater than the sum of static formulas during prefill. At target utilization U, reserve (1−U) for dynamic spikes and deployment variability rather than treating nominal GPU size as free.

Edge cases & failure modes

“8B” is sometimes approximate and excludes multimodal encoders or heads; INT4 theoretical weights are not necessarily 4 bits/parameter after metadata.

lessons.title: Quantization: FP32, FP16, BF16, INT8 and INT4
lessons.subtitle: Understand numerical formats and why fewer bits do not guarantee faster inference.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Compare FP16 exponent limits with BF16 exponent limits.
  2. Why are INT8 and INT4 not drop-in equivalents to floating-point formats?
  3. When should weights, activations and KV cache use different precisions?
sections.text: Compare FP16 exponent limits with BF16 exponent limits. Why are INT8 and INT4 not drop-in equivalents to floating-point formats? When should weights, activations and KV cache use different precisions?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism & data flow

FP32 has 8 exponent bits and 23 explicit fraction bits; FP16 has 5 exponent and 10 fraction bits; BF16 has 8 exponent and 7 fraction bits. Lower-bit integer quantization maps floating values into discrete codes using scale and possibly zero point, often per tensor, channel or group. Inference dequantizes or uses fused integer GEMM kernels. Weight-only INT4 is common when weights dominate memory, whereas activations and KV may need their own calibration and kernel support. Mixed-precision accumulations matter for numerical stability.

Equations and assumptions

Symmetric quant: q=clip(round(x/s), qmin, qmax), x_hat=s·q. Idealized weight GiB = P·bits/(8·2³⁰), plus scales/zero-points/metadata. BF16 and FP16 both use 2 bytes/value but have different dynamic range/precision.

Architecture alternatives

BF16 is often robust for large activation ranges; FP16 can offer greater mantissa precision near unity but narrower range. INT8 vs INT4 trades compression for quantization error; FP8/FP4 and mixed-kernel variants depend on GPU support.

Implementation & instrumentation

Use representative calibration/evaluation data; compare per-layer outlier distributions and sensitive attention/output heads, run structured-output and reasoning regressions, check actual chosen kernel and quantization metadata.

Latency, memory, compute & cost

Compression of model weights can allow more replicas or longer KV, but dequant arithmetic and unfused kernels can hurt p95 TPOT; different batch sizes may reverse the result.

Edge cases & failure modes

Quantization is not a guaranteed 4× RAM reduction for 16→4 bits due to metadata and runtime overhead, nor a guaranteed speedup. Distinguish accuracy and calibration failure from implementation bugs.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. What statistics does PTQ calibration collect and how are scales selected?
  2. How does fake quantization in QAT expose the optimizer to quantization error?
  3. When is QAT cost justified over mixed-precision PTQ?
sections.text: What statistics does PTQ calibration collect and how are scales selected? How does fake quantization in QAT expose the optimizer to quantization error? When is QAT cost justified over mixed-precision PTQ?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism & data flow

Post-training quantization (PTQ) takes a pretrained checkpoint and selects scales/zero points using weight statistics and optionally representative activation traces; deployment runs a quantized/fused graph. In quantization-aware training (QAT), forward operations simulate low-precision rounding/clipping—often via fake-quant operations—while trainable parameters stay in higher precision. Straight-through estimators approximate gradients through discrete rounding. QAT can adapt weight distributions to the quantizer but needs training resources, data and careful verification.

Equations and assumptions

For symmetric per-channel weights W_c, s_c ≈ max|W_c|/(2^{b−1}−1). FakeQuant(W)=s·round(clip(W/s)). Straight-through gradient often approximates ∂FakeQuant/∂W as 1 within clipping range and 0 outside (variant-dependent).

Architecture alternatives

PTQ is cheaper and preferable if quality stays within tolerance; QAT can help aggressive low-bit deployment when data/compute are available. Weight-only and weight+activation PTQ have different calibration needs.

Implementation & instrumentation

Create a representative calibration set from production input distributions; compare per-channel vs per-group scales and quantization-aware finetune only for failing layers. Measure task-level effects, not just weight MSE.

Latency, memory, compute & cost

PTQ requires limited calibration time; QAT adds gradient storage, optimizer state and training cost. Total cost must include serving savings amortized over expected token volume.

Edge cases & failure modes

QAT does not magically restore all low-bit quality; train/serve kernel mismatch or nonrepresentative calibration remains harmful. Beware embedding/outlier layers and embedding-logit ties.

lessons.title: Continuous batching and request scheduling
lessons.subtitle: Track changing membership, token budgets and fairness.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why does static batch padding waste work for variable-length generations?
  2. Design an iteration-level scheduler with a max batched-token budget.
  3. What can starve when decode requests are always prioritized?
sections.text: Why does static batch padding waste work for variable-length generations? Design an iteration-level scheduler with a max batched-token budget. What can starve when decode requests are always prioritized?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism & data flow

Static batching waits for all members and pads shorter requests; one long generation delays the entire group. Continuous or in-flight batching reevaluates admissions and completions at every scheduling iteration. New requests enter as capacity frees; finished or canceled sequences leave. The scheduler accounts for active KV blocks, prompt chunks, decode tokens and priority/fairness. A decode-first policy can stabilize existing streams while starving new prompts, so waiting-age limits or weighted fairness are needed. Correctness requires protecting each sequence’s mask, position offsets and KV block ownership.

Equations and assumptions

Iteration token budget: Σ_i decode_token_cost_i + Σ_j prefill_chunk_tokens_j ≤ scheduler_max_tokens. KV admissibility: Σ_requests (current_cached_tokens + reserved_growth) × bytes/token ≤ KV_budget (plus allocator slack).

Architecture alternatives

Static batching can be adequate for homogeneous offline workloads. Continuous batching excels for mixed latency-sensitive online traffic. Priority policies trade starvation risk and service tier isolation.

Implementation & instrumentation

Build a toy scheduler with waiting/running/finished queues; track request IDs, positions, EOS, cancellation, block allocation and preemption. Instrument requests/step, queue wait, preemptions and tokens/step.

Latency, memory, compute & cost

Increased concurrency improves weight reuse up to bandwidth/compute saturation but may increase memory pressure and per-user ITL. Throughput optimum rarely coincides with best solo latency.

Edge cases & failure modes

Blind first-come-first-served can cause head-of-line blocking; greedy decode-first can starve prefill; too-large batches cause KV OOM and thrashing.

lessons.title: Chunked prefill and prefill-decode disaggregation
lessons.subtitle: Diagnose and isolate interference between long prompts and streaming tokens.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How does chunked prefill improve tail ITL in mixed workloads?
  2. What is transferred between prefill and decode workers in a disaggregated deployment?
  3. Under what conditions can disaggregation reduce performance?
sections.text: How does chunked prefill improve tail ITL in mixed workloads? What is transferred between prefill and decode workers in a disaggregated deployment? Under what conditions can disaggregation reduce performance?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism & data flow

A naive scheduler runs a long prefill operation before servicing decode streams, causing inter-token stalls. Chunked prefill partitions the prompt into sequential chunks and schedules bounded work between decode iterations; attention for each chunk accesses earlier cached chunks under correct causal masking. Prefill-decode (P/D) disaggregation uses separate worker pools: prefill workers build KV and first-token state, then move or expose KV to decode workers via connectors/network/storage. This permits independent resource profiles, routing and scheduling but adds KV transfer and orchestration overhead.

Equations and assumptions

Chunk budget: prefix = ceil(N / chunk_tokens) chunk operations; each chunk must attend causally to preceding K/V. Rough transfer bytes for disaggregation ≈ 2L·Hkv·Dh·N·kv_bytes (unless compression/shared prefix alters it). Total TTFT may include prefill+KV transfer+remote dispatch.

Architecture alternatives

Chunked prefill is simpler when same GPUs can handle both phases. Disaggregation is useful when phase interference dominates and infrastructure/network permits fast KV transfer. It is not inherently a throughput improvement; system shape matters.

Implementation & instrumentation

Test large/small chunk sizes, KV connector latency, flow control and retry idempotency; record per-stage TTFT and p99 ITL, transfer bytes/s and worker utilization.

Latency, memory, compute & cost

Too-small chunks add overhead; too-large chunks reintroduce stalls. Disaggregation may require high-bandwidth GPU networking and duplicated scheduler/worker capacity.

Edge cases & failure modes

KV transfer compatibility requires matching model version, dtype, cache layout and position metadata. vLLM documentation explicitly notes experimental disaggregated prefill and does not promise increased throughput.

lessons.title: Speculative decoding: draft models, Medusa, EAGLE, N-grams
lessons.subtitle: Explain exact verification, acceptance and when speculation is counterproductive.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How does draft-and-verify preserve a target model’s output distribution?
  2. Compare Medusa heads, EAGLE hidden-state proposals and N-gram drafting.
  3. What determines the break-even point for speculation?
sections.text: How does draft-and-verify preserve a target model’s output distribution? Compare Medusa heads, EAGLE hidden-state proposals and N-gram drafting. What determines the break-even point for speculation?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism & data flow

Classic speculative decoding uses a cheaper draft model to propose K tokens autoregressively; a target model evaluates those positions together. Acceptance/rejection is computed from the draft and target conditional distributions, with a correction distribution after rejection; with correct sampling math, the final distribution matches the target. Greedy verification compares argmax paths rather than claiming stochastic exactness. Medusa adds candidate heads/tree proposals to a base model; EAGLE proposes in feature or hidden-state space; N-gram speculation uses matches in recent text or prompt history without a trained draft model. Real systems manage tree masks, cache rollback and acceptance stats.

Equations and assumptions

For conditional per-step acceptance aᵢ, expected accepted prefix length E[A]=Σ_{i=1}^K∏_{j=1}^i aⱼ. Speedup depends on target verification cost, draft cost, accepted tokens and batch/hardware occupancy; A is not the same as generated tokens per iteration (a correction/bonus token may be included).

Architecture alternatives

Model-based drafts work where a small model predicts target-compatible continuations; N-gram drafts help repetitive text/code. Medusa/EAGLE require supported heads/training and kernel integration. Speculation can lose at large batches or poor acceptance.

Implementation & instrumentation

Implement a reference verifier for tiny categorical distributions to test sampling parity statistically, log accepted/proposed ratio, time per verification, rollback and output token rate.

Latency, memory, compute & cost

Accepting multiple tokens per expensive target pass can reduce latency, but overhead and cache traffic may negate it. Report net p95 TPOT and dollar cost rather than “draft acceptance” alone.

Edge cases & failure modes

Using naive accept-on-top-1 in a stochastic sampler changes the target distribution. Failure to undo rejected tentative KV corrupts later output. Tree verification and sampler settings must match.

lessons.title: Tensor, pipeline and data parallelism
lessons.subtitle: Distinguish memory sharding, execution scheduling and replica scaling.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. What communication does tensor parallel attention/MLP introduce?
  2. Why does pipeline parallelism need microbatches to achieve utilization?
  3. Which parallelism technique actually increases serving replicas?
sections.text: What communication does tensor parallel attention/MLP introduce? Why does pipeline parallelism need microbatches to achieve utilization? Which parallelism technique actually increases serving replicas?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism & data flow

Tensor parallelism (TP) partitions matrix weight dimensions across GPUs. Column-parallel and row-parallel layers require all-gather or all-reduce at certain boundaries; each token crosses interconnect links. Pipeline parallelism (PP) assigns layer ranges to GPU stages; microbatching can overlap stages but incurs bubbles, activation transfers and stage imbalance. Data parallelism (DP) replicates model-serving workers so different requests run independently; load balancing chooses replicas, each requiring its own compatible weight and KV memory. Expert parallelism shards MoE experts and adds all-to-all routing as a separate consideration.

Equations and assumptions

Idealized TP per-GPU weight ≈ W/P, plus replication/comm buffers. PP bubble fraction for m microbatches across p identical stages ≈ (p−1)/(m+p−1) under a simple synchronous 1F1B-like timing model (not a universal serving formula). Aggregate replicas R ideally offer R×single-replica capacity only until upstream/shared bottlenecks intervene.

Architecture alternatives

TP is used when layers/weights do not fit, often within high-bandwidth NVLink; PP can fit deeper models across devices but may hurt small-batch latency; DP is simplest for scale-out when full replicas fit.

Implementation & instrumentation

Map weight shards and attention head ownership explicitly; test layer collectives, NCCL timeouts and network topology. Profile communication overlap and imbalanced GPU stages.

Latency, memory, compute & cost

Parallelism is not free: interconnect latency, KV partitioning, host synchronization and pipeline bubbles can outweigh compute savings. Model size and context determine the best mix.

Edge cases & failure modes

“Add GPUs = linear speedup” is invalid. Even if weights shard perfectly, embeddings, logits, KV metadata and buffers may not; per-request decode often suffers from collective latency.

lessons.title: vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, llama.cpp and Ollama
lessons.subtitle: Choose a serving stack based on measured deployment needs, not library popularity.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How do vLLM paged KV and SGLang prefix caching improve serving utilization?
  2. Where might TensorRT-LLM win and where does its deployment complexity matter?
  3. Why are llama.cpp and Ollama not interchangeable with a multi-node inference service?
sections.text: How do vLLM paged KV and SGLang prefix caching improve serving utilization? Where might TensorRT-LLM win and where does its deployment complexity matter? Why are llama.cpp and Ollama not interchangeable with a multi-node inference service?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism & data flow

vLLM targets throughput-oriented GPU serving with paged KV allocation, continuous scheduling, prefix caching and optional disaggregated prefill. SGLang combines efficient serving with structured generation and prefix/radix-cache scheduling; its supported attention/speculation backends vary by device and version. TensorRT-LLM provides NVIDIA-oriented optimized runtime kernels, quantization, parallelism, in-flight batching and advanced inference features, often requiring more deployment-specific tuning. llama.cpp supports GGUF-based lightweight inference across CPU/GPU and constrained or local hardware. Ollama packages model lifecycle and local serving ergonomically, frequently using llama.cpp-family components but is a product/runtime layer rather than a replacement for a production router, scheduler and SLO stack.

Equations and assumptions

Serving decision score must reflect weighted quality constraints and measured p95 TTFT/TPOT, generated tokens/s, failure rate, engineering hours and total cost. Any feature matrix is version/architecture dependent; verify current supported model, kernels and license.

Architecture alternatives

Managed GPU fleet: shortlist vLLM/SGLang/TensorRT-LLM with equivalent model + workload. Local/privacy-first prototype: llama.cpp or Ollama often lowers setup burden. Use format compatibility and observability to choose.

Implementation & instrumentation

lessons.title: GPU utilization, bandwidth and roofline profiling
lessons.subtitle: Connect low-level telemetry to a causal bottleneck hypothesis.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why can GPU utilization be 100% while useful throughput is low?
  2. Calculate arithmetic intensity and identify the memory/compute roof.
  3. How can kernel launch overhead dominate short decode iterations?
sections.text: Why can GPU utilization be 100% while useful throughput is low? Calculate arithmetic intensity and identify the memory/compute roof. How can kernel launch overhead dominate short decode iterations?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism & data flow

Utilization typically reports that a device had some work scheduled over sampling intervals; it does not establish high tensor-core efficiency. Useful profiling includes per-kernel achieved FLOP/s, SM occupancy, HBM bandwidth, L2 hit rate, memory reads, synchronization stalls, CPU scheduler work and end-to-end TTFT/ITL. Plot performance against arithmetic intensity and compare to compute and bandwidth roofs. In mixed traffic, separate prefill GEMMs, decode GEMV/GEMM, attention KV reads, sampling kernels and communication.

Equations and assumptions

Operational roofline: attainable FLOP/s ≤ min(peak_compute_FLOP/s, arithmetic_intensity FLOP/byte × bandwidth bytes/s). Estimate time ≥ max(FLOPs / attainable_compute, bytes / attainable_bandwidth). Distinguish achieved bandwidth from vendor peak.

Architecture alternatives

Kernel fusion can reduce launch and memory traffic; batching can increase arithmetic intensity; FP8/INT8 kernels may improve throughput only when dimensions and GPU support align.

Implementation & instrumentation

Profile PyTorch/Nsight traces with NVTX spans for queue/prefill/decode and token batch shape. Link kernel metrics to p95 per-request spans and memory allocator events.

Latency, memory, compute & cost

Weight bytes are usually read once per kernel launch, not necessarily once per request when batching. Effective token bandwidth must include KV, activations, collectives and cache effects.

Edge cases & failure modes

100% GPU util can mask stalled kernels or low tensor-core use. Floating-point theoretical peaks without actual dtype/kernel and batch assumptions produce misleading estimates.

lessons.title: Self-hosted inference vs managed LLM APIs
lessons.subtitle: Compare operations and economics with quality and privacy constraints.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. What factors determine the cost crossover between API inference and self-hosting?
  2. How do data residency and audit requirements affect the decision?
  3. What are the hidden costs of running your own GPU fleet?
sections.text: What factors determine the cost crossover between API inference and self-hosting? How do data residency and audit requirements affect the decision? What are the hidden costs of running your own GPU fleet?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism & data flow

Managed APIs transfer model hosting, some serving optimization, scaling and availability responsibilities to a provider, but have token-price variability, rate limits, data routing constraints, dependencies and uncertain hardware/internal telemetry. Self-hosting offers checkpoint and runtime control, local data boundaries and tuning opportunities but requires GPU provisioning, capacity planning, failover, on-call support, red-team processes, monitoring, model upgrades, security and quality evaluation. Hybrid routing can direct predictable/sensitive workloads locally and bursty/complex cases to approved APIs if policies allow.

Equations and assumptions

Illustrative self-host compute $/1M output tokens ≈ (instance $/hour)/(useful generated tok/s × 3600) × 10⁶, then add idle ratio, replicas, networking, storage and support. API cost ≈ input_tokens×input_price + output_tokens×output_price + cache/tool charges (under contract).

Architecture alternatives

APIs tend to be simpler for uncertain low volume or rapidly changing models; self-hosting can help high steady volume, residency needs or proprietary model adaptation, but only with measured efficiency.

Implementation & instrumentation

Estimate load by input/output distributions and peak RPS; compare price per successful completed workflow rather than token price alone. Include provider failover plans, data handling approvals and deprecation migration.

Latency, memory, compute & cost

Idle reserved GPU capacity can dominate spend. One self-host model rarely matches the model family, tool ecosystem or SLA of every API model; routing costs and quality differences matter.

Edge cases & failure modes

Rate limit quotas and API prices change. Treat “no data retention” or regulatory compliance as contract-specific, never infer from architecture.

lessons.title: Capacity planning, concurrency and inference cost
lessons.subtitle: Build an admission and scale model with uncertainty and explicit SLO gates.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Estimate concurrency from 20 RPS and 3-second mean latency; what assumptions apply?
  2. Build a peak-load KV budget using token lengths rather than request count.
  3. How can autoscaling based only on GPU utilization fail?
sections.text: Estimate concurrency from 20 RPS and 3-second mean latency; what assumptions apply? Build a peak-load KV budget using token lengths rather than request count. How can autoscaling based only on GPU utilization fail?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism & data flow

Start with input/output token distributions, arrival rate by time, average and tail service time, allowed queue wait, model mixture and quality SLOs. Little’s law estimates average in-flight requests for a stable system. Translate active contexts into KV bytes and account for prefill workspace, weight residency and fragmentation. A queue dispatcher admits only requests that fit token/VRAM reservations; autoscaling watches outstanding work, goodput, latency and instance warm-up time, not just averaged GPU occupancy. Separate peak capacity from efficient average batch size.

Equations and assumptions

L = λW for stable long-run flow. Active KV bytes ≈ Σ_r 2·layers·kv_heads·head_dim·(input_r+generated_r)·bytes/value. Capacity tokens ≈ usable_KV_bytes / bytes_per_token. Cost/request ≈ GPU-instance-hours×$/hour / completed_successful_requests, plus API/network/ops.

Architecture alternatives

Queue vs reject decisions: bounded queue protects GPUs but increases TTFT, 429/load shedding preserves SLA for admitted traffic, autoscaling adds warm capacity after startup delay. Route simpler tasks to smaller models where eval proves adequacy.

Implementation & instrumentation

Load-test open-loop Poisson/bursty arrivals and length-heavy tails; log admission denials, wait ages, KV reserved/live tokens, TTFT/TPOT, output failures and replica spin-up. Deploy with canary and rollback thresholds.

Latency, memory, compute & cost

Nonlinearity matters: latency and memory explode near saturation. More decoding requests increase weight amortization but grow KV simultaneously. Plan safety margin against worst expected percentile, not just mean.

Edge cases & failure modes

Linear extrapolation from a batch=1 benchmark fails under mixed prefill. Percentile SLOs cannot be deduced from averages. Do not invent latency numbers without hardware profiling.

title: Production Reliability
description: Debugging, evaluation, observability, safety, and emerging methods.

lessons.title: Diagnose incorrect or inconsistent LLM outputs
lessons.subtitle: Separate request reproducibility, factual accuracy, nondeterministic sampling, prompt state, and model drift.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. A customer receives two different answers to the same prompt. What exact evidence do you collect before debugging?
  2. How would you isolate decoding stochasticity from provider changes or retrieval nondeterminism?
  3. How do you distinguish a model failure from a prompt-template or tool-output regression?
sections.text: A customer receives two different answers to the same prompt. What exact evidence do you collect before debugging? How would you isolate decoding stochasticity from provider changes or retrieval nondeterminism? How do you distinguish a model failure from a prompt-template or tool-output regression?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism and data flow

Model output is conditional on the COMPLETE effective request: system/developer messages, chat history, retrieved text, tools, model snapshot, sampler, seed (when supported), and inference backend. Capture redacted request identifiers, model and prompt versions, tool calls, sampled tokens where permitted, outputs and trace timing. Reproduce a golden input with retrieval snapshot and fixed parameter configuration; minimize the failing case. Classify error as knowledge/retrieval gap, reasoning, instruction hierarchy conflict, formatting, unsafe tool use or evaluation artifact. Compare failing vs passing traces one variable at a time. Temperature zero or a seed may reduce variance, but GPU kernels, tie-breaking, batching and API changes can still prevent bitwise reproducibility.

Mathematics and invariants

For N independently sampled responses: empirical failure rate p̂ = failures/N. For regression contrast use Δ = p̂_new − p̂_base with confidence intervals, ideally on paired prompt cases; a single divergent output cannot establish a degradation.

Architecture and alternatives

Start with deterministic preprocessing and stable retrieval + prompts before fine-tuning. Escalate to better model, tool verification or SFT only when failure slices prove simpler controls insufficient.

Implementation and instrumentation

Store privacy-safe trace IDs, prompt hash, effective template hash, model checkpoint, sampler config, retrieval document IDs/versions, token counts and structured evaluator results. Use stratified test cases with human adjudication.

Latency, memory, cost and scaling

Repeatability requires data/version pinning and an eval budget; exhaustive logging raises storage and PII exposure risk. Sample traces and redact sensitive inputs while retaining correlation IDs.

Failure modes and traps

Avoid claiming all nondeterminism is temperature; provider routing, safety filters, retrieval indexes, compaction, lossy OCR and schema changes can alter effective context. Never debug from screenshots alone.

lessons.title: Debug structured-output failures and malformed JSON
lessons.subtitle: Differentiate syntactic JSON, schema compliance, business semantics, and partial streamed output.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why can a JSON-mode response parse successfully but still fail downstream?
  2. How do constrained decoding and schema validation differ?
  3. What does your retry strategy do when a tool call has already caused a side effect?
sections.text: Why can a JSON-mode response parse successfully but still fail downstream? How do constrained decoding and schema validation differ? What does your retry strategy do when a tool call has already caused a side effect?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism and data flow

Structured output has multiple gates: (1) transport and streamed frame completeness, (2) valid JSON syntax, (3) schema-level types, required fields, enums, ranges, and extra-field policy, (4) semantic invariants such as sum of marks or consistent IDs. Prefer model-native constrained decoding for a supported JSON Schema subset where available, followed by application-side validation. Streaming JSON is often incomplete until the finish event; buffer or use incremental parsers that track object boundaries. A refusal or truncation is not the same as a malformed payload. On failure, return a typed error or repair only with budgeted, non-side-effecting retries. Persist idempotency tokens before tool execution and never replay a completed side effect merely to fix serialization.

Mathematics and invariants

End-to-end structured success = valid_transport ∧ valid_syntax ∧ valid_schema ∧ valid_semantics. Track conditional failure counts for each gate, not a single parse-error bucket.

Architecture and alternatives

Schema-first generation is stronger than prompting “return JSON”; locally validated parser retries are a fallback if provider lacks constrained decoding. For safety-critical commands, no free-form auto-repair without approval.

Implementation and instrumentation

Illustrative schema: {status: enum["ok","abstain"], answer: string|null, evidence_ids: string[]}; reject unknown keys, validate evidence IDs against an authorized list, and enforce status="abstain" ⇒ answer=null. For Python use json.loads plus explicit schema/domain validators.

Latency, memory, cost and scaling

Retries add latency and token cost; bad retry design causes retry storms. Schema compilation and constrained decoding can have startup/complexity costs. Monitor parse-fail rate and number of repair attempts.

Failure modes and traps

A syntactically valid but wrong ID is still unsafe. Streaming chunks are not independent complete JSON documents. Supported JSON Schema features depend on model/provider; do not promise arbitrary regular expressions or complex constraints.

lessons.title: Reduce hallucinations and implement evidence-based abstention
lessons.subtitle: Engineer evidence-conditioned answers and an explicit unanswerable path, not only better prose.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How do you know a retrieved passage actually supports an answer?
  2. What should an LLM do when sources disagree or contain no answer?
  3. How can you tune abstention without sacrificing all useful coverage?
sections.text: How do you know a retrieved passage actually supports an answer? What should an LLM do when sources disagree or contain no answer? How can you tune abstention without sacrificing all useful coverage?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism and data flow

A grounded QA system retrieves candidate sources using authorization-aware search, reranks passages, checks whether any evidence entails the requested claim, and either answers with traceable spans or abstains. An LLM can fabricate citations even when provided evidence, so cited spans must be checked against retrieved document text and version IDs. Separate retrieval miss, unsupported generation, false entailment and unsupported authority claims. A confidence or answerability classifier may be calibrated using labeled answerable/unanswerable cases; prompt text saying “say I do not know” is not a guarantee. For contradictory evidence, disclose disagreement and source recency rather than silently picking one.

Mathematics and invariants

Selective accuracy(τ) = correct_answered(τ)/answered(τ); coverage(τ) = answered(τ)/all_questions. Evaluate risk-coverage curves as abstention threshold τ varies. Calibration must use held-out data.

Architecture and alternatives

RAG addresses missing/updated facts; entailment or verification addresses unsupported claims; deterministic tools cover arithmetic and database truth. Fine-tuning style alone cannot guarantee factual grounding.

Implementation and instrumentation

Store citations as {document_id, version, span_start, span_end}; verify each quoted phrase substring/source access. Add answerability labels and counterfactual unanswerable prompts to golden sets.

Latency, memory, cost and scaling

Verifier and reranker calls can dominate latency; evaluate marginal gains by domain and cache where safe. Overly aggressive abstention lowers utility even when hallucination rate falls.

Failure modes and traps

High embedding similarity does not imply entailment. A linked source may contradict a claim. A model self-reported numeric confidence is not necessarily calibrated.

lessons.title: Handle outdated model knowledge and deprecated code generation
lessons.subtitle: Choose live retrieval, version pinning, and executable validation instead of pretending model weights auto-update.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. A code assistant writes deprecated SDK syntax. What fixes the root cause?
  2. How do you safely answer questions about current policy or API versions?
  3. What should you do if the latest documentation is unavailable?
sections.text: A code assistant writes deprecated SDK syntax. What fixes the root cause? How do you safely answer questions about current policy or API versions? What should you do if the latest documentation is unavailable?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism and data flow

Base-model knowledge is bounded by training and adaptation; prompting for “latest” does not fetch current data. Route queries requiring freshness to official documentation, known releases or authenticated APIs with citation and retrieval timestamps. Tag sources with publication time, effective date, library version, and validity window. For code, use the project’s actual dependency lockfile, resolve docs for its pinned version, compile/test generated code in a sandbox with permission-safe tools, and return diagnostics rather than untested guarantees. Handle doc conflicts by version and release channel; do not assume a later publication supersedes the active runtime.

Mathematics and invariants

Freshness age = now − source_verified_at. An effective policy version must satisfy valid_from ≤ decision_time < valid_to (if valid_to exists); recency alone is insufficient.

Architecture and alternatives

Retrieval and official tools excel at mutable facts. Fine-tuning can improve syntax/style but should not be the only source of changing release APIs or legal requirements.

Implementation and instrumentation

Provide dependency-aware search with allowlisted vendor docs, package metadata, code lint/type checks and integration tests. Record doc URI, SDK version, timestamp and test command exit status.

Latency, memory, cost and scaling

Extra retrieval and sandbox testing cost latency; asynchronous background refresh can pre-index authoritative docs, but must keep permission/version boundaries. Cache keys include requested version.

Failure modes and traps

An API endpoint existing in the latest guide may not exist in production. Web page freshness, effective date and user environment are different clocks.

lessons.title: Diagnose tokenizer inefficiencies in specialized domains
lessons.subtitle: Measure token inflation, routing failures and the real costs of domain vocabulary fragmentation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why can a medically meaningful term be split into many subwords?
  2. How would you prove tokenizer inefficiency is causing money or accuracy issues?
  3. Would you retrain the tokenizer of a frozen base LLM?
sections.text: Why can a medically meaningful term be split into many subwords? How would you prove tokenizer inefficiency is causing money or accuracy issues? Would you retrain the tokenizer of a frozen base LLM?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism and data flow

Tokenizers map bytes or normalized strings into vocabulary IDs according to learned segmentation and merge rules. Rare domain identifiers, low-resource scripts, code symbols, and Unicode normalization can produce longer token sequences. Token inflation increases prefill length, attention/KV demand, context truncation risk, and billable tokens. But a fragmented term may still be correctly represented through multiple subwords; splitting alone does not prove low accuracy. Audit corpus token-per-character/byte distributions by language and term class; compare segmentations across candidate tokenizers and test end-task retrieval/generation metrics.

Mathematics and invariants

Inflation ratio R = tokens_domain / tokens_baseline for a matched corpus, or tokens per UTF-8 byte. Transformer full-attention prefill pair count scales ≈ N² per head, though optimized kernels reduce memory materialization.

Architecture and alternatives

Keep the pretrained tokenizer unless you can jointly adapt embeddings/model weights and safely migrate serving tools. Domain abbreviations can be handled via preprocessing, aliases, retrieval and terminology lexicons.

Implementation and instrumentation

Inspect exact Unicode input bytes and normalized output; run tokenizer.encode over realistic logs, outliers and multilingual/code fixtures. For any tokenizer change, update embedding matrices and retrain/adapt embeddings; migrate dependent indexes and templates.

Latency, memory, cost and scaling

Vocabulary expansion changes checkpoint compatibility and serving dimensions, may break prompt caching or fine-tunes. Increased token length inflates runtime, not just input billing.

Failure modes and traps

Byte-level tokenization generally avoids truly unknown bytes but may use more tokens; WordPiece systems can use [UNK]. Avoid asserting all tokenizers share one unknown-token policy.

lessons.title: Resolve context-window exhaustion in long-document applications
lessons.subtitle: Build explicit budgeting, retrieval, progressive summarization, and invariant preservation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How would you budget context when tools, conversation, documents and output all compete for tokens?
  2. When does retrieval outperform simply increasing the context window?
  3. How do you stop context compaction from deleting a safety-critical approval?
sections.text: How would you budget context when tools, conversation, documents and output all compete for tokens? When does retrieval outperform simply increasing the context window? How do you stop context compaction from deleting a safety-critical approval?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism and data flow

Count the true rendered model input: system/developer instructions, tool specs and responses, current task, selected documents, chat history, delimiters and reserve for generation. Reject or compact BEFORE overflow, not after the API throws. For long evidence, chunk and retrieve with metadata; use hierarchical map/reduce summaries with retained citations and a versioned manifest of omitted material. Maintain a separate durable state store for approved actions, constraints, access boundaries and current objective. If the task requires global document coverage, use multi-pass extraction rather than treating top-k retrieval as complete.

Mathematics and invariants

Budget constraint: T_system + T_history + T_tools + T_evidence + T_output_reserved + T_margin ≤ T_context. For ordinary full attention, arithmetic work includes O(N² d) attention terms; actual memory depends on kernels and cache.

Architecture and alternatives

Long-context stuffing minimizes infrastructure but can degrade relevance. RAG trades retrieval omissions for lower context cost; hierarchical summarization trades exactness for compression. Use hybrid designs when appropriate.

Implementation and instrumentation

Write a deterministic context assembler with priority tiers, document IDs, source spans, per-segment token counts and a hard output reserve. Test adversarial and late-position facts; never summarize secrets into a less protected store.

Latency, memory, cost and scaling

Long prompts raise TTFT and memory; repeated large histories increase cost. Chunking and summarization add preprocessing overhead and can accumulate factual drift.

Failure modes and traps

A reported context limit is not a guarantee of reliable utilization; “lost in the middle” is an empirical quality effect. Sliding windows do not magically preserve discarded evidence.

lessons.title: Optimize KV cache memory under high concurrency
lessons.subtitle: Translate architecture into per-token bytes and use token-aware admission.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Estimate KV memory for a 32-layer, 8-KV-head, 128-dim, BF16 model at 32k tokens.
  2. Why can page allocation help fragmentation but not eliminate KV growth?
  3. What risks arise when evicting a KV span while the model is still decoding?
sections.text: Estimate KV memory for a 32-layer, 8-KV-head, 128-dim, BF16 model at 32k tokens. Why can page allocation help fragmentation but not eliminate KV growth? What risks arise when evicting a KV span while the model is still decoding?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism and data flow

At every layer, each retained token stores one K vector and one V vector per KV head; memory scales with active sequences, layers, KV heads, head dimension and element bytes. GQA reduces KV heads relative to MHA while preserving query heads, lowering stored bytes, though weights/attention compute have other costs. With paged KV, a logical token sequence maps to physical fixed-size blocks; free blocks are recycled on completion. Prefix reuse can share immutable KV blocks only with exact matching model, position and authorization constraints. Eviction/quantization/offload can save VRAM but introduces accuracy, bandwidth and implementation trade-offs.

Mathematics and invariants

KV bytes = 2 × L × H_kv × d_head × N_live_tokens × b. Example: 2×32×8×128×32768×2 = 4,294,967,296 bytes = 4 GiB for one 32k-token sequence (no metadata/headroom).

Architecture and alternatives

Options: limit maximum active tokens, reduce batch size, use a GQA/MQA-compatible model, supported KV quantization, paging, prefix sharing or CPU offload. Rank by quality impact and measured bottleneck.

Implementation and instrumentation

Track resident and allocated KV blocks, fragmentation, per-request live token count, prefix reuse, swap/page faults and OOM. Account for active generation growth, allocator overhead, weights, CUDA graph buffers and activation workspaces.

Latency, memory, cost and scaling

Per-sequence 4 GiB × concurrency grows fast; 20 conversations at max context would need 80 GiB KV alone in this example. Aggressive offload adds HBM/PCIe copy stalls.

Failure modes and traps

Do not confuse KV cache with logits cache or per-step compute elimination; one-token queries still attend to historical keys. PagedAttention is primarily a memory management mechanism, not an asymptotic attention complexity reduction.

lessons.title: Handle OOM from long-context attention
lessons.subtitle: Distinguish quadratic attention-score materialization from weight/KV/activation OOM.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why can a naive attention kernel OOM at long sequence lengths even when weights fit?
  2. How does FlashAttention change HBM traffic without making exact full attention O(N)?
  3. When is sliding-window attention a functional change rather than a free optimization?
sections.text: Why can a naive attention kernel OOM at long sequence lengths even when weights fit? How does FlashAttention change HBM traffic without making exact full attention O(N)? When is sliding-window attention a functional change rather than a free optimization?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism and data flow

Naively computing QKᵀ for N tokens makes an N×N matrix per head, and softmax/probability intermediates can require O(HN²) HBM bytes. IO-aware tiled kernels compute exact attention with online softmax statistics while avoiding persistent full score matrices. Complexity of exact full attention arithmetic remains O(N² d), even if memory footprint falls. Training additionally stores/derives activations and gradients; activation checkpointing trades recompute for memory. In decode, a KV cache requires O(N) storage per stream, and attention scans keys linearly per generated step. Sliding-window/local attention reduces interactions by limiting visibility and may lose long-range facts.

Mathematics and invariants

Naive fp16 score buffer alone ≈ B×H×N²×2 bytes; with B=1,H=32,N=32768 this is 64 GiB (single materialized score tensor). Exact full-attention FLOPs still scale approximately with N².

Architecture and alternatives

Use optimized exact kernels first if quality requires global attention; try sparse/sliding patterns only with a model supporting the mask and evaluated long-range tasks. Reduce prompt length, microbatch and parallelism when appropriate.

Implementation and instrumentation

Profile peak allocated/reserved VRAM by kernel and stage, prefill vs decode, activation checkpointing, unsupported attention fallback, masking shape and backend. Stress high-head/high-length cases.

Latency, memory, cost and scaling

FlashAttention may shift the OOM source to KV, weights or workspaces. Larger context can overwhelm latency even when memory fits. Alternative masks change inductive bias and usually require matching training.

Failure modes and traps

Do not claim FlashAttention reduces asymptotic exact attention FLOPs to O(N); it reduces memory traffic and peak intermediate storage. A GPU OOM stack trace may point downstream from the earlier allocation.

lessons.title: Diagnose latency spikes, throughput degradation, and excessive token usage
lessons.subtitle: Connect user-visible percentiles to queueing, stages, bandwidth and unnecessary context.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Your p99 doubled after a deploy without changing model weights. Where do you look?
  2. Why does GPU utilization alone not tell you whether the model is fast?
  3. How do you detect a guardrail or agent loop that repeatedly resends unchanged context?
sections.text: Your p99 doubled after a deploy without changing model weights. Where do you look? Why does GPU utilization alone not tell you whether the model is fast? How do you detect a guardrail or agent loop that repeatedly resends unchanged context?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism and data flow

Trace request stages: admission queue, tokenize, retrieval/tool calls, prompt assembly, prefill, decode, postprocess/guardrails and stream flush. Separate TTFT, ITL, total duration, input/output token counts and retry count. Stratify by user tenant, prompt size, output budget, KV occupancy, cache hit, model route, release and GPU node. Compare deployed builds and workload distributions before attributing regression to a kernel. Token explosion can come from redundant tool payloads, repetitive history, runaway generation, failed structured-output retries or agent loops.

Mathematics and invariants

Approximate throughput goodput = successful SLO-meeting completions/time. Little’s law: average in-flight L=arrival_rate λ×mean response time W, for a stable steady-state queue.

Architecture and alternatives

Solutions differ by bottleneck: caching/batching for repeated prefixes, chunked prefill for interference, smaller context, better scheduler, token caps, async I/O, or targeted fallback routing. Optimize quality and cost jointly.

Implementation and instrumentation

Use distributed traces with per-span token counts, model request IDs, queue depths, GPU memory/HBM counters, OTel-style attributes and billable token reconciliation. Load test bursty open-loop traffic.

Latency, memory, cost and scaling

Near saturation queue wait becomes nonlinear; retries can amplify load and create a positive-feedback collapse. Content inspection and extra moderation can change latency budgets.

Failure modes and traps

p50 alone hides tails. High device occupancy can be memory stalls or poor kernels. Lower tokens per answer can be achieved by cutting needed evidence, degrading quality.

lessons.title: Investigate catastrophic forgetting after fine-tuning
lessons.subtitle: Use held-out capability slices and change-isolation experiments to find over-specialization.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How would you detect domain gains that conceal a general reasoning regression?
  2. What are the roles of learning rate, dataset mix and adapter placement?
  3. When would you choose routing between two models over one fine-tuned model?
sections.text: How would you detect domain gains that conceal a general reasoning regression? What are the roles of learning rate, dataset mix and adapter placement? When would you choose routing between two models over one fine-tuned model?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism and data flow

Continued parameter updates for narrow tasks can degrade older capabilities by shifting shared representations and output preferences. Compare base model, previous checkpoint and new candidate on contamination-controlled general reasoning, safety, format, multilingual and domain tasks. Check data mixture, label quality, target formatting, effective token distribution, optimizer schedule and adapter ranks. Use layer-wise or adapter ablations and test whether failures are prompt-format mismatches instead of actual lost knowledge. Mitigations include lower learning rate, early stopping, rehearsal mixtures where permitted, regularization toward base parameters, smaller adapters, selective layer freezing or routing to the base model for vulnerable tasks.

Mathematics and invariants

Model-selection objective can use Pareto constraints: maximize domain Δquality subject to general_regression ≤ ε and safety_regression ≤ δ, rather than averaging unrelated scores.

Architecture and alternatives

LoRA lowers trainable parameter count but does not guarantee zero forgetting. SFT, DPO and continual pretraining can all alter behaviors; simpler prompt/RAG changes may solve target needs without weight updates.

Implementation and instrumentation

Version datasets/checkpoints; run paired golden-case evaluation with confidence intervals and blinded human review. Compare deterministic baselines, compute drift by task slice and identify earliest failing checkpoint.

Latency, memory, cost and scaling

Extra rehearsal raises data licensing/compute burdens, serving multiple adapters increases management cost, and maintaining base fallback may double deployment footprint.

Failure modes and traps

Fine-tuning evaluation should not rely on training loss or benchmark averages. Generic public benchmarks might miss production tasks or include contaminated examples.

lessons.title: Detect reward hacking and unintended alignment behavior
lessons.subtitle: Separate optimization of a proxy reward from verified task success and safe action semantics.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How could an RL-aligned model get a higher reward while solving fewer user tasks?
  2. How would you distinguish reward hacking from an annotation mistake?
  3. What tests catch overly long reassuring answers that dodge hard questions?
sections.text: How could an RL-aligned model get a higher reward while solving fewer user tasks? How would you distinguish reward hacking from an annotation mistake? What tests catch overly long reassuring answers that dodge hard questions?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism and data flow

RLHF-style policies optimize signals learned from preferences or verifiable checks, and may exploit misspecified metrics: verbosity preference, superficial formatting, answer leakage, evaluator contamination, or tool side effects that game success criteria. Inspect policy outputs and full trajectories rather than scalar rewards. Establish independent gold outcomes and rule-based checks, measure differences between reward and verified completion, and run adversarial tasks where shortcuts are attractive. Use holdout human reviewers, reward-model ensembles or uncertainty where justified, leakage barriers, explicit action constraints, and multi-objective evaluations.

Mathematics and invariants

Proxy gap = average_reported_reward − calibrated_verified_task_utility on matched cases (scale units must be comparable); better compare ranks/correlations if reward scales differ. KL constraint D_KL(π_new || π_ref) can limit drift but does not guarantee correctness.

Architecture and alternatives

DPO avoids online RL reward optimization but can still inherit preference biases. Verifiable rewards are stronger where there is a truly correct external test, yet flawed tests can also be gamed.

Implementation and instrumentation

Capture reward decomposition, actor traces, hidden evaluator seeds, independent test cases and policy snapshots. Separate training and audit oracles; validate tool effects in sandbox.

Latency, memory, cost and scaling

Overly strict constraints create alignment tax; overly weak constraints can induce shortcut behavior or policy collapse. Each reward component needs a failure hypothesis and held-out sensitivity test.

Failure modes and traps

A rising reward curve is not a success metric. No reward-model ensemble can prove safety, and no KL penalty automatically prevents exploitation.
