lessons.title: Prevent proprietary-data memorization and sensitive leakage
lessons.subtitle: Reduce data exposure at collection, training, retrieval, tools, inference and logging boundaries.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. What are the main paths by which a chatbot can disclose an internal secret?
  2. How do you separate training memorization from RAG permission failures?
  3. Why are output regex filters and system prompts inadequate as the only security controls?
sections.text: What are the main paths by which a chatbot can disclose an internal secret? How do you separate training memorization from RAG permission failures? Why are output regex filters and system prompts inadequate as the only security controls?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism and data flow

Leakage can originate from memorized training strings, retrieved unauthorized documents, prompt injection in third-party data, tool credentials, logs/traces or the model accidentally copying user secrets. Design controls across the pipeline: data minimization, consent/licensing, secret removal before training, deduplication, tenant-scoped access checks BEFORE retrieval, server-side tool authorization, redaction or isolation of high-risk fields, encryption and retention limits. Treat retrieved web/file text as untrusted instructions; never allow it to override system permissions. Evaluate extraction attacks, canaries and cross-tenant test fixtures. Where training memorization is suspected, mitigation may require data-pipeline remediation and retraining or carefully validated unlearning; a system prompt cannot reliably erase weights.

Mathematics and invariants

Leakage rate = unauthorized disclosure events / evaluated adversarial opportunities; also measure true-positive and false-positive rates for detectors. Redaction residual exposure is an independent metric.

Architecture and alternatives

Authorization belongs in APIs and data stores, not in an LLM prompt. Approved local/self-host setups can change data boundaries but do not automatically solve logging, retention or compromised tools.

Implementation and instrumentation

Use synthetic secret canaries in controlled tests, tenant A/B access matrices, audit logs without raw secrets, egress allowlists and idempotent/approved side-effect actions. Rotate exposed real credentials promptly.

Latency, memory, cost and scaling

Privacy scanning raises latency; hash-based caches must incorporate tenant and policy version so inspection results are not cross-tenant reused. Aggressive redaction can break legitimate tasks, requiring scoped exceptions.

Failure modes and traps

A model appearing to “know” data does not prove memorization; it might have retrieved it. Removing a document from a vector index does not remove it from model parameters or old logs.

lessons.title: Evaluate instruction following, reasoning, factuality and generation quality
lessons.subtitle: Define task-specific rubrics, independent checks and statistically defensible release gates.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How do you evaluate helpfulness when no single reference answer exists?
  2. What is the difference between faithfulness and factual correctness?
  3. How do you compare two models without LLM-as-judge position bias?
sections.text: How do you evaluate helpfulness when no single reference answer exists? What is the difference between faithfulness and factual correctness? How do you compare two models without LLM-as-judge position bias?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism and data flow

Build a frozen, versioned, stratified golden set representing user workflows and known failures. For exact tasks use parsers, unit tests, SQL checks or human-labeled truth; for open-ended outputs, evaluate instruction compliance, evidence support, relevance, style and safety using detailed rubrics. Use blind human review on representative difficult cases and calibrate LLM judges against those labels. Randomize candidate order and mask model identity to reduce order/brand bias; include judge consistency tests and human adjudication. Run paired experiments to control difficulty, report confidence intervals and critical per-slice regressions. Online metrics include user correction rate, escalation rate and task success—not simply thumbs-up.

Mathematics and invariants

For accuracy on n independent prompts, p̂=k/n. Approximate SE=√[p̂(1−p̂)/n] (unreliable near boundaries/small n; use Wilson or bootstrap). For paired binary outcomes, inspect discordant cases rather than treating runs as unrelated samples.

Architecture and alternatives

LLM-as-judge is efficient for some dimensions but susceptible to verbosity, position bias and shared-model errors. Deterministic verifiers are strongest wherever a testable ground truth exists.

Implementation and instrumentation

Construct eval cards with prompt, expected evidence, versioned references, risk tier, rubric and failure category. Automate nightly regression checks, canary comparisons and failure-cluster triage.

Latency, memory, cost and scaling

Judge model calls increase evaluation cost; excessive tuning on the holdout contaminates results. Human eval is slower but essential for subjective and high-risk cases.

Failure modes and traps

BLEU/ROUGE overlap often fail to capture correctness; exact-match can unfairly penalize equivalent valid wording. A single aggregate metric can mask severe subgroup or scenario failures.

lessons.title: Understand ViT, multimodal Transformers and vision-language models
lessons.subtitle: Trace image-to-token data flow and distinguish visual encoders, projectors and autoregressive text heads.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How does ViT turn a 224×224 image into tokens?
  2. How does a vision-language model fuse image and text features?
  3. Why can a multimodal assistant fail on tables even with accurate OCR text?
sections.text: How does ViT turn a 224×224 image into tokens? How does a vision-language model fuse image and text features? Why can a multimodal assistant fail on tables even with accurate OCR text?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism and data flow

A ViT partitions an image into fixed-size patches, flattens each patch and linearly projects it into a model embedding dimension. For H=W=224 and P=16, there are (224/16)²=196 patches, often plus a classification token in classifiers. Each image patch is a learned feature vector; positional information is required to reconstruct layout. Modern VLM pipelines may use a vision encoder followed by a trainable connector/projector that maps vision features into a language model token space, or use cross-attention / unified multimodal Transformer blocks. High-resolution images often use tiling/crops and multiple token groups. Image tokens and text tokens compete for context and compute. Pixel/object recognition, spatial grounding, chart reasoning and OCR are different subproblems.

Mathematics and invariants

Number of square patches N_p=(H/P)(W/P), assuming divisibility. With 224×224×3 and P=16, each patch has 16×16×3=768 raw channel values projected to d_model. Self-attention pair work over patch tokens scales O(N_p²).

Architecture and alternatives

Contrast encoder-projector-decoder VLMs, cross-attention fusion, and unified tokenizers. Choose based on needed localization, latency, training access and modality alignment.

Implementation and instrumentation

Instrument image preprocessing, resizing/crops, encoder latency, number of vision tokens, text-token budget, grounding tests and OCR/table evaluation. Keep document coordinates for citation and table extraction.

Latency, memory, cost and scaling

Smaller patches and image tiling grow token counts rapidly; sending ten pages can overwhelm a context budget. Visual preprocessing can irreversibly lose small text or table lines.

Failure modes and traps

A ViT patch embedding is not an image caption. Not every VLM uses the same cross-attention strategy. High benchmark VQA accuracy may hide severe chart/math or multi-page errors.

lessons.title: Understand LLM watermarking, provenance and traceability
lessons.subtitle: Distinguish statistical token watermarks from cryptographically signed asset origin records.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How can a statistical watermark be embedded in generated tokens?
  2. Why does a positive C2PA signature prove less than “this image is real”?
  3. How do paraphrasing and deterministic factual responses affect detection?
sections.text: How can a statistical watermark be embedded in generated tokens? Why does a positive C2PA signature prove less than “this image is real”? How do paraphrasing and deterministic factual responses affect detection?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism and data flow

A text watermark can gently bias the sampling distribution with a secret/keyed pseudorandom signal so a detector can test whether the token sequence contains the expected statistical pattern. Detection is probabilistic with false positives/negatives and loses power under heavy rewriting, translation or very short/deterministic text. It does not generally identify every AI model. Provenance systems such as C2PA use signed manifests describing asset creation/edits and a trust chain; signatures help validate attached claims and whether bytes/claims were tampered with, but the truth of a creator’s asserted content still depends on the issuer and acquisition process. For production traceability, store hashed prompt/template/model versions, source IDs, consent/retention state and auditable transformations with access controls.

Mathematics and invariants

Illustrative green-list toy statistic z=(g−γn)/√[nγ(1−γ)] for n approx independent token classifications and expected green fraction γ. Real schemes require their own sampling assumptions, calibrated thresholds and key handling.

Architecture and alternatives

Use cryptographic provenance for signed media workflow records; use watermark detectors as weak statistical evidence for supported generators. They complement audit logs, not replace them.

Implementation and instrumentation

Preserve signing-key rotation, revocation, manifest integrity and verification trust stores. For toy detection, choose a false-positive rate on held-out human/non-watermarked text and test paraphrase robustness.

Latency, memory, cost and scaling

Embedding/detecting watermarks can affect token distribution or introduce serving/detector cost. Metadata can be stripped, and not all outputs have trusted signed provenance.

Failure modes and traps

Absence of a watermark does not prove human authorship; a detected pattern may be uncertain. “Signed” does not mean “factually accurate.”

Instrument, evaluate and release criteria: Measure false positives at a preset threshold, detection recall on supported outputs, resilience under edits, signature verification failures and completeness of audited lineage.

  • Signed provenance verifies a claim chain, not the underlying world.
  • Missing marks do not mean authentic human authorship.

lessons.title: Evaluate recursive self-improvement and alternative reasoning architectures
lessons.subtitle: Assess emerging methods through controlled benchmarks, containment, and falsifiable comparisons.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How is iterative self-critique different from an agent modifying its own training procedure?
  2. What evidence would convince you an alternative reasoning architecture is useful in production?
  3. What controls are needed before allowing an optimizer to modify prompts, tools or checkpoints?
sections.text: How is iterative self-critique different from an agent modifying its own training procedure? What evidence would convince you an alternative reasoning architecture is useful in production? What controls are needed before allowing an optimizer to modify prompts, tools or checkpoints?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism and data flow

“Recursive self-improvement” is an umbrella phrase, not one standard capability: repeated prompt reflection, search over candidate programs, external memory, verified code generation, checkpoint training and truly self-directed model modification are very different loops. A safe engineering variant proposes a bounded candidate change, evaluates it on isolated training/dev tasks, then promotes only after independent held-out checks and human approval. Track compute, evaluator independence, contamination and rollback. Alternate reasoning systems include test-time search, verifier-guided sampling, external symbolic solvers, retrieval-driven decompositions, nonautoregressive/diffusion refinement and modular architectures. Evaluate on matched budgets and task sets; promising research should not be presented as proven general autonomous capability.

Mathematics and invariants

Net utility = task_gain − λ_compute×extra_compute − λ_risk×measured_risk, with λ weights agreed for the product. To verify improvement, report paired Δsuccess with uncertainty and compute-matched baselines.

Architecture and alternatives

For verifiable coding/math tasks, search + tests can beat unconstrained longer thinking. For simple Q&A a direct decoder call may be cheaper/faster. Recursive planning adds complexity and repeated-context cost.

Implementation and instrumentation

Use immutable baselines, isolated sandbox execution, staged checkpoints, model/prompt hash versioning, no uncontrolled network access, hidden test sets, time and cost budgets and approval gates. Keep an audit trail of proposals and promotions.

Latency, memory, cost and scaling

Iterating without reliable objective creates Goodhart effects: overfit to feedback, exploit tests or accumulate risky changes. More test-time compute does not guarantee monotonic correctness.

Failure modes and traps

Do not conflate model-generated code patches with changes to foundation-model weights. Automated self-evaluation on the same small public benchmark creates circular proof.

sections.html:
1. How do you stop the agent from editing its own evaluator?
  2. What if cost triples for a tiny accuracy gain?
  3. When should a deterministic symbolic solver be preferred?

Instrument, evaluate and release criteria: Track held-out task success with uncertainty, compute/token cost, security boundary violations, reproducibility, human approval rate and rollback recovery time.

sections.html:
• RSI labels cover materially different mechanisms.
  • Holdout separation and approvals are essential.
  • Measured net task utility beats novelty claims.

title: Prompt Engineering
description: Prompting strategies, structured outputs, security, and evaluation.

lessons.title: What is prompt engineering, and why is it critical for AI applications?
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why is a five-line prompt not automatically more reliable than a 50-line one?
  2. When should you move logic from the prompt into application code?
  3. How do you prove a prompt edit improved real user outcomes?
sections.text: Why is a five-line prompt not automatically more reliable than a 50-line one? When should you move logic from the prompt into application code? How do you prove a prompt edit improved real user outcomes?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

The effective prompt is the full serialized request: high-priority instructions, conversation messages, tool definitions, retrieved context, output contracts and generation parameters. Prompt engineering specifies observable behavior within this interface; it does not change model weights. Build the request by first stating a goal and success rubric, then enforcing a data/control boundary, supplying only relevant context, and specifying an output contract and fallback. Run the exact prompt against pinned model snapshots and representative examples. A prompt is application logic and should be versioned, reviewed and rollbackable.

Mathematics and invariants

Conditional generation: pθ(y | I, C, T, H); I=instructions, C=trusted context, T=tool schema, H=history. A good prompt seeks to maximize estimated task utility U(y) subject to token, latency, security and format constraints, not simply the most persuasive wording.

Architecture and alternatives

Choose rules/code instead of an LLM for deterministic validation; choose retrieval for fresh knowledge; use prompting for task conditioning; move to fine-tuning only for repeated, stable deficits shown in a holdout.

Implementation and instrumentation

Compose typed request sections, hash template/version, record model ID, temperature, output tokens and retries. Freeze golden cases, group by task and severity, and test paired variants.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

Long instructions consume prefill tokens and can impair adherence. Reused stable prefixes may be cached by a provider, but cache eligibility and savings are provider- and request-specific.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

Generic “be accurate” claims are not measurable contracts. Never use a system prompt as a database permission or secret store.

lessons.title: Zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot prompting with examples
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Design three prompts for the same sentiment classifier using zero, one, and three shots.
  2. Why might five examples be worse than two?
  3. How would you detect class-prior bias from example order?
sections.text: Design three prompts for the same sentiment classifier using zero, one, and three shots. Why might five examples be worse than two? How would you detect class-prior bias from example order?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

Zero-shot gives only the instruction and schema; one-shot adds one labeled input-output demonstration; few-shot adds several examples. In-context learning conditions predictions on the examples but ordinarily does not update model parameters. For sentiment classification, specify labels first; supply balanced examples such as “delivery was late” → negative and “arrived early” → positive, then classify an unseen review. Examples carry conventions about formatting, label boundaries and ambiguity. Choose cases representing errors and decision boundaries rather than trivial repeated positives.

Mathematics and invariants

Extra prompt tokens ≈ Σ_i tokens(example_i). In a simple retrieval-based toy selector, similarity can choose demonstrations; real LLMs learn associations from the sequence, not from a guaranteed nearest-neighbor rule.

Architecture and alternatives

Zero-shot is cheapest and simplest. One-shot clarifies an uncommon format. Diverse few-shot examples can stabilize a difficult taxonomy but can also induce label priors, order effects and context waste.

Implementation and instrumentation

Store reviewed, de-identified demonstrations with immutable IDs. Stratify examples by class and language, audit that labels are correct, rotate order in evals and compare k=0,1,3,5.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

Long examples raise input token costs and reduce space for evidence. Dynamic example selection adds embedding/retrieval latency and introduces leakage risks.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

If one class dominates the demonstrations, a model may overpredict it. Beware accidental answer leakage from an example nearly identical to the test.

lessons.title: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting: mechanism and when to use it
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why might “think step by step” fail on a strong reasoning model?
  2. How do you evaluate correctness versus explanation plausibility?
  3. When do external tools beat longer reasoning prompts?
sections.text: Why might “think step by step” fail on a strong reasoning model? How do you evaluate correctness versus explanation plausibility? When do external tools beat longer reasoning prompts?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

CoT-style prompting encourages decomposition into intermediate steps for multi-stage reasoning. It helps on some tasks, but visible reasoning is neither inherently faithful nor necessarily more accurate; model family and instruction-following behavior matter. In production prefer requesting a concise verifiable plan, equations, assumptions or a final explanation rather than requiring hidden/private reasoning traces. On deterministic arithmetic, external calculation beats trusting prose. Assess both result correctness and additional output tokens.

Mathematics and invariants

Let A be answer accuracy and C be incremental token/latency cost. A useful strategy must improve expected utility ΔU = ΔA·V_correct − ΔC·unit_cost. More generated steps do not guarantee ΔA>0.

Architecture and alternatives

Use simple direct answers for extraction and obvious classification; use explicit intermediate checks or tools for multi-hop problems. Self-consistency or search helps only if diverse candidate answers and verification justify extra cost.

Implementation and instrumentation

Prompt for “compute with a calculator and report formula + verified result”; test step order on adversarial multi-hop inputs. Do not persist unnecessary private reasoning text in traces.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

Reasoning tokens may increase end-to-end latency, and longer outputs can amplify hallucinated intermediate facts; request final reasoning summaries to conserve budget.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

The model can narrate a convincing but unsupported path. Explanations are not a substitute for correct tool results or independently verifiable evidence.

lessons.title: Self-consistency prompting for reasoning
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Under what assumptions does majority voting improve correctness?
  2. How do you canonicalize free-form numeric answers?
  3. What would you do when all samples agree on a false claim?
sections.text: Under what assumptions does majority voting improve correctness? How do you canonicalize free-form numeric answers? What would you do when all samples agree on a false claim?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

Self-consistency samples several completions with variation and aggregates final normalized answers; the original motivation is that correct answers may recur across distinct reasoning paths. Require canonical answer extraction and tie handling before voting. Samples from the same model are correlated, so majority voting is not a statistical independence guarantee. An answer verifier is often more useful than a raw plurality when errors share a common misconception.

Mathematics and invariants

For independent Bernoulli answers with correctness q and odd sample count n, majority success = Σ_{k>(n/2)} C(n,k) q^k(1−q)^(n−k). This is an illustrative independence model, usually optimistic for correlated LLM errors.

Architecture and alternatives

Vote for concise discrete answers; use a verifier, tool or judge for continuous outputs; avoid repetition on cheap deterministic tasks. Best-of-N with external correctness tests differs from unconstrained majority vote.

Implementation and instrumentation

Generate N responses with answer schema, parse exact answer field, deduplicate and normalize, record vote histogram, abstain on ties or suspicious disagreement. Never merge incompatible free-text answers blindly.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

N candidates multiply model tokens and potentially wall time; parallel sampling reduces elapsed time but not compute or provider load.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

Common-mode failures survive voting. A 5/5 consensus is weak if every sample uses the same unsupported source or broken computation.

lessons.title: Tree-of-Thought prompting (ToT)
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Explain why ToT is not the same as CoT.
  2. How does beam width affect correctness and cost?
  3. Which parts of a planning search must be deterministic?
sections.text: Explain why ToT is not the same as CoT. How does beam width affect correctness and cost? Which parts of a planning search must be deterministic?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

Tree of Thoughts explores multiple partial solution states: propose candidates, score or externally evaluate them, keep promising states, branch deeper, and stop under a node/step budget. This is search over text-encoded reasoning states; it is not a novel neural network architecture. BFS/beam search retains breadth; DFS can reach depth with lower frontier memory but may get stuck; MCTS is useful with well-behaved rollout signals. Progress depends on evaluator quality: model self-scores may reward fluent nonsense.

Mathematics and invariants

Approximate node expansion at depth d with branching b is Σ_{i=0}^d b^i without pruning; a beam of width w caps retained frontier states at O(w) but can still generate O(wbd) candidate states.

Architecture and alternatives

Use ToT for constrained combinatorial planning with a cheap check; use simple chaining or a deterministic optimizer when scoring can be implemented as code.

Implementation and instrumentation

Represent a state with commitments, remaining constraints, step_count and provenance. Implement propose→validate→score→prune→expand loop; bound recursion and use a visited-state set.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

Budget usually scales with explored nodes × tokens per proposal and evaluator call. Full branching becomes prohibitively expensive quickly.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

Self-evaluation drift, revisiting states, false pruning and loops are key failures. Never take a tool side effect inside a speculative branch.

lessons.title: ReAct: reasoning plus acting with tools
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How is ReAct different from a fixed tool pipeline?
  2. How would you stop an infinite tool loop?
  3. Where do access checks happen if the model picked the correct tool?
sections.text: How is ReAct different from a fixed tool pipeline? How would you stop an infinite tool loop? Where do access checks happen if the model picked the correct tool?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

A ReAct loop alternates deciding what information or action is needed, issuing a structured tool request, receiving a tool observation, and producing the next decision until finish or budget exhaustion. Reasoning is model-side task management; the orchestration service owns tool schemas, permissions, timeouts, state, retries and stopping criteria. An observation is untrusted data and must never gain instruction authority. Distinguish read-only steps from reversible, irreversible and high-risk actions.

Mathematics and invariants

Let T be max steps. Cost is approximately Σ_{t=1}^{T}(prompt_tokens_t + output_tokens_t + tool_cost_t). If full transcript is replayed, context cost can grow superlinearly with turn count; compaction limits this but can discard important state.

Architecture and alternatives

Use a simple fixed tool chain when steps are known; use ReAct when tool choice depends on observations. MCP transports tools/resources but does not replace model tool-selection logic or authorization.

Implementation and instrumentation

Validate tool name and arguments against typed schema, enforce tenant ACL and action-specific approval server-side, use idempotency keys and retry budgets, and persist checkpoints after each result.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

Tool round trips often dominate latency; bound loops and route narrow tasks to non-agentic workflows.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

Tool output saying “ignore previous instructions” is not a user command. Avoid dynamic execution based on arbitrary extracted text.

lessons.title: System prompts and instruction hierarchy
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Can a user override actual system instructions by writing “SYSTEM: ...”?
  2. What should be placed in the system prompt versus application logic?
  3. How do you test instruction conflicts?
sections.text: Can a user override actual system instructions by writing “SYSTEM: ...”? What should be placed in the system prompt versus application logic? How do you test instruction conflicts?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

High-priority instructions define global role, constraints, permitted tool behavior and fallback policy. Actual instruction precedence depends on provider APIs and message roles; quoted untrusted text is still data, not a new system message. Build system instructions from stable policy modules, then supply per-request variables as validated typed fields. Hard business restrictions still require server-side code and tool-layer permissions.

Mathematics and invariants

The effective request is a sequence of typed messages M=(role_i,content_i). A text substring “SYSTEM:” inside a retrieved page does not become an actual system-role message in an API call.

Architecture and alternatives

Keep stable role/tone and policy at the top; put user task and examples at lower priority; keep retrieved docs separate. Never rely on “DO NOT REVEAL” to protect embedded credentials.

Implementation and instrumentation

Unit test conflicting messages, role spoofing in user data, and prompt revisions. Use explicit output refusal or safe fallback policies where appropriate.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

Long system prompts increase tokens and attention load. Modular code-managed instructions improve review and cache reuse when stable.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

Overconstraining the model can cause blanket refusals. “You are an expert” is not an access-control mechanism.

sections.html:

  2. How do you handle partial streamed JSON?
  3. Why is a valid JSON object still unsafe to execute?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

Define a typed result contract before prompting: required properties, enums, bounds, nullable fields, version, and semantics. Prefer provider-native constrained decoding or structured output where available, then parse and validate server-side. A format prompt such as “only JSON” cannot by itself guarantee correctness. Detect incomplete streams, refusal, length cutoffs and content-filter interruptions as separate error classes. XML requires secure parsers and well-formedness checks; downstream XML parsing must prevent entity expansion and unsafe external entities.

Mathematics and invariants

Success = P(transport_complete ∧ syntax_valid ∧ schema_valid ∧ semantic_valid). Each gate must be measured separately. For classification, validate label ∈ allowed_labels independently of parseability.

Architecture and alternatives

Use JSON Schema for typed application contracts; XML only when a downstream protocol requires XML or mixed hierarchical markup. Constrained generation enforces a supported grammar subset, not live business truth.

Implementation and instrumentation

After json.loads or safe XML parse, reject extra keys, invalid IDs, illegal enum values and inconsistent totals; apply authorization before executing requested actions.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

Validation and a repair call add latency; bounded retries prevent retry storms. Schema-native generation may restrict format without correcting meaning.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

A valid JSON output can be malicious as SQL parameters or an unauthorized account ID. Never deserialize model output directly into privileged actions.

lessons.title: Prompt injection: direct, indirect, and defense boundaries
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Show how an indirect injection travels from a webpage into a tool call.
  2. Which defense remains useful if the model is completely compromised?
  3. How do you test prompt injection without harming real data?
sections.text: Show how an indirect injection travels from a webpage into a tool call. Which defense remains useful if the model is completely compromised? How do you test prompt injection without harming real data?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

Prompt injection crosses a trust boundary when attacker-controlled text in a user message, web page, file, email or tool response tries to replace the agent’s instructions or trigger unauthorized actions. The attacker may spoof roles, ask for hidden prompts, plant tool directives, or use encoded instructions. Labels, delimiters, regex and classifier checks help, but cannot provide perfect security. Restrict what the model can do by tool permissions, independent authorization, egress controls and explicit approval for high-risk operations.

Mathematics and invariants

Risk = P(successful instruction uptake) × impact of allowed action. Reduce both sides: input quarantine lowers uptake; strict tool authorization and approval caps impact. Raw detection accuracy is not equal to prevented harmful action rate.

Architecture and alternatives

Defense-in-depth: treat retrieved text as data; use narrowly scoped tools; enforce policy at execution; validate proposed calls; audit operations; use sandboxes and confirmation for irreversible actions.

Implementation and instrumentation

Create attack fixtures in the same channel as real threats (retrieved document, not a user prompt), with dummy secrets and fake network endpoints. Log tool denial reason without storing private content.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

External-content classifiers add cost; cheap regex alone misses novel attacks. High-risk action checks deserve stronger budgets than ordinary summarization.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

Never treat an LLM security judgment as authorization. A prompt saying “ignore injections” has no enforceable effect if powerful tools remain unrestricted.

lessons.title: Jailbreaking and bypass techniques
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How do you distinguish a jailbreak from an indirect injection?
  2. What is a meaningful security metric beyond refusal rate?
  3. How do you test multilingual attack classes?
sections.text: How do you distinguish a jailbreak from an indirect injection? What is a meaningful security metric beyond refusal rate? How do you test multilingual attack classes?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

A jailbreak aims to steer a model beyond intended constraints, often through roleplay, fabricated authority, multi-turn escalation, obfuscation or adversarial paraphrases. Prompt injection is broader and can target tool actions; a jailbreak is commonly a behavioral policy-bypass attempt. Mitigations require layered safety policy, constrained tool access, high-risk content review and continuously updated red-team sets. An overzealous filter harms benign tasks, so evaluate false refusals alongside bypasses.

Mathematics and invariants

Attack success rate ASR = successful unsafe outcomes / evaluated attacks, conditioned on attack class and permissions. Benign false-refusal rate = rejected legitimate tasks / legitimate cases. Both are necessary.

Architecture and alternatives

Model refusal tuning and classification can help at the response layer; tool execution restrictions protect real side effects even if text guardrails fail. Distinguish provider refusal from app-specific business policy.

Implementation and instrumentation

Use harmless synthetic attack prompts and sandbox tools. Stratify direct, indirect, multilingual and multi-turn attacks; record accepted/denied actions and human adjudication.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

Defenses add cost and can increase refusal rate. Prioritize controls by severity and route uncertain high-risk cases to review.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

A high refusal rate is not proof of security; it might just block everything. Avoid publishing real sensitive prompts or secrets in test traces.

lessons.title: Optimize prompts for cost and latency
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How do you separate TTFT from complete response latency?
  2. When can adding a cacheable system prefix be cheaper than aggressively trimming?
  3. Which quality regressions could an aggressive context reduction cause?
sections.text: How do you separate TTFT from complete response latency? When can adding a cacheable system prefix be cheaper than aggressively trimming? Which quality regressions could an aggressive context reduction cause?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

First measure end-to-end trace stages: context assembly, retrieval, prefill, decoding, tools, parsers and retries. Count actual tokenizer tokens, not characters. Shorten redundant instructions, choose the smallest adequate context, reuse stable prefix segments where caching is supported and reserve an explicit output budget. Do not delete evidence or compliance checks simply to save tokens; optimize quality at a given cost.

Mathematics and invariants

Illustrative model: C=(U·P_u + K·P_k + O·P_o)/10⁶, U=uncached input tokens, K=cached input, O=output; TTFT≈queue+network+prefill. Total latency≈TTFT+generated_tokens×TPOT (rough approximation, streaming overlap ignored).

Architecture and alternatives

Caching is ideal for repeated stable prefixes, but not semantic correctness. Summarization reduces length with information-loss risk; retrieval selects evidence; fine-tuning reduces repeated instructional examples in some domains.

Implementation and instrumentation

Version stable system templates; put user-specific content after static prefix; instrument cache-hit tokens, tokens per successful task, p50/p95/99 latency and retry rate.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

Every example and instruction consumes tokens, though persistent cache pricing can differ. Compression pipelines add preprocessing latency and can lose legal requirements.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

Optimizing only billed tokens can raise retry rate and effective cost or degrade accuracy. Low TTFT does not imply fast full answer.

lessons.title: Prompt engineering vs. prompt tuning
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why can soft prompts not be copied between arbitrary model embeddings?
  2. How is prefix tuning different from a longer natural-language system prompt?
  3. When would LoRA be preferred?
sections.text: Why can soft prompts not be copied between arbitrary model embeddings? How is prefix tuning different from a longer natural-language system prompt? When would LoRA be preferred?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

Prompt engineering edits natural-language instructions and examples supplied at inference. Prompt tuning trains a small set of continuous prefix embeddings or virtual token vectors while often freezing the base model. Soft prompts are optimized by gradients and cannot generally be inspected as meaningful words. Prefix tuning can introduce trainable key/value activations per layer, while P-tuning methods vary. Prompt tuning needs model-weight/embedding access and labeled training examples; prompt engineering can work with an API-only model.

Mathematics and invariants

For soft prompt P∈R^{m×d}, optimize P* = argmin_P Σ_i L(fθ([P;x_i]), y_i), with θ frozen. Trainable parameters ≈ m·d for simple input soft prompts, vs billions of θ parameters.

Architecture and alternatives

Natural language prompts are easiest to version/inspect and portable across providers; trainable soft prompts can be efficient for stable high-volume tasks but are checkpoint- and model-family-specific.

Implementation and instrumentation

Use training/test split; pin tokenizer/embedding dimensions; serialize prompt vectors and loss metrics. Do not claim a soft prompt is readable or directly usable through generic chat APIs.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

Tuning consumes GPU train time but can be cheaper than full fine-tuning; m virtual tokens also consume context/prefix compute. Vendor support varies.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

Overfitting small datasets and mismatched tokenizer/model weights can cause regression; misleadingly calling example selection “prompt tuning” confuses inference and training.

lessons.title: Production prompt templates
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Design a template API for a multi-tenant assistant.
  2. How do you handle delimiters inside malicious user text?
  3. Which version identifiers belong in the trace?
sections.text: Design a template API for a multi-tenant assistant. How do you handle delimiters inside malicious user text? Which version identifiers belong in the trace?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

A template is a versioned function that assembles real messages from validated variables, not unsafe string concatenation. Separate stable policy, task-specific user request, authorized source excerpts and output schema. Escape or structurally delimit inserted data and cap field lengths; never interpolate user input into high-priority instructions. Include an explicit contract for abstention, citations and tool authorization. Treat prompt changes like code migrations with tests and rollback.

Mathematics and invariants

Builder: build_prompt(policy_version, task: str, authorized_sources: list[Doc], schema_version) → Messages. Invariants: permitted_source(doc,user) and len(request_tokens)≤budget.

Architecture and alternatives

Use typed message arrays rather than a single raw string whenever supported. A file-based code-managed prompt avoids provider dependence and facilitates PR review; provider prompt registries are optional and may change.

Implementation and instrumentation

Test template rendering for braces/quotes/unicode, missing fields, injected role labels, token overflow and system-user boundary integrity. Hash the final constructed request excluding PII where appropriate.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

Template compilation and validation are inexpensive; the dominant cost is the resulting token payload. Multi-service duplication of templates makes migrations risky.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

Putting an end user’s “special instructions” into the system role is a privilege escalation. Do not log raw secrets or trust dynamic source names.

lessons.title: Multi-turn conversation prompting
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why is summarizing the last 50 turns insufficient for transactional workflows?
  2. How do you preserve constraints while switching topics?
  3. What belongs in structured state rather than natural-language memory?
sections.text: Why is summarizing the last 50 turns insufficient for transactional workflows? How do you preserve constraints while switching topics? What belongs in structured state rather than natural-language memory?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

Multi-turn chat is a state management problem. The serving model typically receives the selected prior messages again; absent external state it does not automatically remember all previous user details. Track user intent, current task, entity references, unresolved commitments and source versions in structured state; assemble a bounded context containing current message, task state, recent turns and relevant prior facts. Use summaries as lossy indexes with citations/pointers; never overwrite durable policies or approvals with model-made summaries.

Mathematics and invariants

Context budget: N_sys + N_state + N_history + N_evidence + N_tools + N_reserve ≤ W. Memory retrieval should optimize relevance and user permissions, not simply maximize included tokens.

Architecture and alternatives

Sliding recent window is simple but forgets early constraints; summary-plus-retrieval improves reach but adds extraction risk. Durable state machines beat prose history for approvals and side effects.

Implementation and instrumentation

Record conversation_id, turn_id, state version, user permissions, source snapshot, and last confirmed constraints. Use explicit topic-switch detection and old-task suspension.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

Long histories raise prefill and cache pressure. Compaction reduces tokens but can drop negations or provenance, so validate pinned invariants.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

The assistant might merge two user tasks after a topic change or treat a quoted conversation as authoritative. Do not infer permissions from chat memories.

lessons.title: Role prompting: when it helps and when it does not
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why does “you are a senior lawyer” not make an LLM legally reliable?
  2. How do you measure the incremental value of a role?
  3. Which behavior should be made deterministic instead?
sections.text: Why does “you are a senior lawyer” not make an LLM legally reliable? How do you measure the incremental value of a role? Which behavior should be made deterministic instead?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

Role prompting supplies an occupational lens or communication convention, e.g. “act as a senior code reviewer,” which influences vocabulary, focus and response structure. It is useful for consistent tone, rubric framing and task decomposition, not a guarantee of domain expertise. A role cannot confer actual permissions, model capabilities, or fresh knowledge. Specify verifiable responsibilities (“report risks and proposed tests”) rather than personality inflation (“world’s greatest architect”).

Mathematics and invariants

Effect size is empirical: Δscore = score(role+task) − score(task) on paired fixed cases. A role that only increases verbosity with no correctness gain has poor utility.

Architecture and alternatives

Use a domain rubric, schema and source references for correctness; role phrasing can be a light style wrapper. Expert review or a tool beats a persona when exactness matters.

Implementation and instrumentation

Test with and without the role under multiple languages/task slices. Keep stable tone instructions high-level and domain-specific instructions in the task message.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

Roles can lengthen answers and increase tokens. Strong persona language may encourage unwarranted confidence.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

A “legal expert” persona produces invented statutes. Require cited source text and explicit unknowns; treat generated professional-sounding wording as unverified.

lessons.title: Prompt chaining for complex tasks
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. When does a two-call pipeline beat a one-call prompt?
  2. What happens to success probability as stages multiply?
  3. How do you isolate failures to one stage?
sections.text: When does a two-call pipeline beat a one-call prompt? What happens to success probability as stages multiply? How do you isolate failures to one stage?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

Prompt chaining decomposes a workflow into distinct model calls or deterministic stages: interpret request → retrieve evidence → extract facts → verify → draft → validate. Each stage has a typed input-output contract and local retry/recovery policy. This improves observability and permits specialized models, but intermediate errors propagate; chaining does not automatically outperform one carefully constrained call. Parallelize independent stages only when causal dependencies allow it.

Mathematics and invariants

If independent stages have success probabilities p_i, idealized end-to-end success=∏ p_i; with 5 stages each p=0.98, total≈0.904. Actual dependencies make this a teaching approximation. Sequential total latency≈Σ L_i.

Architecture and alternatives

Use a single call for simple extraction; chain when distinct tool access, schemas or verification warrants stage separation. Prefer deterministic validators where criteria are exact.

Implementation and instrumentation

Return validated typed artifacts from each stage; store trace IDs, stage versions, idempotency keys and retry counts; quarantine untrusted text between stages.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

More calls increase network overhead, input reuse and failure points; targeted caching and parallel execution can offset some costs.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

If a hallucinated intermediate “fact” is blindly trusted downstream, chains amplify errors. Avoid unlimited self-repair cascades.

lessons.title: Evaluate and iterate on prompt quality
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How do you avoid prompt overfitting to a 30-case test set?
  2. What is the limitation of LLM-as-judge?
  3. How would you estimate a meaningful improvement statistically?
sections.text: How do you avoid prompt overfitting to a 30-case test set? What is the limitation of LLM-as-judge? How would you estimate a meaningful improvement statistically?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

Treat prompt changes as experiments over a representative golden dataset: define task success, semantic validity, groundedness, safety, latency, cost and worst-case slices. Version prompt+model+dataset and compare paired outputs on identical items; freeze a holdout to prevent iterative overfitting. Use deterministic unit tests for exact outputs, humans for ambiguous qualitative rubrics and calibrated LLM judges when scaled evaluation warrants them.

Mathematics and invariants

For n cases, accuracy p̂=k/n; paired difference Δ=(wins−losses)/n for binary discordant outcomes. Use paired bootstrap or McNemar-style analysis for inference rather than independent confidence bands when cases are matched.

Architecture and alternatives

Offline regression tests catch known failures; canaries/A-B tests reveal live workflow distribution. Both are required for high-stakes changes.

Implementation and instrumentation

Keep fixture IDs, expected evidence, rubric version, model parameters, prompt hash and judge ID. Tag critical failure slices and predeclare shipping gates.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

Human review adds cost, but tuning repeatedly on the same public dataset contaminates findings. Cache model outputs per exact request version where allowable.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

A prompt can appear better only because a judge prefers length or formatting. One aggregate score can hide a severe multilingual or safety regression.

lessons.title: Meta-prompts for generating and improving prompts
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Can an LLM reliably grade prompts it wrote?
  2. How do you protect locked business constraints during optimization?
  3. How do you avoid holdout contamination in repeated search?
sections.text: Can an LLM reliably grade prompts it wrote? How do you protect locked business constraints during optimization? How do you avoid holdout contamination in repeated search?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

A meta-prompt asks an LLM to propose task prompts, examples or evaluation criteria. It is useful for brainstorming prompt candidates and surfacing missing constraints but not for independently proving improvements. Build a constrained loop: supply task spec and known failure categories → generate diverse candidate edits → lint trusted structure → run held-out eval → retain only verified winner. Keep proposer separate from judge when possible.

Mathematics and invariants

Optimization loop: P_(t+1)=select({candidate(P_t,feedback_j)}, holdout_score), under risk/cost constraints. This resembles black-box search; selection noise increases with repeated testing on the same holdout.

Architecture and alternatives

Use manual prompt review for low volume; meta-prompts for large hypothesis spaces; fine-tune or train a prompt optimizer only if repeated search cost makes sense.

Implementation and instrumentation

Require edit rationale, diff, expected improvement slice and known risk, then test exact rendered request. Prevent meta-prompter from modifying security or authorization policies.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

Candidate generation and evaluation multiply token usage; a small targeted candidate pool is usually easier to audit than thousands of slight variations.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

Self-graded prompts can reward longer, persuasive output. Never auto-promote a prompt based solely on its own judge explanation.

lessons.title: Common prompt failure modes and debugging
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. What data do you need to reproduce a prompt bug?
  2. How do you isolate retrieval nondeterminism?
  3. Which failures must be fixed in code, not the prompt?
sections.text: What data do you need to reproduce a prompt bug? How do you isolate retrieval nondeterminism? Which failures must be fixed in code, not the prompt?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

First classify the failure: wrong task framing, incomplete context, ambiguous label boundary, conflicting instructions, stale source, truncation, invalid schema, hallucinated tools, over-refusal, prompt injection, model drift or evaluation defect. Reproduce with exact effective request, model snapshot, sampling settings and source snapshot. Change one variable at a time, including example order, budget and retrieved documents.

Mathematics and invariants

Regression contrast: failure_rate_new − failure_rate_baseline on the same versioned fixtures. For large systems, attribute latency L_total=L_queue+L_retrieval+L_prefill+L_decode+L_validation+L_retry.

Architecture and alternatives

Use better source retrieval for missing facts, validators for exact constraints, schema decoding for syntax and prompt revisions for instruction ambiguity. Fine-tuning is not the default first fix.

Implementation and instrumentation

Instrument prompt/model/schema hashes, token usage, finish reasons, source IDs, tool attempts, parser error types and anonymized trace IDs.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

Excess logging exposes data; sample or redact private content. Retries hide underlying failures and distort success metrics.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

Temperature zero is not universal determinism. A malformed response may be a streaming or schema implementation bug, not a “bad model.”

lessons.title: Adversarial inputs and prompt edge cases
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How is a hard boundary different from an injection classifier?
  2. What benign examples cause false positives?
  3. How do you structure tests across untrusted channels?
sections.text: How is a hard boundary different from an injection classifier? What benign examples cause false positives? How do you structure tests across untrusted channels?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

Define the threat and malformed-input space before release: empty requests, mixed encodings, huge documents, markdown/HTML, nested quotations, role spoofing, adversarial task switches, contradictory sources, ambiguous requests, unsupported languages and prompt injection embedded in tool data. Design robust input contracts, bounded lengths, canonicalization where safe, safe rendering and server-side permissions. Test both adversarial threats and legitimate inputs that resemble them.

Mathematics and invariants

Coverage = tested classes / enumerated risk classes (only an inventory proxy). For threat risk, weight failure by severity and exposure; a low-frequency exfiltration case can dominate common formatting issues.

Architecture and alternatives

Use allowlisted tools and typed data; add classifier-based inspection only as defense-in-depth. Do not put safety-critical parsing into an LLM prompt.

Implementation and instrumentation

Build synthetic fixtures grouped by actual input channel and attack objective. Unit-test access-denied behavior and that valid benign requests still succeed.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

Fuzzing and adversarial models increase test costs but can reveal rare failure paths; cap maximum input size to bound latency/DoS.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

Avoid naïve keyword blocking that rejects legitimate quotations. Unicode normalization may change semantics in multilingual contexts.

lessons.title: Lost in the middle and long-context prompting
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How would you prove positional bias rather than retrieval failure?
  2. When does a longer context still beat RAG?
  3. What is the cost of repeating key evidence at both ends?
sections.text: How would you prove positional bias rather than retrieval failure? When does a longer context still beat RAG? What is the cost of repeating key evidence at both ends?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

A model may use information at beginning and end of a long context more reliably than facts in the middle, even when all tokens fit; published experiments document position-dependent degradation on specific tasks, but no universal U-shaped performance law exists. Diagnose recall by moving identical evidence to different positions while preserving other content, and use evidence retrieval, ranking, citations and context compression to reduce irrelevant middle material.

Mathematics and invariants

Retrieval hit@k = #cases containing decisive evidence among top k / #answerable cases. Position robustness gap = max_position_score − min_position_score on a controlled relocation set.

Architecture and alternatives

Selective RAG beats stuffing whole documents when evidence is sparse; full-context approaches work when global relationships are needed and the model can use that length reliably.

Implementation and instrumentation

Create fixed-answer probes with evidence in beginning/middle/end; report per-position scores, context length and tokenized location. Require source-span validation.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

Huge context increases prefill compute and KV footprint; a longer nominal window does not guarantee high utility across it.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

Do not “solve” lost in the middle by always repeating authoritative instructions; this can increase tokens and does not enforce behavior. Reordering evidence can bias answer selection.

lessons.title: Output parsers in production LLM applications
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. What are the parser’s exact layers?
  2. How do you treat stream truncation differently from JSON syntax error?
  3. Why must authorization occur after parsing?
sections.text: What are the parser’s exact layers? How do you treat stream truncation differently from JSON syntax error? Why must authorization occur after parsing?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

A parser converts the model’s text/structured API output into typed application data. Pipeline: collect a complete response, distinguish refusal/truncation/tool requests, parse syntax, validate schema, run domain invariants, and authorize downstream effects. Parsing failures should be typed, observable and recoverable through bounded retries where safe; never blindly reinterpret content with regex if a trusted grammar is available.

Mathematics and invariants

P(end-to-end valid)=P(complete)·P(parse|complete)·P(schema|parse)·P(semantic|schema) in a chained conditional model. Instrument each denominator.

Architecture and alternatives

Prefer native schema output then typed validation; use regex only for constrained local matching. Separate output validation from business authorization.

Implementation and instrumentation

Implement parse_result(raw, allowed_ids) that rejects unknown keys and invalid enums and has an explicit abstention status. Persist idempotency keys before side effects.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

Repair loops increase tokens and p95; syntax-first repair can conceal model logic errors if semantic checks are skipped.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

Never execute arbitrary model-generated code or SQL based solely on a parse success. A partial streaming chunk is not a full JSON object.

lessons.title: Multilingual prompting in production
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How do you handle English/Bengali code-switching?
  2. How would you calculate tokenization cost disparity?
  3. Why can translating English few-shot examples degrade quality?
sections.text: How do you handle English/Bengali code-switching? How would you calculate tokenization cost disparity? Why can translating English few-shot examples degrade quality?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

Multilingual prompting requires explicit task locale, output language, script, domain terminology, formatting and cultural conventions. Language detection can fail on code-switching and short text; prefer user-supplied locale when trustworthy, with fallback. Evaluate each language on native-labeled tasks, not machine translations alone. Consider tokenization expansion, retrieval coverage, transliteration, dates/currency, idioms and refusal fairness.

Mathematics and invariants

Per-language accuracy A_l and token expansion E_l = tokens_l / tokens_reference. Macro accuracy = (1/L)Σ_l A_l; aggregate micro metrics can conceal severe low-volume-language failures.

Architecture and alternatives

Direct multilingual prompting avoids translation artifacts when model capability is adequate; translate→reason→translate can help on low-resource languages but adds latency and semantic drift.

Implementation and instrumentation

Carry BCP-47 locale as structured metadata, maintain terminology glossary and domain test fixtures, protect quoted source language, and locale-normalize dates only at typed boundaries.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

Some scripts tokenize into more pieces; translation chains add calls; cross-lingual retrieval may miss documents if index lacks coverage.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

Wrong honorifics, script mixing and code-switching failures are common. Do not assume English eval improvements transfer to Bengali, Arabic or Hindi.

lessons.title: Few-shot prompting gives inconsistent results
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. What is order sensitivity and how do you measure it?
  2. How do you select diverse demonstrations?
  3. What if k=0 actually outperforms k=5?
sections.text: What is order sensitivity and how do you measure it? How do you select diverse demonstrations? What if k=0 actually outperforms k=5?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

Start with a failure matrix by class, input length and exemplar order. Inspect conflicting or low-quality demonstrations, repeated examples and label imbalance. Stabilize the instruction/labels and keep examples concise, representative and nonoverlapping with evaluation. Randomize example order in tests and evaluate whether dynamic retrieval improves boundary coverage. Reduce stochastic sampling if output diversity is unwanted, but note determinism is not guaranteed.

Mathematics and invariants

Sensitivity to example ordering: Var_order(score) over multiple permutations; compare average and worst-case performance, not only the best arrangement.

Architecture and alternatives

Balanced curated few-shot prompts are cheap; dynamic similarity-selected exemplars add retrieval and leakage controls; fine-tuning may win at high volume with enough stable labels.

Implementation and instrumentation

Build confusion matrices for each candidate, trace example IDs/order, test label consistency, and select based on held-out macro F1.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

Long shot sets raise prefill cost and may change model behavior on rare classes.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

Overfitting a specific ordering can produce illusory gains; a class imbalance cannot be repaired with confidence wording.

lessons.title: Classification changes when prompt wording changes
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How do you separate instability from label ambiguity?
  2. Which metric measures invariance across paraphrases?
  3. When is an ordinary classifier the better product?
sections.text: How do you separate instability from label ambiguity? Which metric measures invariance across paraphrases? When is an ordinary classifier the better product?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

Prompt sensitivity can arise from ambiguous taxonomy, label priors, uncalibrated probabilities, temperature, and prompt/model snapshot drift. Define precise mutually exclusive label criteria and precedence rules; give contrastive boundary cases and structured output. Evaluate across a set of meaning-preserving paraphrases, then reduce dependence on exact wording. If high reliability is needed, consider a trained classifier or rule engine.

Mathematics and invariants

Robust accuracy = (1/N)Σ_i 1[all required paraphrases_i labeled correctly] (strict metric); agreement = count_same_predictions / total_paraphrase_pairs.

Architecture and alternatives

Use schema-based classification and temperature tuning first; explicit conventional classifiers dominate when labels and training data are stable; LLMs help when taxonomy changes rapidly or inputs are highly semantic.

Implementation and instrumentation

Create paraphrase groups with identical gold label, compare confusion matrices and confidence calibration, and keep locked label definitions in trusted instruction modules.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

Paraphrase ensembles raise cost; a dedicated classifier may offer lower per-request cost and latency at volume.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

High paraphrase agreement can be consistently wrong; robustness must be paired with gold accuracy.

lessons.title: A chatbot leaks a proprietary system prompt
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why is a system prompt an unsafe secret store?
  2. How would you distinguish a fabricated leaked prompt from genuine exposure?
  3. What hard controls reduce impact even if prompt text is disclosed?
sections.text: Why is a system prompt an unsafe secret store? How would you distinguish a fabricated leaked prompt from genuine exposure? What hard controls reduce impact even if prompt text is disclosed?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

A system prompt is part of the model input and may be partially reproduced or inferred. Never store secrets, cryptographic tokens or privileged proprietary business rules whose disclosure would be catastrophic in model-visible instructions. Put enforcement logic, restricted documents, rate limits and permission checks behind APIs. Prompt hardening or leakage filters may reduce accidental disclosure, but should not be represented as complete secrecy.

Mathematics and invariants

Exposure impact is bounded by where the sensitive facts are stored and what privileges the model can invoke. In an ideal design, model-visible prompt contains no exploitable credential or authorization secret.

Architecture and alternatives

Separate guidance (“answer concisely”) from sensitive policy (“user A is allowed to transfer $X”). Restrict retrieval and secure tool services.

Implementation and instrumentation

Test extraction attempts with synthetic prompt canaries; log leaked canary IDs only, not the entire private prompt. Rotate actual exposed credentials.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

Heavier leakage detectors raise latency and may block legitimate requests for transparency; eliminating sensitive prompt content removes the most severe risk.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

A model refusing to print its prompt is not a secret-keeping guarantee. Redaction after generation does not prevent covert disclosure through tool arguments.

lessons.title: An agent is injected into revealing hidden instructions
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Where does the untrusted instruction become a dangerous capability?
  2. What if a summarizer rewrites the attack as a recommendation?
  3. How do you test action boundaries independently of model compliance?
sections.text: Where does the untrusted instruction become a dangerous capability? What if a summarizer rewrites the attack as a recommendation? How do you test action boundaries independently of model compliance?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

With tools, the critical risk is not just revealing words but allowing an external observation to cause privileged actions. Attack path: retrieve third-party content → model misclassifies it as instructions → suggests a tool call → orchestration executes. Defense path: data-channel isolation, tool ACL and egress restrictions, independent argument validation and human approval. Persist a trust label and source reference for each observation; do not let summaries silently launder instructions into durable memory.

Mathematics and invariants

Outcome measure = unauthorized executed actions / adversarial opportunities, supplemented by proposed forbidden calls, detector recall and benign-task success. Zero executed actions is the security gate; lower attempted calls is a secondary signal.

Architecture and alternatives

ReAct with guarded tools can be safe enough for read-only research; high-risk email/file deletion requires explicit approval and idempotent execution outside model.

Implementation and instrumentation

Include cross-turn, web/tool-output, markdown-link and encoded attack fixtures in a sandbox; record source ID and the exact authorization denial point.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

Tool validation adds tiny overhead compared with an LLM call; approval may add user latency but protects high-impact actions.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

Prompt sanitization alone misses malicious semantics. A “summarizer” tool can produce instruction-like output if trust labels are lost.

lessons.title: CoT prompting is not improving reasoning accuracy
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why might reasoning text not reflect causal reasoning?
  2. When should you remove a CoT instruction entirely?
  3. How do you distinguish reasoning failure from missing facts?
sections.text: Why might reasoning text not reflect causal reasoning? When should you remove a CoT instruction entirely? How do you distinguish reasoning failure from missing facts?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

A reasoning prompt may fail when the task is not reasoning-limited, the model already performs internal deliberation, demonstrations contain false steps, tokens are budgeted poorly, or the metric rewards fluent explanations rather than correct answers. Segment tasks into arithmetic, symbolic logic, retrieval, ambiguity and multi-hop; verify tool use and answer extraction. Compare direct, concise step summary, external calculator and multiple-sample strategies on paired, untouched cases.

Mathematics and invariants

Net value per task ΔV = task_success_gain·value − added_tokens·rate − added_latency·penalty. If reasoning only lengthens wrong answers, ΔV<0.

Architecture and alternatives

For exact math choose verified computation; for evidence missing choose retrieval; for combinatorial reasoning consider bounded search; for easy extraction choose direct generation.

Implementation and instrumentation

Collect correctness, tokens, p95 latency, unsupported intermediate claims and failure categories with prompt/model versions.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

Reasoning can increase output/hidden computation and provider cost; retries multiply the effect.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

Beware falsely inferring reasoning quality from verbal detail. Inspect whether gold answers are unambiguous and the benchmark is uncontaminated.

lessons.title: AI works in English but fails in other languages
lessons.subtitle: Applied engineering mechanisms, evidence, trade-offs and operational decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How do you isolate retrieval vs generation language failures?
  2. What if OCR fails before the LLM sees the content?
  3. Why is English-backtranslation insufficient to evaluate Bengali?
sections.text: How do you isolate retrieval vs generation language failures? What if OCR fails before the LLM sees the content? Why is English-backtranslation insufficient to evaluate Bengali?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
Internal operation and data flow

Root causes include uneven model data, token fragmentation, poor translated labels, regional conventions, script normalization, language-mismatched retrieval and biased guardrails. Establish native-language golden cases with bilingual reviewers; compare input processing, retrieval recall, model answer quality and output formatting separately. Prefer locale-specific instruction/examples and terminology lists only when validated.

Mathematics and invariants

Error decomposition by language: P(success_l)≈P(retrieve_l)·P(generate_correct_l|evidence)·P(parse_l|correct), as an approximate diagnostic factorization.

Architecture and alternatives

Direct multilingual vs translation pivots must be compared on native gold; a domain-specific small model may improve one language but sacrifice other coverage.

Implementation and instrumentation

Record locale, source language, embedding-model version, tokenizer statistics, script form, and expected numeric/date conventions.

Latency, cost, memory and scaling

Longer tokens may elevate costs and shrink context. Translation pipelines add overhead and introduce semantic drift.

Failures, misconceptions and mitigation

English-aligned LLM judges often favor English phrasing; avoid only back-translated English ground truth.
