lessons.title: Your RAG system fails on domain-specific jargon. How do you fix it?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism → proof → architecture → debugging → measurable decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. When is a glossary safer than embedding fine-tuning?
  2. How do you select hard negatives?
  3. What failure mode comes from ambiguous acronyms?
sections.text: When is a glossary safer than embedding fine-tuning? How do you select hard negatives? What failure mode comes from ambiguous acronyms?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step mechanism / data flow

Domain jargon causes semantic mismatch when embeddings see uncommon acronyms, product codes or specialized usage. Analyze failures by tokenization, abbreviations, lexical matching, ontology synonyms, multilingual vocabulary and versioned terminology. Build hard negatives around terms that look similar but mean different things.

2 · Equations, symbols and invariants

Query expansion may create q’=q∪synonyms(q), but expansion precision matters. Contrastive fine-tuning minimizes loss over positive/hard-negative pairs to reshape representation of domain terms.

3 · Architecture, options and when they win

Start BM25+dense hybrid, curated synonym/alias maps and field boosts; domain embeddings or ColBERT only when paired evaluation shows persistent misses.

4 · Implementation, APIs and instrumentation

Build glossary with exact product IDs, approved aliases and disallowed synonym collisions. Include glossary version in trace; preserve literal query terms in search.

5 · Latency, compute, memory, cost and scaling

Query expansion adds candidate volume and rerank cost; fine-tuning requires data and retraining infrastructure. Hybrid index may increase footprint.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions and mitigation

Over-expanding “RA” in medical vs finance contexts can retrieve dangerously incorrect passages; blind model fine-tuning may forget general semantic retrieval.

lessons.title: Your text-only RAG system now needs to handle images and tables. How do you extend it?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism → proof → architecture → debugging → measurable decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How do you index a chart with no extractable text?
  2. Why is flattening a table dangerous?
  3. How do you cite an image-derived claim?
sections.text: How do you index a chart with no extractable text? Why is flattening a table dangerous? How do you cite an image-derived claim?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step mechanism / data flow

For images/tables, extraction must represent visual evidence rather than pretend all content is flat text. Parse PDF geometry, detect figures/table regions, preserve captions and header hierarchy, add OCR for scanned text and image embeddings/VLM captions where needed. Index text and modality-specific representations with shared source/page coordinate IDs.

2 · Equations, symbols and invariants

A multimodal pipeline uses modality-specific e_text=f_t(text), e_img=f_v(image) or aligned space; similarity scores across uncalibrated spaces cannot be mixed directly. Aggregate answer evidence per source object and cell/region.

3 · Architecture, options and when they win

Text extraction for selectable PDFs, table-aware processors for tables, VLM image analysis for diagrams, and cross-modal retrieval when questions refer to visual content.

4 · Implementation, APIs and instrumentation

Store page bbox, cell row/column, OCR confidence, image crop hash, caption and original PDF version. Do not run VLM OCR on everything if selectable text is high quality.

5 · Latency, compute, memory, cost and scaling

Image embeddings and VLM vision passes increase storage and cost. Selective routing and cached extracted artifacts lower recurring expenses.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions and mitigation

Hallucinated chart labels, swapped column order and missing units are high-risk. Require original image/table verification for critical numeric claims.

lessons.title: Your RAG knowledge base gets updated frequently and needs versioning. How do you manage it?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism → proof → architecture → debugging → measurable decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. What exactly must a reproducible retrieval trace record?
  2. Can old index snapshots still serve deleted sensitive data?
  3. How do you dual-read during embedding migration?
sections.text: What exactly must a reproducible retrieval trace record? Can old index snapshots still serve deleted sensitive data? How do you dual-read during embedding migration?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step mechanism / data flow

Version the raw source, extracted page artifacts, segmentation settings, embedding model, index generation, ACLs, and graph summaries independently. Use immutable identifiers and content hashes; queries bind to a coherent published snapshot. Derived artifact lineage enables targeted rebuilding after parser/model changes.

2 · Equations, symbols and invariants

Lineage identity can be (source_id, source_version, parser_version, chunker_version, embed_version, acl_version). Query snapshot S must not join incompatible derived versions.

3 · Architecture, options and when they win

Content-addressed object storage + versioned index aliases is simple; event sourcing supports audit history; full reindex is easiest to reason about but too costly at high update frequency.

4 · Implementation, APIs and instrumentation

Run idempotent upserts with compare-and-swap publication pointer, tombstone deleted sources, reprocess impacted chunks and attach version to citations.

5 · Latency, compute, memory, cost and scaling

Multiple generations cost additional disk until garbage collection; incremental updates save compute but create reconciliation and compaction complexity.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions and mitigation

Embedding model dimension changes invalidate old vectors; silently mixing them will yield meaningless similarity. ACL revocations must override historical snapshots in live queries.

lessons.title: Your RAG system fails on multi-hop questions that require combining multiple facts. How do you fix it?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism → proof → architecture → debugging → measurable decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. What does a hop-by-hop trace look like?
  2. When can a graph edge be trusted?
  3. How do you handle a missing hop?
sections.text: What does a hop-by-hop trace look like? When can a graph edge be trusted? How do you handle a missing hop?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step mechanism / data flow

For multi-hop misses, inspect per-hop retrieval, not just the final answer. Translate question into entity- and relation-specific subgoals, retrieve evidence for each hop, disambiguate referents and verify all joins before composing an answer. Try deterministic query decomposition first; bounded agent/graph traversal for uncertain dependencies.

2 · Equations, symbols and invariants

If hop i has recall r_i, idealized P(all hops found)≈Π r_i under independence; correlated errors, shared documents and adaptive searches break the approximation. Measure joint hop coverage directly.

3 · Architecture, options and when they win

Parent-child can restore local multi-fact context; multi-query handles distributed facts; graphs help typed relations; agents add adaptive sequencing at cost of control and latency.

4 · Implementation, APIs and instrumentation

Record hop graph, query transformations, candidate passages, entity IDs, version constraints and derived join; prohibit conclusions with unverified dependency.

5 · Latency, compute, memory, cost and scaling

Multiple rounds multiply latency and retrieval cost; parallel independent hops and early-stop on insufficiency help meet budget.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions and mitigation

Entity/coreference drift, stale timelines and single-hop-only evaluation lead to confident false joins. A plausible conclusion is not proof.

lessons.title: Your enterprise RAG system returns contradictory answers from different source documents. How do you resolve conflicts?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism → proof → architecture → debugging → measurable decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why not always trust the newest document?
  2. How do you represent authority and scope?
  3. When should the assistant show two conflicting answers?
sections.text: Why not always trust the newest document? How do you represent authority and scope? When should the assistant show two conflicting answers?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step mechanism / data flow

Contradictory answers arise from outdated versions, regional policies, authority hierarchy differences, effective dates, source errors and genuinely unresolved conflicts. Resolve facts by explicit precedence policies (effective period, owner authority, document status and principal scope). If conflicts remain, present both with provenance or abstain rather than silently selecting by similarity.

2 · Equations, symbols and invariants

A precedence key may be (scope_match, authoritative_rank, effective_date, publish_status); apply a domain-approved partial order. Similarity score must never define legal or policy authority.

3 · Architecture, options and when they win

Use version-aware rerank and contradiction detection with source metadata. For unresolved business policies require escalation to document owner/human.

4 · Implementation, APIs and instrumentation

Extract claims to typed records with entity, valid interval, scope, claim text and source. Detect mutually exclusive claims and compare precedence/authorization.

5 · Latency, compute, memory, cost and scaling

Contradiction detection adds model work; metadata-only resolution is cheaper but may not recognize substantive conflicts.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions and mitigation

Do not always choose newest file: a current regional exception may override global policy; two sources may be valid for different tenants.

lessons.title: Your RAG system returns outdated answers from an evolving knowledge base. How do you keep it current?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism → proof → architecture → debugging → measurable decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How is freshness different from recency?
  2. What invalidates semantic answer caches?
  3. What fallback is safe if ingestion is behind SLA?
sections.text: How is freshness different from recency? What invalidates semantic answer caches? What fallback is safe if ingestion is behind SLA?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step mechanism / data flow

Outdated answers need a freshness policy across connector ingest, derivative index, cache, selection and prompt. Record effective dates and source timestamps, and ensure the latest applicable published document wins. For mutable high-risk facts, bypass stale answer caches and optionally check a live authoritative API.

2 · Equations, symbols and invariants

End-to-end freshness lag = source_change→query_visible. Cache TTL bounds time-only expiration but does not ensure revocation; event invalidation and generation-bound cache keys reduce stale exposure.

3 · Architecture, options and when they win

Scheduled reconciliation ensures eventual repair; event-driven update reduces latency; live tools are best for highly volatile state when safe and available.

4 · Implementation, APIs and instrumentation

Trace source_version, published_index_generation, answer_cache_generation and policy_valid_at. Reject stale version if user requests “latest” and no verified current source is available.

5 · Latency, compute, memory, cost and scaling

Short TTL increases source and embedding load; aggressive caching improves p95 but may violate freshness SLO. Separate low-risk historical queries from time-critical policy.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions and mitigation

The most recently ingested doc may not be most authoritative or currently effective; timestamps can refer to ingestion, not policy validity.

lessons.title: Your RAG system struggles with PDF documents containing tables and layouts. How do you fix PDF parsing?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism → proof → architecture → debugging → measurable decisions.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Explain a layout-aware PDF parsing pipeline end to end.
  2. When is OCR insufficient even at high character accuracy?
  3. How do you measure correct table-to-answer grounding?
sections.text: Explain a layout-aware PDF parsing pipeline end to end. When is OCR insufficient even at high character accuracy? How do you measure correct table-to-answer grounding?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step mechanism / data flow

Complex PDFs encode information spatially: multiple columns, tables with spanning cells, headers, footers, equations, figures and scanned pages. Extraction pipeline detects born-digital vs image-only pages, reads glyph geometry, infers layout/reading order, recognizes tables as structured objects, uses OCR selectively, and preserves page coordinates for citations.

2 · Equations, symbols and invariants

Table fidelity is not simply text recall. Evaluate cell extraction precision/recall, row-column header association and numeric exact match; for OCR use character error rate CER = edit_distance(pred,true)/|true|.

3 · Architecture, options and when they win

Prefer native text and layout extraction for digital PDFs; OCR/layout models for scans; multimodal document models for graphics and highly complex formatting. Hybrid page-specific routing avoids overusing expensive vision models.

4 · Implementation, APIs and instrumentation

Emit typed blocks: TextBlock(page,bbox,reading_order), Table(rows,columns,header_paths,spans), Figure(crop,caption), and references. Visual-check low-confidence pages against originals before indexing.

5 · Latency, compute, memory, cost and scaling

Full-page vision passes are expensive; OCR may add hundreds of ms per page depending on hardware. Background ingestion hides runtime cost but must meet freshness SLO.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions and mitigation

Linearized tables can swap numbers, orphan footnotes or read columns in wrong order; confident text cannot validate visual semantics. Do not cite OCR output alone when critical values are unclear.

title: AI Agents & Agentic Systems
description: Agent loops, MCP, orchestration, memory, tool governance, and safety.

lessons.title: What is an AI agent, and how does it differ from a simple LLM call?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Trace a request from user goal through model, tool, observation and final state.
  2. When is an agent unnecessary?
  3. What must remain deterministic outside the model?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: Trace a request from user goal through model, tool, observation and final state. When is an agent unnecessary? What must remain deterministic outside the model? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

An agent is a closed-loop controller over an environment: a runtime assembles goal and state; an LLM proposes a response or typed action; a policy gateway validates tool, arguments and caller permissions; an executor performs the operation; an observation is recorded; the loop repeats until a verifiable terminal condition or budget stop. One model completion without observation/action feedback is a workflow step, not a full autonomous tool-use loop.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Model as partially observable decision process with state s_t, observation o_t, action a_t and transition P(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t). Practical tool agent is a bounded approximation, not necessarily an RL policy. Total cost C=Σ_t(C_model,t+C_tool,t); retries and dependent steps compound delay.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Use a direct LLM call for extraction/summarization; deterministic pipeline for known steps; agent loop when the next action depends on evidence not known up front. An agent is not inherently more accurate.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Store objective, approved tool list, principal, budgets, message/observation ledger and terminal validator separately. Tool side effects happen only in host application, not because model emitted text.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Latency increases with sequential LLM/tool round trips, token replays and queueing. Measure per-run success, steps, cost, side-effect errors and p95 latency.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Infinite loops, hallucinated tools, unwanted actions, stale observations and prompt injections are dominant risks. Bounded loops, scoped credentials and fail-closed execution mitigate them.

lessons.title: AI Agent Memory
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Design short- and long-term memory for a multi-tenant agent.
  2. How can memory make performance worse?
  3. How do you support right-to-delete and corrections?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: Design short- and long-term memory for a multi-tenant agent. How can memory make performance worse? How do you support right-to-delete and corrections? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Agent memory exists in at least four layers: working context for current reasoning, checkpointed task/conversation state, persistent user/project facts and historical episode records. A retrieval policy selects memory based on relevance, freshness, source and authorization; a write policy determines what may become durable.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

One retrieval objective: score(m,q)=α·relevance(m,q)+β·recency(m)+γ·confidence(m)−δ·privacyRisk(m). Weights are policy parameters, not model-internal constants. Memory precision and stale-memory rate matter more than raw stored fact count.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Window summaries are cheap; structured database state fits transactional tasks; vector memory enables semantic recall; graph memory tracks relations. Do not conflate a KV cache with persistent agent memory.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Memory record: {tenant,principal,kind,source,created_at,expires_at,confidence,version,content}. Permission checks apply at retrieval and writes; add deletion, provenance and conflict resolution.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Cross-session search adds retrieval latency and storage; repeated embedding and unbounded history raise cost. Cache stable summaries but invalidate on edits and ACL changes.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Confident false memories, cross-user leakage, forgotten corrections and polluted episodic logs cause failures. Verify consequential memories against authoritative sources before acting.

lessons.title: Harness Engineering in AI
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Draw the minimum harness around an LLM to edit files safely.
  2. Which correctness properties must be independent of model obedience?
  3. How do you evaluate harness improvements without model confounding?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: Draw the minimum harness around an LLM to edit files safely. Which correctness properties must be independent of model obedience? How do you evaluate harness improvements without model confounding? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

A harness is all non-weight software surrounding the model: prompt/context assembly, tool catalog and dispatcher, state machine, checkpoints, permission enforcement, sandboxing, failure recovery, observability, verification and evaluation. The model proposes; the harness turns proposals into safe, reproducible actions.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

End-to-end reliability is limited by product of conditional stage success probabilities under an independence approximation: P(success)≈∏_i p_i. Actual stages are dependent, so use traced end-to-end tests.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

A thin harness improves speed for narrow read-only tasks; a durable policy-rich harness is needed for side-effecting, long-running enterprise agents. Avoid adding orchestration layers that do not remove a measured failure.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Wrap every tool with typed validation, explicit principal, deadline, idempotency key, structured result, replay log and risk-based approval. Persist commit status independently from LLM messages.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Harness overhead increases initial complexity, but can reduce destructive incidents and retry waste. Budget queueing, serialization and sandbox startup, not only model latency.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

A clever system prompt cannot replace authorization, idempotency or rollback. Side-effect replay after crash is a classic harness defect.

lessons.title: What matters more for an agentic coding tool like Claude Code: the model or the harness?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How would you isolate the model effect from tool/harness effect?
  2. What evidence shows that better tools beat better reasoning?
  3. When does harness complexity reduce performance?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: How would you isolate the model effect from tool/harness effect? What evidence shows that better tools beat better reasoning? When does harness complexity reduce performance? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Model and harness are complementary, not competitors. A stronger model may plan, reason and choose tools better; a better coding harness exposes repository topology, diffs, targeted search, tests, sandbox and feedback so the model can verify work. Their interaction determines delivered value.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Counterfactual experiment: a 2×2 factorial design over model M₁/M₂ and harness H₁/H₂ isolates main effects and an interaction term in success ~ M+H+M×H. Report task-mix and uncertainty.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Improve model when reasoning/tool-selection errors dominate; improve harness when missing context, invalid interfaces, absent tests, repeated work or unsafe writes dominate.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Record git baseline, patch diff, tests, trace, tool results and human verdict. Run the same benchmark tasks across fixed code snapshots with matched budgets.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Larger models may cost more and still fail when file access or test tooling is broken. More tooling may inflate context and tool-choice error.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Do not claim a proprietary coding assistant’s entire private architecture is public. Discuss observable product patterns and general harness primitives.

lessons.title: Explain the ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) agent architecture.
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Walk through a three-step ReAct trace with actual observations.
  2. Why might ReAct perform worse than fixed chains?
  3. How would you detect no progress?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: Walk through a three-step ReAct trace with actual observations. Why might ReAct perform worse than fixed chains? How would you detect no progress? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

ReAct alternates language-model deliberation with actions and external observations: goal → proposed tool call → execution → observation → updated choice. Modern systems usually encode actions as structured tool calls rather than parsing fragile textual “Action:” lines. Observations are untrusted data and are appended only after validation.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

At each step choose a_t ~ π(a|goal,history_t); history_{t+1}=history_t⊕observation(tool(a_t)). Terminate on final answer validated, no useful action, error, time, steps or cost cap.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

ReAct suits exploratory tasks with unknown next evidence; a precomputed plan suits stable dependencies; deterministic DAG wins for known business processes. ReAct has high serial latency.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

A loop dispatches action only if in allowlist, schema-valid and authorized; captures tool_call_id and result; writes checkpoint; checks stop predicates before next model call.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Worst-case model round trips bounded by max_steps. Tool latency can dominate; parallelize independent reads but serialize dependent writes.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Loops can repeat identical failed searches, mistake page text for instructions, or stop before verifying success. Add progress detection, loop fingerprints and evidence validators.

lessons.title: What is the Plan-and-Execute agent pattern?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How do you model dependencies and parallel tasks?
  2. When should the agent replan rather than retry?
  3. How does a checkpoint prevent duplicate publication?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: How do you model dependencies and parallel tasks? When should the agent replan rather than retry? How does a checkpoint prevent duplicate publication? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Plan-and-execute separates a planning stage that creates an explicit dependency graph from execution of its nodes. A controller tracks states pending/running/succeeded/failed/blocked; a replanner runs only when a dependency changes or evidence invalidates the plan.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

For DAG G=(V,E), earliest start(v)=max_{u∈pred(v)}finish(u). Critical-path latency is Σ weights along the longest dependency path, not the sum of all parallel tasks.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Choose fixed DAG for repeatable work; plan-and-execute for partially known multistep tasks; ReAct for high uncertainty and cheap exploratory probes. Replanning can be expensive and unstable.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Plan node schema {task_id,inputs,dependencies,tool,verification,side_effect,risk}; enforce monotonic node-state transitions and idempotent writes.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Excessively fine-grained plans generate many model calls. Batch adjacent cheap tasks and parallelize independent nodes under rate and quota constraints.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Plans drift from current state; stale success markers propagate downstream. Require revalidation on changed artifacts and compensating actions for irreversible steps.

lessons.title: What is tool use (function calling) in LLMs, and how does it enable agents?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why is a function call not necessarily an action?
  2. Where do you enforce ownership checks?
  3. How should tool errors be presented to the model?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: Why is a function call not necessarily an action? Where do you enforce ownership checks? How should tool errors be presented to the model? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Function calling is a model emitting a structured request such as {name:"lookup_invoice",arguments:{id:"INV-9"}}. The application—not the model—validates arguments, authorizes the operation, invokes the implementation, captures output and returns it as an observation. It can be used by a simple one-shot assistant or within a full agent loop.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Let action proposal a=(name,args). Execute only if name∈Allowed(principal) ∧ validate(args,schema) ∧ authorize(principal,resource,action). Schema validation is necessary but not authorization.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Tool calls outperform prose parsing when providers support typed interfaces. Prefer narrow high-level domain APIs over exposing shell, SQL or unbounded generic HTTP.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Define strict schemas, enums, bounds, required fields, stable description, effect class, timeouts and error contracts. Bind principal server-side rather than let model supply user ID.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Each call adds network, serialization and backend latency; repeated tool descriptions consume tokens. Tool discovery limits can reduce prompt overhead.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Model may hallucinate a name or arguments; “syntactically valid” can still cause an invalid business action. Fail safe without allowing the model to override policy.

lessons.title: What is the difference between structured output and function calling?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Show an output-schema example and a tool schema example.
  2. Why is JSON validity insufficient for safety?
  3. When is tool calling a poor abstraction?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: Show an output-schema example and a tool schema example. Why is JSON validity insufficient for safety? When is tool calling a poor abstraction? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Structured output constrains or validates the model’s returned data object, commonly to a JSON schema; function calling asks the model to request an application operation with typed parameters. Both may use similar decoding constraints but have different semantics: representing a result versus triggering a capability.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

For schema S, syntax validity is Parse(y)∈S; semantic validity requires predicates such as total≥0, currency known, customer ownership. No decoder grammar alone proves factual correctness.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Use schema output for classification/extraction. Use tool calling for read/write effects. A function can return a schema but must still be explicitly dispatched.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Validate JSON with a parser, enforce additional business constraints, produce machine-readable errors, and cap repair attempts. Ignore unexpected additional properties when strictness is required.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Constrained decoding reduces parse failures but can increase retries if impossible schemas are requested. Latency depends on schema complexity and provider support.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Valid JSON can contain invented invoice IDs. A tool call should never automatically run just because it is valid JSON in ordinary message text.

lessons.title: How do you design and define tools for an AI agent?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Rewrite a dangerous raw SQL tool into a safer domain API.
  2. What makes a tool schema easy for the model to use?
  3. How do you evaluate tool catalog growth?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: Rewrite a dangerous raw SQL tool into a safer domain API. What makes a tool schema easy for the model to use? How do you evaluate tool catalog growth? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Design tools around meaningful domain capabilities with clear preconditions, side effects and expected results. Inputs should minimize ambiguity, outputs should be bounded, and exposed operations should obey least privilege. Split read vs write and make irreversible operations require explicit approval.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Tool selection quality depends partly on overlap in descriptions and schema entropy. Reduce ambiguous choices: maximize distinguishability of intent→tool mapping and constrain parameter domains.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

A few domain-specific tools often beat dozens of low-level primitives. Tool combinatorics can be necessary for unknown workflows but raises selection and latency risks.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Contract includes name, purpose, schema with enums and ranges, principal from runtime, idempotency semantics, timeout, retriable error codes, observability, audit category and data classification.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Many unused schemas increase prompt tokens. Coarse tools reduce round trips but hide intermediate validation; balance granularity against observability.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Dangerous tools such as unrestricted shell, delete_any, raw_sql or send_email_without_review are authorization mistakes, not prompt-design problems.

lessons.title: How does an agent decide when to call a tool versus answering from its own knowledge?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. What makes a tool mandatory regardless of model confidence?
  2. How do you train/evaluate a retrieval router?
  3. What is the harm of eager tool calling?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: What makes a tool mandatory regardless of model confidence? How do you train/evaluate a retrieval router? What is the harm of eager tool calling? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

An agent’s retrieval/tool decision should depend on freshness, task uncertainty, availability of authoritative evidence, risk of hallucination and cost. A model can propose this decision, but the application must enforce mandatory checks for regulated, mutable or high-impact facts.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Expected value of tool: EV(call)=P(tool changes decision)·benefit−latencyCost−moneyCost−riskCost. This is a decision-theoretic heuristic, not a calibrated LLM probability unless measured.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Use deterministic routing for obvious database lookups; a learned router for ambiguous requests with strong offline labels; default to human escalation when action risk is high.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Record reason-for-call, required source freshness, chosen tool, confidence proxy, rejection reason and alternative no-tool outcome. Add forced verification before irreversible writes.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Over-calling tools inflates latency and cost; under-calling causes unsupported answers and stale knowledge. Optimize under task-level quality gates.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Model uncertainty estimates are often poorly calibrated. “I know this” does not satisfy mandatory evidence requirements.

lessons.title: What is the difference between single-agent and multi-agent systems?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. What is the difference between workers and role-play?
  2. Why can three agents be slower than one?
  3. How would you merge contradictory outputs?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: What is the difference between workers and role-play? Why can three agents be slower than one? How would you merge contradictory outputs? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

A single-agent system maintains one decision policy and shared task state; multi-agent systems delegate specialized subtasks to separate contexts or workers and combine their outputs. Multiple named roles are not automatically independent agents unless each has a meaningful decision/execution boundary.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

If m independent workers have duration L_i, ideal fanout critical path≈L_setup+max_i L_i+L_merge; serial coordination approaches Σ_i L_i. Communication and verification add overhead.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Use single agent when shared context and strong global consistency matter. Use multi-agent for bounded independent tasks, diverse expertise, isolation, or parallel evidence acquisition.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Coordinator assigns task IDs, contracts, deadlines, scope and evidence requirements; workers return structured artifacts with provenance; merger validates conflicts.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Multi-agent increases model invocations, context duplication, contention and merge cost. Parallelism helps only when dependencies allow it.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Role chatter, circular delegation, untrusted peer messages, conflicting edits and unclear ownership can decrease task success.

lessons.title: When do multi-agent systems break down, and when is a single agent the better choice?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Calculate the Amdahl upper bound for a partially parallel task.
  2. What signals show multi-agent overengineering?
  3. Why can majority vote be misleading?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: Calculate the Amdahl upper bound for a partially parallel task. What signals show multi-agent overengineering? Why can majority vote be misleading? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Multi-agent breakdown often comes from state fragmentation, stale plans, communication overhead, correlated model errors, handoff ambiguity and inconsistent permissions. Multiple workers reading the same low-quality evidence can amplify an identical mistake rather than diversify reasoning.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Useful parallelism bound by Amdahl: speedup≤1/[(1−p)+p/n], before coordination/merge overhead. With small parallelizable fraction p, more workers do little.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Prefer a single agent with good tools for sequential, low-entropy and tightly coupled tasks. Escalate to multi-agent only when a benchmark proves better quality or latency after cost.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Instrument per-worker inputs, task ownership, cross-agent message count, convergence loops and edit conflicts. Create an explicit coordinator quorum/merge policy.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Token usage commonly scales with replicated context; plus orchestration and verification. Enforce team-wide budgets, not only per-worker limits.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Consensus among identically prompted workers is not independent evidence. Groupthink and copying mistaken evidence create false confidence.

lessons.title: What is Model Context Protocol (MCP), and how does it standardize tool integration?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Draw the MCP client/server boundary and model boundary.
  2. Is MCP the same as function calling?
  3. How do remote server permissions and credentials work?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: Draw the MCP client/server boundary and model boundary. Is MCP the same as function calling? How do remote server permissions and credentials work? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

MCP standardizes how a client discovers and interacts with servers that expose tools, resources and prompts. In an agent host, the client discovers capabilities, advertises approved tools to a model, validates a proposed tool call, sends a protocol request to a server and returns structured results. MCP is an interoperability layer, not an authorization bypass or agent reasoning algorithm.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Separation of concerns: LLM action selection → host-side policy → MCP client transport/protocol → MCP server capability → external system. Protocol JSON-RPC-style calls do not prove user consent or data ownership.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Choose MCP when integrating a changing ecosystem of external capabilities; direct library calls may be simpler for one stable internal API. Resource and prompt surfaces have different trust and discovery expectations.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Pin a spec/SDK version, negotiate capabilities, validate schemas, control server trust, scope credentials, log resource provenance and restrict dangerous calls. July 2026 spec introduced stateless core and authorization changes; version-specific behavior must be checked.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Tool-list refresh, server startup and remote network hops affect latency. Many MCP servers increase tool-token catalog size and trust surface.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Tool metadata and returned documents are untrusted. A malicious server can inject instructions in descriptions; host approval and identity controls remain mandatory.

lessons.title: How does MCP differ from traditional function calling?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Can you use function calling without MCP?
  2. Can MCP expose resources without a callable function?
  3. Where should user consent be enforced?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: Can you use function calling without MCP? Can MCP expose resources without a callable function? Where should user consent be enforced? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Function calling is the model-to-host request format used to express a desired tool invocation. MCP describes a host/client-to-server integration protocol and discovery model. An MCP tool can be wrapped as a model function; the two layers are complementary and sometimes both are present on the same execution path.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Two contracts: proposal={name,args} and execution request={server,capability,args,caller}. Both must pass independent schema and authorization checks; do not confuse provider tool schema with MCP protocol envelope.

lessons.title: What are AI SubAgents?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How do you avoid recursive spawn storms?
  2. What state should a subagent be allowed to mutate?
  3. How should workers return evidence?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: How do you avoid recursive spawn storms? What state should a subagent be allowed to mutate? How should workers return evidence? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Subagents are specialized workers invoked by a supervising agent. They receive a scoped task, narrower context and tools, produce a bounded deliverable and return control to the supervisor. They may run concurrently for independent tasks or sequentially when results depend on one another.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Total context cost C≈C_supervisor+Σ C_worker_i. Context isolation lowers irrelevant information per worker but duplication and summarization can increase total tokens.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Use subagents for parallel read-only research or separate test/debug tasks; avoid them for tiny tasks or writes to overlapping resources without coordination.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Contract: run_id, parent_run_id, task, permitted tools, authorized data scope, cost/step deadline, output schema and stop reason. Supervisor verifies outputs instead of blindly forwarding.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Subagents add startup and handoff latency. Async fanout helps only if independent and within provider concurrency limits.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Recursive spawning can explode costs; a worker may conceal tool failures in a cheerful summary. Bound depth, fanout and evidence requirements.

lessons.title: What are the different types of agent memory (short-term, long-term, episodic)?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. What distinguishes a checkpoint from episodic memory?
  2. How do you resolve contradictory memories?
  3. When should the agent refuse to store a fact?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: What distinguishes a checkpoint from episodic memory? How do you resolve contradictory memories? When should the agent refuse to store a fact? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Short-term memory tracks current conversation/task; semantic long-term memory stores durable facts and preferences; episodic memory stores past action/outcome trajectories; procedural memory stores reusable instructions or skills. These classifications overlap but have different read/write, decay and verification policies.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Retrieval accuracy=correct memories retrieved / all memories retrieved; usefulness also depends on action impact and freshness. Treat memories as hypotheses with provenance, not immutable ground truth.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Checkpoints store exact execution state; a vector database provides fuzzy fact lookup; a relational store suits durable declarative state; skill files represent procedures. No single store serves every role.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Partition by principal and tenant, assign TTL/status/verification, implement consent and deletion; use search + re-ranking for recall and explicit contradiction handling.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Writing every observation to long-term storage causes noise, stale beliefs and embedding cost. Summarize episodic traces only after outcome verification.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

A memory can be accurate at creation but harmful later; stale professional role, deleted document and changed user preference require time scope.

lessons.title: How do you handle agent failures and implement error recovery?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How do you distinguish timeout from failure?
  2. How do you resume after a process crash?
  3. Which failures should never be retried automatically?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: How do you distinguish timeout from failure? How do you resume after a process crash? Which failures should never be retried automatically? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Classify failures: invalid model schema, tool rejection, network timeout, transient rate limit, external side-effect ambiguity, policy denial, state conflict and human cancellation. The controller should map each class to retry, replan, escalate, compensate or terminate; one catch-all retry is unsafe.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

For exponential backoff t_n=min(t_max,t_0·2^n)+jitter; retry bound and deadline constrain amplification. Expected attempts for independent transient failure p (uncapped) =1/(1−p), but side effects make blind repetition dangerous.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Idempotent GET-like reads can retry automatically; writes need idempotency keys, status queries or a transactional outbox. Noncompensable operations require explicit approval.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Persist intent + effect ID + state before executing; on restart reconcile UNKNOWN effects against authoritative system. Emit structured ToolError(code,retriable,occurred,correlation_id).

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Retries worsen incident load and p99 if not bounded; circuit breakers and backpressure protect dependencies.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

A timeout does not prove a payment failed. Retrying an unkeyed charge can double-bill. Never have the LLM infer effect status from missing response.

lessons.title: What is an agent loop, and how does it decide when to stop?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. What are all legitimate stop conditions?
  2. What should happen on budget exhaustion mid-task?
  3. Can the LLM decide its own success?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: What are all legitimate stop conditions? What should happen on budget exhaustion mid-task? Can the LLM decide its own success? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

The agent loop is an explicit state machine: PREPARE → MODEL → VALIDATE → EXECUTE → OBSERVE → CHECKPOINT → MODEL or TERMINATE. Stop on verifiable goal completion, explicit refusal, human cancel, no-progress threshold, wall-clock deadline, step/tool/token limit or unsafe condition.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Termination condition = goal_verified ∨ deadline_hit ∨ steps≥S_max ∨ cost≥B_max ∨ unsafe ∨ cancelled. A budget check belongs before every billable/model and tool action.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Rule-based workflow can stop deterministically; open-ended ReAct needs progress estimation and safety caps. Model’s own “finished” claim must be checked for consequential tasks.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Keep immutable run_id, step index, action hash, observed evidence, cumulative usage and current state in transactional storage. Reconcile after crash.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Worst-case calls S_max; long tool timeouts consume wall time even if token budget is untouched. Enforce both.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

A partial plan may be marked done without its side effects; identical observations may create loops. Detect repeated state+action signatures.

lessons.title: Context Engineering
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. What belongs in a prompt versus the database state?
  2. How do you decide what to evict?
  3. How do you prevent untrusted retrieved text from modifying policy?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: What belongs in a prompt versus the database state? How do you decide what to evict? How do you prevent untrusted retrieved text from modifying policy? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Context engineering is the runtime process of selecting, ordering, sanitizing and budgeting everything the model sees: durable task intent, recent observations, relevant documents, policies, tool contracts, partial results and memory. The boundary between trusted instructions and untrusted content is as important as relevance.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Token budget: T_input=T_policy+T_goal+T_history+T_tools+T_evidence+T_state ≤ T_window−T_output_reserve−T_safety_margin. Rank content by expected marginal task utility per token, subject to mandatory safety/context constraints.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Full history is easiest but costly; targeted retrieval plus typed working state scales better. Summaries compress but may erase crucial negations and identifiers.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Maintain a typed context manifest including source, priority, age, trust class and token count. Keep a separate authoritative state object outside the prompt; never let retrieved text redefine tool permissions.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Excessive context raises prefill cost and may worsen answer quality. Cache immutable tool descriptions/long stable prefixes where supported.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Lost-in-middle, contaminated summaries, stale context, hidden source versions and quote-to-instruction promotion lead to failures.

lessons.title: How does context compaction work?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Show your compaction schema.
  2. What must never be summarized away?
  3. How do you quantify compaction hallucination?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: Show your compaction schema. What must never be summarized away? How do you quantify compaction hallucination? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Compaction converts a long trajectory into a shorter state representation. Freeze a checkpoint, identify invariant instructions and pending obligations, extract verified facts and unresolved questions, serialize a structured summary with references, validate it against state and then replace redundant history while retaining a replay log.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Compression ratio r=T_before/T_after; quality must be measured as retained-task-fact recall and constraint preservation, not just r. A simple cost criterion favors compact if saved future prefill > compaction inference + verification cost.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Sliding window is cheap but forgets distant constraints; rolling summary retains narrative but may distort facts; event-sourced state + targeted retrieval is more auditable.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Separate facts vs hypotheses; preserve exact IDs, dates, permissions, pending tool effects and approval state. Include summary version and pointers to raw events for audit/recovery.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Periodic compaction adds a model call but prevents quadratic replay-like cost over long sessions. Compact at measured thresholds rather than every turn.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Lossy summaries can silently convert “customer requested draft” into “customer approved send.” Verify critical state mechanically.

1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Loop engineering tunes the model–tool execution cycle: routing, action validation, observation formatting, feedback quality, stop policy and cost/retry limits. It treats progress as an engineering signal rather than hoping more reasoning steps help.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Progress p_t may combine verified completed milestones, newly acquired evidence and reduction of open blockers. Trigger stagnation if Δp_t≈0 for r successive steps; use calibrated task-specific thresholds.

React-style dynamic loop is flexible; deterministic loops with branching win when transitions are known; adaptive loops choose routes based on observed errors.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Long loops explode cumulative prompt and tool cost. Summaries, tool result truncation and early verified stop limit amplification.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Overly aggressive stop rules kill solvable tasks; too generous limits invite runaway compute. Optimize failure-aware task success against p95 and dollars.

lessons.title: Graph Engineering
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Compare a durable graph to a while-loop agent.
  2. What does a state reducer do?
  3. How do you safely re-enter a node after restart?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: Compare a durable graph to a while-loop agent. What does a state reducer do? How do you safely re-enter a node after restart? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Graph engineering models agent workflows as named nodes, typed shared state and conditional transitions. Nodes may be deterministic functions, model calls, tools, approvals or subgraphs. Checkpointing records transitions so work can resume after failure or human interruption.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

For directed graph G=(V,E), execution trace is path v₀→…→v_k with branch predicates over state; termination and liveness require bounded cycles or a monotone progress measure. For parallel branches specify merge algebra to avoid lost updates.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Use a graph when branching, durable interruptions, concurrency or auditability justify it. A straight pipeline is clearer than graph orchestration for two trivial calls.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Define typed state fields and reducers; make transition contracts explicit; checkpoint before risky external effects and after confirmed completion; support thread-scoped concurrency locks.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Graph checkpoints cost I/O; excessive node granularity adds orchestration overhead. Parallel branches lower wall-time if they do not fight over shared state.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Race conditions, nondeterministic reducers, repeated side effects during replay and stale approvals are key hazards.

lessons.title: How AI Agents Communicate?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Design a multi-agent message envelope.
  2. How does peer trust differ from system trust?
  3. When is a shared state store better than chat messages?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: Design a multi-agent message envelope. How does peer trust differ from system trust? When is a shared state store better than chat messages? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Agents communicate by passing typed messages, artifacts or shared-state events. Communication needs sender identity, correlation ID, task ownership, evidence provenance, schema and deadline. A coordinator routes work and resolves conflicts; direct peer exchange increases flexibility but complicates trust.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Communication overhead grows with topology: central star O(n) coordinator connections; unrestricted all-to-all can have O(n²) pairwise channels. Message count is a workload property, not automatically O(n²).

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Prefer structured artifact handoffs over long prose. Shared blackboard fits collaboration; request-response fits delegation; event bus fits asynchronous lifecycle integration.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Envelope {sender,run_id,task_id,artifact_type,version,evidence,deadline,signature} and schema validation; treat every peer’s text as untrusted even within the company.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Serial handoffs slow critical path; large broadcast messages duplicate tokens. Limit scope and use artifact references rather than copying full documents.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Unclear ownership, stale messages, compromised workers and circular delegations cause failures. Apply per-agent privileges and max conversation turns.

lessons.title: What are Agent Skills?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. What is progressive disclosure?
  2. Is a skill the same as a tool or an MCP server?
  3. How would you verify a file-changing skill?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: What is progressive disclosure? Is a skill the same as a tool or an MCP server? How would you verify a file-changing skill? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Agent Skills package reusable task knowledge in a discoverable directory. A typical portable structure has SKILL.md with YAML name/description and procedure, optional references, scripts and assets. An agent first sees lightweight metadata, loads the procedure when relevant, then consults resources on demand (progressive disclosure).

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Context economy: catalog cost≈Σ metadata tokens; loading all full skill bodies upfront costs Σ full_body_tokens; progressive loading pays only for selected skills. Overlapping descriptions raise activation ambiguity.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Skills are procedural knowledge, not automatically executable tool privileges. Tool permissions remain governed by the host; skills can be versioned, reviewed and tested.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Implement skill registry with version, source, content hash, compatibility, provenance and tests. Treat downloaded skills as untrusted; review scripts and disallow silent shell/network execution.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Skill selection can save recurring prompt tokens but activation overhead and broad match rules may trigger wrong workflows.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Unverified skills can inject instructions or run harmful scripts. “Skill passed once” is not evidence for all future tasks; use replay evaluation and permission-bound execution.

lessons.title: How do you evaluate and test AI agents?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. What is a proper agent gold task?
  2. Why is answer-only judging inadequate?
  3. How do you design failure injection?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: What is a proper agent gold task? Why is answer-only judging inadequate? How do you design failure injection? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Agent evaluation must separate outcome, trajectory, safety and efficiency. A task suite has initial environment snapshot, user goal, authorized tools, expected state changes, forbidden effects and deterministic/verifiable success checks. Replay in isolated environments, inspect complete traces and pair offline results with production shadow tests.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Task success=verified completed tasks / evaluated tasks. Tool selection precision = correct selected actions/all selected; recovery rate=successful recovered failures/injected recoverable failures. Track p50/p95 cost and latency and confidence intervals for key rates.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Golden tests are repeatable; randomized/adversarial tasks test robustness; human eval captures usefulness; LLM-as-judge helps scale but must be calibrated on human labels. Avoid benchmark-only optimization.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Capture tool-call graph, arguments, timestamps, sandbox diffs, checkpoints, model/tool versions, final state and human approvals. Inject timeouts, stale evidence, prompt injection and rate limits.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Evaluating long trajectories is expensive; sampling and tiered gates help, but always run critical safety tests fully.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

A correct final answer can hide unauthorized intermediate actions. Outcome-only scoring misses dangerous trajectories and replay bugs.

lessons.title: What are the security risks of agentic systems, and how do you mitigate them?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Draw the trust boundaries of web→model→tool.
  2. Which controls survive a fully compromised model output?
  3. How do you detect cross-tenant memory leaks?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Agent security spans prompt injection, data exfiltration, excessive agency, insecure tools, secrets exposure, compromised connectors, cross-tenant memory, sandbox escapes and irreversible effects. Enforce least privilege and dataflow policy at runtime, not only through a system prompt.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Allow(action)=identity_ok∧authz(principal,resource,verb)∧scope_ok∧policy_ok∧approval_if_required. A prompt cannot change this Boolean policy.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Defense in depth: trusted policy engine, tool allowlist, data classification, origin-bound credentials, outbound network egress limits, sandbox, approval ledger and event audit. Model guardrails are useful detectors but not permission enforcement.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Tag observations with trust origin; validate arguments; redact secrets before model/tool boundary; monitor cross-domain sends; restrict shell/filesystem by namespace and ACL.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Security filters and approvals add latency; apply risk tiers to maintain usability without compromising high-impact operations.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Indirect injected instructions embedded in read-only documents can trigger tool calls if the model treats them as trusted. Reject unsafe operations regardless of model intent.

lessons.title: Your agent reads untrusted content (emails, web pages, documents) and can call tools. How do you prevent indirect prompt injection and data exfiltration?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How does an indirect injection differ from a malicious user command?
  2. What if the malicious content is in a tool description?
  3. Why is escaping text insufficient?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: How does an indirect injection differ from a malicious user command? What if the malicious content is in a tool description? Why is escaping text insufficient? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Indirect prompt injection enters through lower-trust content: email body, web page, PDF, tool description or search result. The model might interpret an instruction inside that content as a higher-priority command. The robust boundary is a policy-enforced executor that makes untrusted text incapable of granting capabilities.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

For any proposed exfiltration e=(src,dest,data), authorize only if principal may read src ∧ destination is allowlisted ∧ purpose is approved ∧ data policy permits transfer. String classifiers alone cannot prove this.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Treat retrieved material as quoted evidence; use isolated render/sandbox, origin labels and no secrets in unnecessary prompts. Avoid broad browser/authenticated sessions when read-only excerpts suffice.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Enforce destination/domain allowlists, per-tool egress policy, server-side credential binding, user confirmation for sending and content filtering. Keep a tamper-evident action log.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Injected content may be obfuscated or encoded. Token filtering has false positives/negatives; add authoritative controls beyond a detector.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Never let a retrieved “system notice” replace runtime instructions. Multimodal screenshots, metadata and tool catalogs are also attack surfaces.

lessons.title: What is the difference between reactive and proactive agents?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. What makes proactive execution riskier?
  2. How do you handle duplicated webhook events?
  3. When should a proactive agent ask a human?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: What makes proactive execution riskier? How do you handle duplicated webhook events? When should a proactive agent ask a human? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Reactive agents respond to a current request or event; proactive agents are scheduled or triggered by policies to pursue standing goals without a new chat message. Both need identity, event deduplication, state and stop conditions. Proactive execution requires stronger consent because actions may occur when the user is absent.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Trigger condition: event∧policy_preconditions∧budget_available∧not_duplicate. Time-based schedule, webhook and event stream have distinct delivery guarantees.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Prefer reactive for one-off user tasks; proactive for monitoring, remediation or scheduled summaries where a standing authorization and clear SLA exist.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Store task schedule/condition, principal, scopes, last event cursor, cooldown, approval tier and idempotency key; separate detection from action.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Polling too frequently increases cost; webhooks reduce latency but need duplicate handling. Cooldowns prevent alert storms.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

A proactive watcher can spam or act on stale alerts; protect with confidence thresholds, expiry and approval for high-impact changes.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why does token cost accelerate over a long conversation?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Every agent step consumes prompt prefill tokens, output tokens, tool calls and potentially worker contexts. A cost controller should estimate the next call from token forecast and model/provider price, choose a model tier, trim irrelevant observations, cache stable prefixes and enforce per-run and per-tenant limits.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Expected run cost C≈Σ_i(p_in·t_in,i+p_out·t_out,i+C_tool,i); growing transcript t_in,i can create superlinear cumulative costs over many turns. This is accounting math, not a performance benchmark.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Use cheap deterministic tools for narrow checks; small model for routing/extraction; stronger model for genuine reasoning bottlenecks. Compaction and subagent isolation require validation.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Reserve budget before dispatch; update actual usage afterwards; store cost ledger and abort at hard limit. Count subagent charges in parent run.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Latency and cost can oppose each other: batching reduces fixed overhead but may delay first result. Optimize cost per verified completed task.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Naive summary may drop safety constraints; aggressive cheap-model routing may harm complex tasks; enforce quality gates for each optimization.
