lessons.title: What is the human-in-the-loop pattern for agents, and when is it needed?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How do you bind approval to exact tool arguments?
  2. How does a run resume safely after a week?
  3. What should an expired approval do?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: How do you bind approval to exact tool arguments? How does a run resume safely after a week? What should an expired approval do? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Human-in-the-loop (HITL) is a controlled interrupt at a risk boundary: proposed action and evidence are shown; authorized human accepts, edits or rejects; signed approval is bound to exact parameters and expiry; execution revalidates against current state.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Approval key H=hash(canonical(action,params,resource_version,principal,scope)). Execute only when validApproval(H)∧notExpired∧policyAllows. This prevents “approve one thing, execute another.”

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Approval is appropriate for payments, deletions, external communications and irreversible changes. Routine read-only retrieval should generally proceed automatically.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Persist WAITING_FOR_APPROVAL in durable state; present diff, effects, source, estimated cost and rollback; resume with a stable run ID and version preconditions.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Human review adds queue wait and abandonment risk; use targeted high-risk checkpoints instead of approving every minor tool call.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Approval screenshots can become stale; user confirmation must not be reinterpreted after parameters change. Never bypass on timeout.

lessons.title: How do you implement guardrails for AI agents to prevent harmful actions?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why are model guardrails insufficient for tool authorization?
  2. Where would you place middleware?
  3. What does fail-closed mean for sensitive data?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: Why are model guardrails insufficient for tool authorization? Where would you place middleware? What does fail-closed mean for sensitive data? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Agent guardrails span pre-input hygiene, tool selection, argument/domain checks, side-effect authorization, output verification and continuous monitoring. Hard safety properties belong in deterministic host checks; LLM-based classifiers handle fuzzy risk signals with calibrated escalation.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Enforce predicate: authorized_user ∧ tool_allowed ∧ action_within_scope ∧ args_valid ∧ dataflow_allowed ∧ risk_approval. Detection score thresholds must be tuned with false-positive and false-negative costs.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Rule engine is predictable for legal constraints; classifier is flexible for ambiguous harmful content. Combine them, but do not let a probabilistic result override legal/permission checks.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Guardrail middleware logs policy version and decision reason; input sanitization cannot replace tool-side identity. Redact secrets at cloud boundary and enforce outbound destinations.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Scanning every repeated unmodified observation can dominate agent latency. Cache only where settings and classification scope make reuse safe.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Fail-open privacy filtering, duplicate scanning, overly broad false blocks and approval bypass under retries are common implementation failures.

lessons.title: What is agent reflection, and how does it improve agent performance?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. When does self-reflection not work?
  2. What makes feedback independent?
  3. How do you keep reflection from looping forever?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: When does self-reflection not work? What makes feedback independent? How do you keep reflection from looping forever? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Reflection adds an explicit review step: inspect current artifact, compare against objective/evidence/tests, produce targeted corrections, and stop when a measurable criterion is satisfied. Reflection that merely asks the same model “Are you right?” often reinforces the original error.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Let Q_t be independent verification quality; reflect only if expected ΔQ exceeds extra token/latency budget. Repeated self-grading scores are not independent observations.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Use unit tests, external calculators, retrieved sources and cross-model critique where useful. Deterministic validators usually outperform vague self-critique for schemas/permissions.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Define checklist with observable tests, targeted retry and max reflection rounds; persist original artifact and patch to detect regressions.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Reflection may double or triple inference calls for little gain on easy tasks. Trigger selectively on high uncertainty/failed tests.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Self-confirmation, critique loops and regressions are common. Never use reflection as a substitute for independent evidence or human review.

lessons.title: What is the difference between code-generating agents and tool-calling agents?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why is generating code sometimes more powerful than a fixed tool set?
  2. How do you sandbox execution?
  3. When should you prefer a fixed tool?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: Why is generating code sometimes more powerful than a fixed tool set? How do you sandbox execution? When should you prefer a fixed tool? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

A code-generating agent emits source artifacts which may later be executed by a build system or sandbox; a tool-calling agent selects from predefined capabilities exposed by its host. Many coding agents combine both: generate a patch, run controlled tools, inspect tests and revise.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Risk surface: generated code can be arbitrary program behavior, while typed tool calls are constrained by available capability semantics. Neither is safe automatically; tool power and execution environment determine risk.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Prefer tools for known business actions and APIs; generate code when task space is open-ended and program synthesis offers expressiveness, but isolate execution.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Use diffs, AST or lint checks, dependency policies, sandbox CPU/memory/network restrictions, deterministic test suite and explicit approval for repository changes.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Code execution startup and testing add latency but can provide stronger verification than pure prose. Tool calling has predictable per-call overhead.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Generated scripts can access secrets or filesystem if sandbox privileges are broad. Narrow capability surface reduces blast radius.

lessons.title: How do you handle multi-modal inputs and outputs in agentic systems?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How do images enter a model-based agent?
  2. Why do screenshot coordinates become stale?
  3. What is the latency budget for a voice agent?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: How do images enter a model-based agent? Why do screenshot coordinates become stale? What is the latency budget for a voice agent? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Multimodal agents ingest image/audio/video/document observations, convert them into representations via vision encoders/ASR/parsers, fuse with task state, select actions, and emit outputs such as text, audio, UI events or modified files. Maintain modality-specific provenance and confidence rather than flattening all inputs into anonymous text.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Video processing cost roughly scales with sampled frames×vision tokens plus audio duration×ASR cost; higher sampling can improve event recall but increase latency/cost.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

OCR/layout parsers suit documents; native VLMs may help visually complex screens; ASR→LLM→TTS is modular, while native speech-to-speech can reduce stages but be harder to inspect.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Associate each observation with timestamp, page/region/bounding box, transcript confidence and access scope; store derived text and original media references separately.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Image/video tokens can exhaust context quickly. Adaptive frame selection, crop grounding and retrieval reduce repeated processing.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

A multimodal agent may ignore a screenshot or invent UI controls; require visual grounding and observed post-action state.

lessons.title: How do you implement state management in complex agent workflows?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How does long-term memory differ from workflow state?
  2. How do you handle concurrent state updates?
  3. What is recorded before executing a payment?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: How does long-term memory differ from workflow state? How do you handle concurrent state updates? What is recorded before executing a payment? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Complex agents require durable state separating user goal, current plan, node status, tool effects, approvals, memory and observation ledger. State transitions should be explicit and checkpointed at safe boundaries; resume must reconcile external writes before rerun.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

A useful state tuple S=(run_id,version,phase,plan,results,approvals,budget,ledger). Apply state update with optimistic check expected_version=v; reject conflicting writes, then merge according to field reducers.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Relational database/event store suits transactional effects; graph runtime coordinates transitions; Redis cache suits ephemeral hints, not single source of truth for approvals.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Event-source important side effects and user approvals; checkpoint graph/task state; use idempotency keys and exclusive ownership where necessary.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Checkpoint frequency trades storage/write overhead against lost progress. Unbounded message histories can make state serialization slow.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Concurrent branches can overwrite each other, replay a completed action or drop an approval. Use versioning and effect reconciliation.

lessons.title: How do you build a customer support agent with escalation logic?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Design the decision to escalate.
  2. How do you avoid duplicate CRM writes?
  3. What context must transfer to a human operator?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: Design the decision to escalate. How do you avoid duplicate CRM writes? What context must transfer to a human operator? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Customer support agent should separate intent classification, policy-aware knowledge retrieval, authenticated account lookup, proposed action, escalation decision and case closure. Escalation policy considers risk, evidence gap, sentiment/urgency and action permissions; account modifications require deterministic authorization.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Escalate if unsafe∨identity_unverified∨no_supported_resolution∨high_impact∨SLA_risk. Route based on verified business conditions rather than uncalibrated model confidence alone.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

A deterministic decision tree may handle narrow tickets; agent helps with ambiguous multi-system cases and ad hoc research. Both need human handoff paths.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Persist case_id, customer_id server-side, conversation summary, evidence citations, actions already taken and escalation reason; transfer these to human representative.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Escalation adds labor cost; premature escalation reduces automation benefits, but false automated closure damages outcomes. Optimize cost subject to resolution/safety.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

False refund eligibility, wrong account, double ticket creation, stale policies and a chat summary lacking critical detail are common failures.

lessons.title: What is agent orchestration, and how do you implement it?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Draw your orchestrator data model.
  2. How do you distinguish retries from replans?
  3. When is a message queue insufficient?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: Draw your orchestrator data model. How do you distinguish retries from replans? When is a message queue insufficient? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Orchestration coordinates who runs, with what inputs, in which order, under what budget and permission. A durable orchestrator tracks task graph, worker leases, checkpoints, retries, approvals and artifact merge. It does not need to be an LLM: deterministic controllers are often preferable for known process requirements.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

For DAG work, critical-path latency L≈max_path Σ(node duration), plus queue/coordination overhead. Throughput depends on worker pools, provider quotas and downstream concurrency, not worker count alone.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Use queue/workflow engine for durable events and retries; graph-based agent runtime for dynamic decisions; both can coexist. Avoid adopting an agent-specific framework for basic cron + ETL.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Define node ownership, transition predicates, fanout caps, per-worker budgets, artifact schemas, cancellation propagation and compensation policy.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Retries, serialization, model call rounds and cross-region connectors dominate latency. Parallelize independent reads but avoid simultaneous writes to the same resource.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Lost callbacks, stuck leases, duplicate effects and missing provenance break long-running flows. Heartbeats, idempotency and audit trails enable recovery.

lessons.title: What is Sakana Fugu, and how does it orchestrate a team of AI models?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. What is query-adaptive scaffolding?
  2. How would you benchmark Fugu-like orchestration fairly?
  3. What are the extra failure boundaries?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: What is query-adaptive scaffolding? How would you benchmark Fugu-like orchestration fairly? What are the extra failure boundaries? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Sakana Fugu is a reported family of orchestrator models trained to create query-adaptive multi-agent scaffolds: a coordinator interprets a task, chooses coordination topology/roles and dispatches specialist model agents, then integrates their outputs. The 2026 technical report describes methods spanning large-scale fine-tuning, evolution and reinforcement learning; public evaluation claims are from the project authors and require independent reproduction.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

The general objective is to optimize orchestration policy π(scaffold|task) for downstream verified reward subject to total latency and model-cost constraints. This describes the abstraction, not the exact unpublished implementation details.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Static multi-agent pipelines always run predetermined roles; a task-adaptive orchestrator may choose serial critique, parallel experts or simpler routes. Adaptive decisions add policy/evaluation complexity.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Implement bounded coordinator output as typed graph proposal: selected models, worker roles, edges, handoff schemas, verification and cost limits. Validate tool/data permissions at every worker.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Coordinating frontier models can substantially increase aggregate token spend and queue pressure. Benchmark against one strong model and simple fixed multi-agent baselines at matched budget.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Reported headline benchmark results may hide task mix and inference spend; never assume cross-provider agent results are independent or automatically secure.

lessons.title: How do you build a code execution agent safely using sandboxed environments?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why is Docker alone not a complete security boundary?
  2. Which secrets can a sandbox access?
  3. How do you preserve artifacts without leaking the host FS?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: Why is Docker alone not a complete security boundary? Which secrets can a sandbox access? How do you preserve artifacts without leaking the host FS? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Safe execution agent has a policy gateway → isolated container/VM/process sandbox → resource-limited execution → captured stdout/stderr/artifacts → host-side validation. Execution context must not inherit host filesystem, secrets, cloud identity or unrestricted egress. Run user/model code as untrusted.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

A practical budget caps CPU time, wall time, RSS, disk bytes, process count and network destinations. Resource exhaustion is a denial-of-service even if shell command is syntactically valid.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

VM/microVM isolation offers stronger boundaries at startup/ops cost; container namespaces/seccomp require careful hardening; WASM can simplify highly restricted workloads.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Use non-root UID, ephemeral rootfs, read-only mounts, no host socket, per-run temp directory, package allowlist, timeouts and cleanup. Sign/verify artifact hashes before copying outputs.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Cold sandbox startup and dependency provisioning affect latency. Reusable pools require strict reinitialization so one tenant never observes another tenant’s files.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Block shell escape, symlink traversal, ZIP bombs, fork bombs, malicious package postinstall, DNS exfiltration and unsafe artifact open.

lessons.title: Your AI agent is stuck in an infinite loop. How do you detect and break the cycle?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. What fingerprint would you store?
  2. What if repeated calls are intentionally part of polling?
  3. How do you separate no progress from slow progress?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Infinite loops often arise from unchanged observations, repeated failed tool calls, contradictory instructions, stale plans or unmet verification criteria. Detect repeated normalized action+state fingerprints and no progress in verified milestones, then replan, ask user or stop with diagnostic context.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Define F_t=hash(normalized_action, relevant_state_version, observation_digest). If F_t repeats ≥r and no new evidence, trigger circuit breaker. Use separate limits for steps, wall time, tokens and external effects.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Deterministic workflows can prove termination with acyclic graph; exploratory loops need practical stopping conditions and uncertainty escalation.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Emit each action hash, failed precondition, retry cause and novelty score; on stagnation, suppress identical calls unless state changed.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Loop amplification increases model spend and tool load. Budget checks must precede retries and subagent spawning.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Blind “try again” prompts are not recovery. They often replicate the same tool call with no new data.

lessons.title: Your AI agent gets conflicting answers from different tools. How does it reconcile them?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How do you resolve contradictions without trusting model confidence?
  2. When do you ask a human?
  3. How do you recognize correlated data sources?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: How do you resolve contradictions without trusting model confidence? When do you ask a human? How do you recognize correlated data sources? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Conflicting tools may differ due to authority, freshness, scope, units, timezone, identifier mapping or outright data corruption. Do not average arbitrary strings or ask the model to guess; construct an evidence matrix with source, scope, timestamp, unit and version, then reconcile by explicit authority rules.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Consensus requires comparable claims. Normalize fact f=(entity,attribute,value,unit,valid_time,source,authority). Conflict exists if two claims refer to same entity/attribute/time scope and values are incompatible.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Prefer transactional source of truth for account balance; prefer latest signed policy for rules; present unresolved conflict to human if risk is high.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Store raw tool responses and authority metadata; re-query with consistent IDs, enforce unit conversion and time scope, and record why one value prevailed.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Extra verification adds latency but prevents costly wrong actions. Cache only with source/version-aware invalidation.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Majority vote among three copied APIs is not three independent sources. “Most recent” is not always “authoritative”.

lessons.title: Your AI agent burns too many tokens per task. How do you reduce token consumption?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Show the quadratic history growth argument.
  2. What should a tool return when logs are huge?
  3. Which cost cuts are risky?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: Show the quadratic history growth argument. What should a tool return when logs are huge? Which cost cuts are risky? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Token explosions stem from repeated full transcript replay, verbose tool outputs, duplicated worker context, indiscriminate retrieval, long self-critique and ineffective caching. Profile tokens at the step/component level before trimming.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

C_run=Σ_t(tokens_in,t·p_in+tokens_out,t·p_out)+tools. If prompt history grows by roughly k each step, input token sum over n turns is O(k n²) without compaction or prompt caching.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Prefer exact deterministic tools where possible, prune stale observations, use structured summaries, compress documents, route by task complexity and set bounded tool output formats.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Track token cost by role, source, tool result, cache hit/miss, step, branch and final result. Enforce a token ledger before making model requests.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Hard budgets control cost; adaptive context packing preserves important evidence. Unnecessarily low output caps can cause incomplete tool arguments.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Over-aggressive compaction can erase approval constraints; smaller model routing can lower critical-task correctness.

lessons.title: Your AI agent keeps exceeding its budget per task. How do you enforce budget limits?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How do you enforce cost limits under concurrency?
  2. How do you handle unknown usage on timeout?
  3. When should you surface partial progress?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: How do you enforce cost limits under concurrency? How do you handle unknown usage on timeout? When should you surface partial progress? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

A hard budget is an authoritative controller state, not a prompt instruction. Reserve worst-case or conservative estimated tokens/cost before calls, debit actual usage after, count all workers and tool charges, and block new actions once budget is insufficient. Persist reservations across crashes.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Available=B_total−spent−reserved. Allow new estimated charge c only if c≤available and time/step quota remain. Refund unused reserve after actual billing arrives, reconcile unknown charges.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Use soft threshold to warn/switch strategy; hard threshold to stop safely. Budget hierarchy can be per request, tenant, day and tool type.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Acquire budget reservation atomically with run_id and call_id; on retry do not silently reset allowance. Store provider usage and fallback estimates.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Budget constraints can reduce success; offer low-cost summary of partial progress and require user consent for extension.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Budget checks only after requests allow overspend during concurrent fanout. Multi-agent budgets must be centrally coordinated.

All numerical examples in this course are illustrative, not measured gains.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Which failures can grammar-constrained decoding prevent?
  2. How do you debug tool confusion?
  3. How do you enforce parameter provenance?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: Which failures can grammar-constrained decoding prevent? How do you debug tool confusion? How do you enforce parameter provenance? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Tool hallucination can mean selecting nonexistent capability or inventing unsupported parameters. Restrict choices to dynamically approved names, use strict schemas, decode typed calls, perform semantic validation, and return descriptive tool errors that permit bounded correction.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Error taxonomy: nonexistent_tool, invalid_schema, invalid_domain, unauthorized, downstream_failure. Each class routes to a different recovery path; do not retry unauthorized calls.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

A short high-quality tool catalog with distinct descriptions may outperform a huge tool list. Retrieval-based tool selection scales catalogs but requires recall evaluation.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Generate tool contracts from canonical backend schemas; test enum/range/ownership constraints; log rejected calls and example confusion pairs.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Large catalogs increase prompt tokens and selection confusion. Multi-step tool discovery adds latency but may lower errors for 100+ tools.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

A correct field name with wrong resource ID can still be a dangerous action. Validate semantics against authoritative database.

lessons.title: Your AI agent deleted a production database. How do you prevent irreversible actions?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How would you redesign the tool surface after such an incident?
  2. Would human approval alone suffice?
  3. How do you prove recoverability?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: How would you redesign the tool surface after such an incident? Would human approval alone suffice? How do you prove recoverability? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

A production DB deletion is a layered control failure. Agents should have read-only credentials by default; destructive operations should use narrowly scoped APIs, least-privilege DB roles, dry-run previews, explicit approval, backups and recoverable transaction or soft-delete patterns.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Risk model: expected loss≈P(bad action)×impact. Low-probability catastrophic writes justify strong authorization gates; prompt compliance alone never drives P to zero.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Use separate privileged service for deletion rather than SQL access. Two-phase intent approval and temporal rollback may be necessary for regulated datasets.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Design delete(resource_id,expected_version,approved_request_id) where backend validates policy, principal and exact approval hash; produce immutable audit and reconcile backups.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Approval and soft-delete cost time/storage but provide auditability and recovery. Test restore procedures rather than merely claiming backups exist.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Database “read/write” role often has more authority than task needs. One malicious document should never be able to expand privileges.

lessons.title: Your AI agent has many tools, but keeps picking the wrong one. How do you improve tool selection?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. What does a tool confusion matrix show?
  2. When is semantic tool retrieval helpful?
  3. How does routing relate to authorization?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: What does a tool confusion matrix show? When is semantic tool retrieval helpful? How does routing relate to authorization? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Incorrect tool selection arises from overlapping names, too many advertised capabilities, vague descriptions, hidden preconditions and poor supervision. Collect confusion matrices, group tools by task, expose only context-relevant capabilities, and make selection examples contrastive.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

For intent i and selected tool j, inspect confusion P(j|i). Optimize macro accuracy across rare high-risk intents, not just overall micro accuracy on frequent easy calls.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Hierarchical routing (category→specific tool) can scale; top-k retrieved tool metadata can shrink prompts; keep mandatory security tools visible at host regardless.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Version tool names and schemas, collect rejected-call traces with user intent, design unambiguous descriptions, and test adversarial near-duplicate choices.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Tool discovery adds round trip or retrieval overhead. Better selection can save expensive failed downstream calls.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Hiding a tool from the model is not sufficient access control; the executor still checks server-side permissions.

lessons.title: Your AI agent takes too long to complete a task. How do you speed it up?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How do you identify the critical path?
  2. Which calls may run in parallel?
  3. What failure appears when concurrency is increased?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: How do you identify the critical path? Which calls may run in parallel? What failure appears when concurrency is increased? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Agent latency is serial dependency cost plus model queue time, prefill/decode, tool calls, retries, approvals and orchestration. Start from traces and critical path. Parallelize independent reads, batch small operations, cache immutable data and reduce unnecessary model turns.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

L_total≈Σ_{critical_path}(L_model_prefill+L_decode+L_tool+L_queue), not the sum of all parallel workers. Little’s Law L=W/λ can relate concurrency W and throughput λ under stable conditions.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Simpler deterministic workflow often beats multi-agent. Parallelize research queries, not ordered financial writes; compact context only when its quality trade-offs are measured.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Instrument spans with run/step ID, tool latency, provider TTFT, output tokens, waits, errors and retry counts. Load-test with realistic external-service distributions.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

High concurrency increases queueing and rate-limit pressure. More parallelism is not free and may worsen p99.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Focusing only on model tokens misses 15-second browser navigation or frozen approval queue. Observe each stage independently.

lessons.title: Your long-running agent drifts after hours and confidently works on the wrong thing. How do you diagnose and fix it?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Which invariants survive compaction?
  2. How do you detect drift early?
  3. How do you recover work already outside scope?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: Which invariants survive compaction? How do you detect drift early? How do you recover work already outside scope? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Long-running drift occurs when the agent’s representation of goal, constraints and current artifact stops matching the original task or environment. Detect by comparing planned milestones and verified artifacts against immutable goal and user approvals, not by asking the model if it is still aligned.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Maintain invariants I(S_t,goal)=true and measure distance to goal via verified milestones. Replan when source versions change; terminate when drift or repeated unapproved scope expansion occurs.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Use durable task contract and checkpoint with artifact lineage; context compaction retains constraints; supervisor can periodically audit objective vs actual write set.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Persist original user goal, approval hashes, changed-files list, evidence links, versions, verification results and current plan. Add periodic state reconciliation.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Drift checks consume tokens/I/O but can prevent hours of wasted work or destructive edits. Prioritize at workflow boundaries rather than every token.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

A confident progress message is not evidence of completed scope; summaries may strengthen a wrong assumption over time.

lessons.title: Your LLM selects the right tool but extracts the wrong parameters. How do you fix parameter extraction?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How do you prove where an argument came from?
  2. What if two entities share the same name?
  3. How do you handle relative dates safely?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: How do you prove where an argument came from? What if two entities share the same name? How do you handle relative dates safely? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Right tool but wrong arguments is a semantic parsing problem: ambiguous entity mentions, stale references, mismatched units/dates, missing required fields or invented IDs. Improve typed schemas, canonical entity resolution, explicit provenance and verification against live authoritative data.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Field-level accuracy=Σ correct required fields / Σ required fields. High schema-validity can coexist with low semantic exact-match; evaluate both per field and by risk.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Use constrained decoding for syntax, extraction examples for mapping, deterministic normalization for dates/money and retrieval for entity IDs. High-risk cases should request clarification/approval rather than guess.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Validate combinations (start≤end, resource belongs to principal, amount≤limit, currency known). Log raw user span supporting each argument.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

An extra lookup adds latency but is cheaper than a wrong financial write. Cache resolved entities with short TTL and ownership scope.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Temperature zero does not guarantee correct parameter extraction. Defaults can be harmful if ambiguous.

lessons.title: How do Computer-Use Agents work?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Why prefer accessibility metadata to pixels?
  2. How do you detect an incorrect click?
  3. How do you secure clipboard and screenshots?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: Why prefer accessibility metadata to pixels? How do you detect an incorrect click? How do you secure clipboard and screenshots? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Computer-use agents turn screenshots/accessibility trees into an actionable UI state, choose clicks/typing/scroll/keyboard input, execute through controlled OS interfaces, capture the next observation and verify. Coordinates are transient; stable semantic accessibility identifiers are preferable when available.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

For click(x,y), reliability depends on correct grounding P(target|screenshot), screen layout stability and post-click verification. Retries should re-observe state; blindly repeating coordinates can click a new control.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Use direct APIs when stable and authorized; computer use for legacy software lacking integrations. Hybrid approaches leverage accessibility trees plus vision grounding.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Enforce app/window allowlist, visible action preview, PII redaction, clipboard isolation, exact approval for destructive steps and step snapshots.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Screenshot/VLM inference and animations add high latency. Use event-driven waits and accessibility-based selectors to reduce polling where possible.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

UI focus shifts, screen DPI, modals, deceptive buttons, tooltips and prompt injection in rendered content cause incorrect actions.

lessons.title: How do Browser Agents work?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. What should a browser agent observe?
  2. How do you handle dynamic-page state?
  3. What is the main security risk of page content?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: What should a browser agent observe? How do you handle dynamic-page state? What is the main security risk of page content? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Browser agents operate on DOM/accessibility trees, network navigation and sometimes screenshots. They must synchronize dynamic pages, identify stable selectors, handle authentication safely and verify effects after each action. Text from the page remains untrusted even when the browser is authenticated.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Action cycle: observe DOM/view → choose selector/action → execute → wait for relevant state change → assert desired condition → checkpoint. Use event-based waiting where possible instead of fixed sleeps.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Browser automation can reliably interact with DOM APIs; pixel computer-use remains fallback for canvas/shadow UI or remote desktops. Direct first-party API may be more robust.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Partition browser contexts by user, enforce domain allowlist, restrict downloads/uploads and external navigation, never exfiltrate cookies, and recheck authorization on checkout/payment.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Page loads, anti-bot challenges, network retries and screenshots dominate wall time. Minimize redundant navigation and cache safe static lookups.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Prompt injection in web pages, clickjacking, auto-submit, stale selectors and duplicated purchase submits are high-risk failure modes.

lessons.title: How does LangChain work?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. What does LangChain provide versus model APIs?
  2. When is a framework overkill?
  3. How would you inspect a tool call through middleware?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: What does LangChain provide versus model APIs? When is a framework overkill? How would you inspect a tool call through middleware? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

LangChain supplies model/provider interfaces, prompt/message abstractions, tools, structured output, middleware and higher-level agent constructors. A typical create_agent loop is model → proposed tool calls → tool execution → tool messages → model, commonly backed by LangGraph runtime components.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

An agent’s tool iteration has dynamic step count N; complexity and cost derive from selected model and tool calls, not the import of LangChain. Its interfaces are a composition layer over API/SDK behavior.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Use LangChain for rapid integration and reusable components; plain Python calls for a tiny predictable service; LangGraph when you need explicit graph control, durable pauses and branching workflows.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Define typed tools with authentication passed at runtime, middleware for dynamic context and policy, response schema, tracing and tests. Pin dependencies; APIs evolve across versions.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Framework abstractions can hide retries, queues and token costs unless instrumented. Benchmark underlying operations rather than attributing latency to a brand.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Tool invocation may be routed through a seemingly harmless wrapper; backend permissions remain your responsibility. Avoid mixing long-term secrets into model context.

lessons.title: How does LangGraph work?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. Distinguish checkpointer and store.
  2. What are reducers and interrupts?
  3. How do you handle replay of a side-effecting node?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: Distinguish checkpointer and store. What are reducers and interrupts? How do you handle replay of a side-effecting node? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

LangGraph models execution as explicit nodes, edges and state reducers, with checkpoint persistence and optional durable interrupts. Nodes can call LLMs, tools or deterministic functions; conditional transitions control workflow. Checkpointers persist thread state, while stores can hold cross-thread long-term data.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Graph G=(V,E), typed state S; node transition f_v(S)→ΔS; reducer merges ΔS. Correctness requires explicit merge semantics and idempotent side effects across replay.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

LangChain high-level agent suits standard model/tool loop; LangGraph suits custom state machines, branch/parallelism, human approval and long-running recovery; event queues may still underlie external integration.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Use unique thread/run ID, durable checkpointer, state schema, explicit conditional edges, interrupt/approval node and effect ledger. Do not assume replay-safe external writes automatically.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Persistence adds storage and serialization overhead; enables recovery instead of restarting long tasks. Tune checkpoint granularity to risk and latency.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

Concurrent state races and rerun of external effects are not solved by merely drawing a graph. Tools remain governed by application authorization.

lessons.title: What is OKF (Open Knowledge Format)?
lessons.subtitle: Mechanism · architecture · math · failure controls · validation.

sections.heading: Interviewer questions
sections.html:
1. How does OKF differ from MCP and RAG?
  2. What belongs in frontmatter?
  3. What happens when files are stale or unverified?
  4. How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?
sections.text: How does OKF differ from MCP and RAG? What belongs in frontmatter? What happens when files are stale or unverified? How would you prove the improvement on a reproducible evaluation suite without inventing benchmark gains?

sections.heading: Deep technical explanation
sections.html:
1 · Step-by-step internal flow and observable state

Open Knowledge Format (OKF) is an open, human- and agent-readable convention for curated knowledge bundles: directories of Markdown concept files with YAML frontmatter, indexes/links and optional provenance, lifecycle, freshness and trust metadata. As of the 2026 v0.2 specification, it aims for portable exchange without a proprietary runtime.

2 · Equations, bounds, symbols & assumptions

Example metadata: type: Policy; title: Refund rules; status: active; verified_at: 2026-10-01; source: signed-policy-v4. Typed fields enable filtering; links form a traversable concept network. It is a format, not a vector index, model tool protocol or factuality guarantee.

3 · Alternative architectures and decision criteria

Use OKF to exchange domain concepts, rules, metric definitions and agent knowledge maps. Pair it with search/graph or MCP tools to access runtime services; plain Markdown may suffice for a tiny static playbook.

4 · Production implementation, schemas & instrumentation

Write bundle index.md, per-concept frontmatter, stable URLs, source references, integrity/version metadata, ACL handling and validators. Pin official spec version and check consumer tolerance for optional fields.

5 · Token, latency, memory, compute & scaling consequences

Portable flat files are cheap to inspect/review, but freshness, indexing, permissions and attestation pipelines still require engineering.

6 · Edge cases, misconceptions, failure & mitigation

A polished OKF bundle can contain stale or invented content. Source lineage, reviews and access enforcement cannot be skipped.
